title: An Integrated Security Analysis Model for Identifying Software and Hardware System Vulnerabilities
authors: Nguyen Minh Khoa; Tran Ngoc Anh
venue: International Journal of Modern Computer Science and IT Innovations
abstract: The increasing interdependence of software, hardware, cloud infrastructures, embedded platforms, and connected systems has transformed cybersecurity vulnerability assessment from an isolated technical activity into a multidimensional security requirement. Software vulnerabilities can arise from insecure code, configuration weaknesses, vulnerable dependencies, and exploitable application interfaces, whereas hardware vulnerabilities may originate from architectural design limitations, processor-level weaknesses, implementation flaws, and hardware-assisted attack mechanisms. This study develops an integrated security analysis model for identifying vulnerabilities across software and hardware system layers. The proposed approach synthesizes vulnerability taxonomy, attack-surface analysis, risk assessment, exploitability evaluation, hardware security analysis, machine-learning-assisted detection, and adaptive defensive mechanisms. The methodology is conceptually grounded in the supplied literature and uses a layered assessment process to connect vulnerability discovery with exploitability, potential impact, and mitigation priority. Particular attention is given to base-image vulnerabilities, processor-level attacks, artificial-intelligence-supported security analysis, HTTPS deployment weaknesses, embedded-system risks, and cyber-hunting relationships between threats and defensive weaknesses. The analysis indicates that isolated software or hardware assessment can overlook cross-layer attack paths, while an integrated model provides stronger contextual understanding of vulnerabilities and their operational consequences. The study further identifies the need for risk-oriented prioritization, continuous monitoring, and coordinated software-hardware defenses. The proposed model provides a conceptual foundation for systematic vulnerability assessment in heterogeneous computing environments.

title: An Intelligent Cybersecurity Architecture for Network Log-Based Intrusion Detection Employing a Hybrid Machine Learning Approach
authors: Dr. Tatsuya Endo; Dr. Honoka Sato
venue: European Journal of Emerging Data Science and Machine Learning
abstract: The increasing sophistication of cyberattacks has significantly challenged traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS), particularly in environments generating large-scale network logs. This study proposes an intelligent cybersecurity architecture for network log-based intrusion detection using a hybrid machine learning approach that integrates statistical learning and deep feature representation techniques. The objective is to enhance detection accuracy, reduce false positives, and improve adaptability to evolving malicious traffic patterns. The proposed architecture leverages multi-stage preprocessing, feature engineering, and ensemble-based classification mechanisms inspired by recent advancements in deep neural networks and hybrid IDS models (Gao et al., 2020; Bendiab et al., 2020).The framework integrates both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms to address labeled and unlabeled log data scenarios. Additionally, it incorporates insights from prior studies on IoT, SCADA, and encrypted traffic detection, emphasizing robustness across heterogeneous network environments (De Lucia & Cotton, 2019; Xin et al., 2022). Experimental design considerations are aligned with machine learning evaluation standards in cybersecurity domains (Rajesh & Satyanarayana, 2021).The results indicate that hybridization of classical machine learning with deep learning feature extractors significantly improves detection efficiency, particularly in high-dimensional log environments. The architecture demonstrates scalability, interpretability, and adaptability for modern enterprise networks. This study contributes a unified and extensible IDS framework suitable for real-time deployment in cloud, IoT, and enterprise infrastructures

title: An Intelligent Hybrid ML System for URL-Based Phishing Threat Detection
authors: Jaganathachar K; Mrs.Sangeetha S; Amudhan M; Keshavaraj S; Lokesh M
venue: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
abstract: Abstract: This project utilizes machine learning techniques to detect phishing URLs by analyzing various features of both legitimate and fraudulent websites. With the rapid growth of internet usage and online transactions such as banking, shopping, and communication, phishing attacks have become one of the most serious cybersecurity threats. Attackers create deceptive websites that closely resemble legitimate ones in order to trick users into revealing sensitive information such as usernames, passwords, and financial details.To address this issue, the proposed system uses a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) algorithm, which is a type of artificial neural network capable of learning complex patterns from data. The system is designed to classify URLs as either phishing or legitimate based on a set of extracted features. These features include URL length, number of special characters, number of subdomains, use of HTTPS protocol, and other structural characteristics that help differentiate between safe and malicious websites.The system is trained using a dataset that contains a large number of URLs labeled as either phishing or legitimate. During the training phase, the model learns the patterns and relationships between the extracted features and the corresponding labels. This enables the system to understand the common characteristics of phishing URLs and distinguish them from legitimate ones.Once the training process is completed, the model is ready for real-time prediction. When a user inputs a URL into the system, it undergoes the same feature extraction process. The extracted features are then passed to the trained MLP model, which analyzes the data and predicts whether the URL is safe or a phishing attempt. The result is then displayed to the user, helping them avoid accessing malicious websites.The proposed system plays an important role in enhancing online security by preventing unauthorized access to sensitive information. It provides a fast and efficient way to detect phishing attempts and reduces the risk of cyber-attacks. Compared to traditional methods, this machine learning-based approach is more flexible and capable of identifying new and previously unseen phishing URLs. Keywords- Phishing Detection, Machine Learning, URL Analysis, Cybersecurity, Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Random Forest, Feature Extraction, Classification, Data Security, Hybrid Model

title: An Intelligent Machine Learning Framework For Detecting QUIC-Based Traffic Flood Attacks In Encrypted HTTP/3 Networks
authors: Mr.M.V.Rajesh; Balla Aarathisree; S S V Sumanvitha Palivela; Nagala Bhavya Pragna; Kamalesh Chitra; Taneti Ritesh
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The rapid growth of encrypted internet protocols such as HTTP/3 and QUIC has significantly improved communication speed and security on modern networks. However, these protocols also introduce new challenges for network security, particularly in detecting Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) traffic flood attacks. Traditional monitoring techniques rely on packet inspection, which becomes difficult when network traffic is encrypted. This study proposes an intelligent machine learning framework for detecting QUIC-based traffic flood attacks in encrypted HTTP/3 network environments. The proposed system analyses network flow behaviour rather than packet content, enabling effective detection even when traffic payloads are encrypted. To build the detection model, network traffic data are captured and processed into flow-based features such as packet rate, packet size distribution, inter-arrival time, and connection statistics. Data preprocessing techniques are applied to prepare the dataset for machine learning training. Multiple classification algorithms including Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), and Random Forest are implemented and evaluated using standard performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC–AUC. Experimental results demonstrate that the Random Forest classifier achieves the highest detection accuracy and provides reliable performance for distinguishing between normal and malicious QUIC traffic patterns. To improve transparency and interpretability of the prediction process, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques such as SHAP and LIME are incorporated into the framework. These methods highlight the most influential network features contributing to attack detection and help security analysts understand the reasoning behind model predictions. The proposed framework enhances the reliability of encrypted traffic monitoring, improves early detection of QUIC traffic flood attacks, and contributes to strengthening the security of next-generation web communication protocols.

title: An Intelligent predictive model system for Real-Time identification and Risk Scoring of Web Application Vulnerabilities
authors: Rajni Tiwari; Debasmita Mishra; Srabana Pramanik; Neha Arora; Priyanka Niranjan Savadekar
abstract: In this study, we designed and implemented a machine learning based system for detecting web application attacks using HTTP request behaviour. Unlike traditional signature-driven scanners, the proposed approach learns traffic characteristics from collected request logs and evaluates threat severity through a dynamic risk scoring model. Experiments were conducted on a dataset containing 10,000 real and synthetically generated requests covering SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and command injection attacks. The developed system achieved improved detection accuracy while reducing false alarms observed in rule-based security tools. The framework demonstrates the feasibility of integrating intelligent threat detection with automated risk prioritization for practical web security monitoring.

title: An IoT Malware Detection Framework Based on Large Language Models and Deep Learning Techniques
authors: Hamza K. Al-Daoud; Adnan H. Al-Helali
abstract: Rapid growth in IoT devices has led to the creation of crucial cybersecurity threats since existing methods of malware detection which use signature matching and numerical feature analysis are incapable of capturing the contextual behavioral semantics of IoT attacks. The presented work proposes an innovative malware detection framework incorporating a pipeline of behavior-to-text transformation together with transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform binary classification of IoT network traffic. Selected through the process of SHAP-based feature importance analysis, the numerical features of network flows from the initial set of 41 features are transformed into natural language descriptions, allowing encoder-based LLMs to capture the context of IoT traffic behavior. Four LLMs, including DistilBERT, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa, were fine-tuned and rigorously tested against four Deep Learning baselines, Neural Network, LSTM, BiLSTM, and CNN, and four Machine Learning baselines, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, using the CIC-IoT-2023 dataset under three experimental setups: balanced classification, realistic imbalanced distribution, and unseen variant detection. Additionally, a four-class multi-class classification experiment and an ablation study were conducted to further validate the framework. On a balanced dataset consisting of 400,000 samples, BERT-base and RoBERTa achieved the highest F1-scores of 98.94% with precision above 99.96%. In the imbalanced case of 90% attack and 10% benign traffic, the precision of all models was equal to 99.99%. The framework attained an F1-score of 99.99% for unseen variant detection on a completely unseen Mirai botnet variant with zero false negatives. The four-class multi-class experiment achieved a Macro F1-score of 88.80%. Statistical analysis across three independent runs confirmed high result stability with standard deviations below 0.03%. SHAP analysis revealed that packet count, ACK flag number, and HTTPS indicator were the most discriminative features, while attention visualization confirmed token-level interpretability. All LLMs consistently outperformed all Deep Learning baselines, providing evidence for the effectiveness of the behavior-to-text transformation paradigm for IoT malware detection, while classical ML models achieved marginally higher F1-scores due to their efficiency with numerical features, providing evidence for the effectiveness of the behavior-to-text transformation paradigm for IoT malware detection.

title: An LDA-Enhanced Machine Learning Approach for Efficient SQL Injection Detection from Web Traffic Logs
authors: Amit Hariyani
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
abstract: SQL injection (SQLI) remains a critical web application security threat, while conventional signature-based detection methods face limitations in identifying evolving attack patterns and handling high-dimensional web request data. This study proposes an improved machine learning framework for SQLI detection based on TF-IDF N-grams and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). HTTP requests from the CSIC-2010 and ECML/PKDD-2007 datasets are processed to extract SQLI-related traffic using SQL keyword-based filtering. TF-IDF trigram features are generated to represent request characteristics, followed by LDA-based dimensionality reduction to obtain a compact latent semantic representation. Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Random Forest (RF) classifiers are employed for classifying malicious and genuine requests. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed LDA-based approach. On the CSIC-2010 dataset, the SVM and RF models achieve 99.90% and 98.13% accuracy, respectively. On the ECML/PKDD-2007 dataset, the improved framework achieves 98.70% accuracy using SVM and 99.85% using RF, with approximately 99% true-positive rate and mean ROC performance. The findings indicate that LDA-based feature reduction can improve the effectiveness and efficiency of machine-learning-based SQLI detection.

title: An optimized blockchain framework with ML-based anomaly detection for distributed access control in IoT networks
authors: Ravikumar Ch; B. N. V. MadhuBabu; C. S. Sowjanya; Burri Naresh
abstract: Abstract The fast rate of adoption of cloud-integrated Internet of Things (IoT) environs poses critical problems to access control because of the resource restrictiveness, heterogeneity, and dynamism of IoT devices, making the traditional centralized security models not applicable. To overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents a blockchain-based distributed access control system CapBlock, which combines the ability-based access control (CapBAC), smart contracts, and machine learning (ML) to provide dynamic, scalable, and resistant security enforcement. The framework applies the Ensemble Cuckoo Search Optimization (ECSO) algorithm, Bloom filters and the public-key cryptography to optimize the usage of resources, reduce the latency associated with authorization and improve the scalability of the system, and the use of a Random Forest-based anomaly detection model is continuously used to monitor the behavior of users to access the system and dynamically update the access policies to prevent malicious activities. The system is tested on a large scale of simulation with 4,000 access transactions on metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, transaction latency, throughput, security of data and preservation of privacy. The user privacy protection rate is considered as the percentage of requests of access where sensitive user attributes are not disclosed during authentication, authorization, and blockchain transaction logging, where the average value is 93 percent. Moreover, the throughput is calculated by scaling loads of request-per-second in HTTP requests to blockchain transactions commits with the assumption of one validated request per one completed transaction, under which the proposed framework can reach the highest throughput of 1,200 transactions per second (TPS) with stable performance. The experimental findings support the notion that CapBlock is a highly secure system capable of promoting security resiliency, privacy protection, and scalable access control in the contemporary cloud-IoT systems.

title: An Unlabeled Netflow Cybersecurity Sandbox Dataset with Attack and Benign Traffic
authors: Vojdan Kjorveziroski; Sonja Filiposka; Anastas Mishev
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Overview This dataset contains 2465 CSV files exported from ntopng, each representing a batch of Netflow records. All files follow the naming pattern: batch-local-only.$id.csv, where $id is between 00001 and 02465. The traffic has been recorded in a sandbox environment, as part of a cybersecurity challenge. Challenge participants were divided into teams, and each team was assigned a VM where purposefully vulnerable software was deployed. Each team was tasked with defending their own VM, while attacking as many other VMs as possible. The provided dataset only includes the internal traffic between the VMs and the traffic between the challenge participants' workstations and the sandbox. Each row represents a network flow with extended metadata, as described below. In total, there are 69 features available. Field Description 1. Flow Timing and Identity Field Description FIRST_SEEN Timestamp when the flow started LAST_SEEN Timestamp when the flow ended DURATION Flow duration TIME_DELTA Inter-arrival time between flows FLOW_ID Unique flow identifier COMMUNITY_ID Flow hash for cross-system correlation 2. Traffic Volume Field Description PACKETS Total packets in the flow TOTAL_BYTES Total bytes in the flow SRC2DST_BYTES Bytes from source to destination DST2SRC_BYTES Bytes from destination to source SRC2DST_PACKETS Packets from source to destination DST2SRC_PACKETS Packets from destination to source THROUGHPUT Estimated throughput 3. Network and Transport Layer Field Description PROTOCOL L4 protocol (e.g. TCP, UDP) IP_PROTOCOL_VERSION IP version (IPv4 or IPv6) IPV4_SRC_ADDR_FORMATTED Source IPv4 address IPV4_DST_ADDR_FORMATTED Destination IPv4 address IPV6_SRC_ADDR_FORMATTED Source IPv6 address IPV6_DST_ADDR_FORMATTED Destination IPv6 address IP_SRC_PORT Source port IP_DST_PORT Destination port SRC2DST_TCP_FLAGS TCP flags (src -> dst) DST2SRC_TCP_FLAGS TCP flags (dst -> src) SRC2DST_DSCP DSCP value (src -> dst) DST2SRC_DSCP DSCP value (dst -> src) VLAN_ID VLAN identifier 4. Application Layer (L7) Field Description L7_PROTO Detected application protocol L7_PROTO_MASTER Parent protocol L7_CATEGORY Application category DOMAIN_NAME Associated domain name PROTOCOL_INFO_JSON Additional protocol metadata 5. Performance and QoE Field Description SCORE Flow score assigned by ntopng QOE_SCORE Quality of Experience score CLIENT_NW_LATENCY_US Client-side latency (microseconds) SERVER_NW_LATENCY_US Server-side latency (microseconds) 6. Security and Alerts Field Description FLOW_RISK Risk classification ALERT_JSON Structured alert information STATUS Flow status INFO Additional descriptive information 7. Autonomous Systems and Geolocation Field Description SRC_ASN Source Autonomous System Number DST_ASN Destination Autonomous System Number SRC_COUNTRY_CODE Source country DST_COUNTRY_CODE Destination country CLIENT_LOCATION Client geographic location SERVER_LOCATION Server geographic location 8. NAT Information Field Description PRE_NAT_IPV4_SRC_ADDR_FORMATTED Source IP before NAT PRE_NAT_SRC_PORT Source port before NAT PRE_NAT_IPV4_DST_ADDR_FORMATTED Destination IP before NAT PRE_NAT_DST_PORT Destination port before NAT POST_NAT_IPV4_SRC_ADDR_FORMATTED Source IP after NAT POST_NAT_SRC_PORT Source port after NAT POST_NAT_IPV4_DST_ADDR_FORMATTED Destination IP after NAT POST_NAT_DST_PORT Destination port after NAT 9. Observation and Probe Metadata Field Description OBSERVATION_POINT_ID Identifier of observation point PROBE_IP_FORMATTED IP of the monitoring probe INPUT_SNMP Input interface index OUTPUT_SNMP Output interface index NTOPNG_INSTANCE_NAME Exporting ntopng instance 10. Network Segmentation and Labeling Field Description SRC_NETWORK_ID Source network identifier DST_NETWORK_ID Destination network identifier SRC_HOST_POOL_ID Source host pool DST_HOST_POOL_ID Destination host pool SRC_LABEL Source label DST_LABEL Destination label 11. Connection State Field Description MAJOR_CONNECTION_STATE High-level connection state MINOR_CONNECTION_STATE Detailed connection state 12. Wireless Context Field Description WLAN_SSID Wireless network SSID WTP_MAC_ADDRESS Wireless access point MAC 13. Fingerprinting Field Description CLIENT_FINGERPRINT Client fingerprint (e.g. TLS fingerprint) Notes Not all fields are populated for every flow. NAT fields are populated only when translation is detected. JSON fields (PROTOCOL_INFO_JSON, ALERT_JSON) can contain nested structures. The Netflow probe IP has been anonymized and hardcoded to 10.10.10.10. Only RFC1918 (private IP) traffic is available.

title: An Unsupervised Machine Learning Approach for Dynamic Anomaly Detection and Risk Defense in Cloud Servers
authors: Chanaka Lasantha; M.W.P Maduranga; Abesekara; Bhattacharyya
venue: International Journal of Research in Computing
abstract: This paper presents a hybrid unsupervised machine learning model for real-time anomaly detection and dynamic risk defense in the cloud environment. Traditional security mechanisms such as Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) and fixed firewall rules are often not sufficient to deal with the emerging threats in cloud computing, especially zero-day exploits and polymorphic malware that evade signature-based detection. The proposed system combines Isolation Forest (IF), Local Outlier Factor (LOF) and Density Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to identify both point and cluster anomalies from unlabeled cloud traffic. Integration with AWS Web Application Firewall (WAF) allows it to update its rules automatically and independently mitigate the threats detected. The model was trained and validated on 2.3 million AWS EC2 traffic records, in addition to the CICIDS2017 dataset which was split into a 70- 30 training-validation split. The computation environment consisted of AWS EC2 t2.xlarge (4vCPUs, 16GB RAM) instances of Python 3.8, scikit-learn 0.24.2, MongoDB 4.4, and TensorFlow 2.6. Experiments showed a detection accuracy of 92 per cent with a false positive rate of four per cent. The comparative analysis demonstrated better adaptability and less manual intervention in comparison to traditional IDS (Snort, Suricata: 88 -90% accuracy, 7-9% false positives) and standalone ML models (IF: 87 -90% accuracy, LOF: 86 -90% accuracy, DBSCAN: 84 -90% accuracy). The system was able to detect and block port scanning, DDoS, brute-force and data exfiltration patterns in real time with latency of less than 50ms. The reduction of false-positive by 43-56% led to 150-200 alerts per day being reduced in enterprise settings. The hybrid unsupervised model makes the cloud more resilient with adaptive defense without the need for labeled data. Removing manual firewall updates will save 15-20 hours per week for security teams. Future directions are encrypted traffic analysis based on metadata-based behavioral profiling, largescale distributed data processing (10M+ requests/minute), and multi-cloud integration between AWS, Azure, and GCP.

title: Analisis Komparatif Penggunaan IDS dan WAF Terhadap Serangan SQL Injection dan Brute Force: Tinjauan Literatur Sistematis
authors: Hermawan Setiawan; Ahmad Muflih Izfatara; Rahadian Ronggo Kusumo; Zamir Achmad Sachio; Moch Radhit Julian Randito
abstract: Aplikasi web merupakan sasaran utama serangan SQL Injection (SQLi) dan Brute Force, sementara Intrusion Detection System (IDS) dan Web Application Firewall (WAF) berbasis tanda tangan terbatas dalam menghadapi serangan tersamar maupun serangan zero-day. Tinjauan Literatur Sistematis ini disusun mengikuti protokol PRISMA 2020 dan kerangka PICOC untuk memetakan tantangan penerapan, metode deteksi yang dominan, serta membandingkan metrik performa IDS dan WAF terhadap SQLi dan Brute Force. Pencarian pada tujuh basis data untuk publikasi 2021–2025, dengan penyaringan oleh dua penelaah independen dan penilaian kualitas lima butir, menghasilkan 14 studi primer yang dianalisis melalui sintesis tematik. Hasil tinjauan mengindikasikan bahwa perbandingan performa kedua sistem secara langsung rentan terhadap bias karena perbedaan lapisan operasional, unit analisis, dan dataset evaluasi. IDS berbasis Deep Learning hibrida melaporkan akurasi biner 99,84%–99,98% pada dataset arus jaringan yang hampir tidak memuat muatan SQLi, sedangkan WAF berbasis Machine Learning melaporkan akurasi 89,34%–97,57% pada muatan HTTP, dan pendekatan AI generatif memblokir 99% serangan SQLi yang sebelumnya lolos dengan 23 aturan tambahan. Penelitian ini mengusulkan kerangka normalisasi perbandingan berbasis strata, analisis base rate, dan daftar periksa pelaporan minimum delapan butir, serta menyimpulkan bahwa IDS dan WAF bersifat komplementer, bukan substitutif.

title: Analisis Serangan Phising Dan Upaya Pencegahannya Pada Sistem Informasi
authors: Fiqri Alwan; Ramzi Al Pasha; Eka Prasetya Kaspandiri; Muhammad Dzaky Al Fariz
abstract: Phishing attacks continue to evolve into increasingly complex cyber threats, particularly with the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies capable of producing realistic fraudulent content. This study highlights the ineffectiveness of traditional blacklist-based security methods in countering dynamic attacks that exploit both technical and psychological vulnerabilities of users. The objective of this research is to analyze the technical characteristics and masquerading patterns of current phishing attacks. Using a descriptive qualitative approach, this study examines 14 active phishing URL samples from the 2024-2025 period through URL Feature Analysis. The results indicate that 80% of the samples have adopted the HTTPS protocol to manipulate user trust. Furthermore, the study identifies a dominance of typosquatting techniques and the abuse of cheap Top-Level Domains (TLDs) that often bypass standard security detection. The research concludes that effective cyber defense requires the integration of adaptive strategies, combining intelligent Machine Learning-based detection systems with comprehensive security awareness training to mitigate risks associated with human error.

title: Analysis of Threats on Web Proxy Servers with an AI Technique
authors: Nitin Kumar; P. Arya; Brijendra Pratap Singh
venue: 2026 5th International Conference on Innovative Sustainable Computational Technologies (CISCT)
abstract: In enterprise networks, web proxy servers play a vital role in traffic monitoring, access control and cybersecurity enforcement [1], [2]. But traditional rule-based security systems are losing their ability to protect against encrypted traffic and the ever-changing cyber threats. In this paper, the proposed intelligent web proxy security framework is a hybrid Random Forest (RF), Isolation Forest (IF) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) based AI system. The framework classifies traffic, detects anomalies in proxy server logs, and analyses users’ sequential behavior in a set of normal and malicious traffic patterns. Experimental results prove greater accuracy of detection, fewer false positives and greater adaptability to dynamic cyber-attacks than other traditional approaches. Modular design also enables near-real-time and scalable deployment in enterprise proxy environments to enable adaptive cybersecurity monitoring.

title: anan5093/ncmm-secure-ai-platform: Securing the Invisible Backbone: How I Built a Classified AI Intelligence Platform for India's Critical Mineral Mission
authors: Anand Raj
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Securing the Invisible Backbone: How I Built a Classified AI Intelligence Platform for India's Critical Mineral Mission When national security meets RAG pipelines — a deep dive into ABAC, hybrid search, and the 3-layer firewall that kept COSMIC TOP SECRET data where it belongs "The next world war won't be fought over oil. It will be fought over lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements." That's not hyperbole. As the world races to electrify everything from cars to power grids, the supply chains for critical minerals have become as strategically vital as oil fields once were. India's National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM) understands this. And so, as a B.Tech capstone project, I set out to build the intelligence platform that could help secure it — without ever sending a byte of classified data to a third-party API. This is the story of that system: the architecture, the engineering decisions, the debug nightmares, and the test metrics that prove it actually works. The Fragility Nobody Talks About When you pull up the supply chain map for lithium carbonate — tracing it from Chilean brine deposits through Chinese refineries to battery gigafactories in Southeast Asia — you're looking at a system with hundreds of single points of failure. A port strike in VIZAG. A transshipment anomaly at JNPT. A shift in Chinese export quotas. Any one of these events can cascade into a shortage that stops electric vehicle production lines on three continents. Intelligence analysts monitoring this landscape deal with classified manifests, geopolitical briefs, stockpile assessments, and inter-ministerial memos — documents spanning five clearance levels, from RESTRICTED (CL1) to COSMIC TOP SECRET (CL5). They need to query this corpus fast, accurately, and across natural language. The standard answer in 2024 is to throw a RAG pipeline at it. Chunk the documents, embed them, stuff them in a vector store, and let GPT-4 synthesize the answer. That answer is unacceptable here. Let me tell you why. The Danger of 'Standard' AI Consider what a typical enterprise RAG stack looks like: documents get embedded via OpenAI's API, vectors live in a cloud-hosted Pinecone index, and queries get synthesized by GPT-4 over HTTPS. Every single one of those steps is a classified data egress event. You cannot send a COSMIC TOP SECRET port manifest to OpenAI. You cannot store vectors encoding sensitive logistics intelligence in a cloud service you don't control. And beyond the egress problem, standard RAG has a deeper flaw: it has no concept of who is asking. A port inspector in VIZAG and a Mission Director at headquarters would receive identical retrieval results, because the pipeline doesn't know — and doesn't care — about access control. Add prompt injection to the threat model, and the picture gets worse. A malicious user who can craft the right input could exfiltrate retrieved context through the model's own output. Standard LLM deployments have no defense against this at the infrastructure level. The NCMM platform had to solve all three problems simultaneously: localization, attribute-based access control, and adversarial prompt defense. And it had to do so on an 8GB RAM developer machine using open-source components. Enter the NCMM Intelligence Platform [INSERT SCREENSHOT: Secure Login & Mandate Vision] The platform is a full-stack, locally-hosted intelligence system built around a hardened RAG pipeline. Here's the elevator pitch: React frontend with JWTs stored strictly in-memory (never localStorage) to prevent XSS exfiltration Node.js/Express API gateway with JWT middleware and a 60 req/min rate limiter Open Policy Agent (OPA) evaluating Rego policies for Attribute-Based Access Control before any document enters the retrieval pipeline Hybrid search engine combining FAISS semantic search and BM25 lexical search, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and re-ranked by a Cross-Encoder 3-Layer Prompt Firewall intercepting queries before they reach the LLM Ollama running a local LLM (or a mock server in dev) — zero data egress, ever The entire developer profile runs on 8GB RAM. No cloud dependencies. No API keys to third-party LLMs. Every computation happens on-device. Five security layers are enforced in sequence. Pass all five, and you get an answer with citations. Fail any one, and you get a denial — logged, audited, and attributed to your JWT. The RAG Pipeline: An Engineering Deep Dive Parent-Child Chunking: The Architecture That Makes It Work Standard chunking makes a brutal tradeoff: large chunks preserve context but dilute semantic precision; small chunks are precise but lose surrounding meaning. The NCMM platform resolves this with a Parent-Child chunking strategy. Every document is split into: Parent chunks — 512 tokens, stored in MongoDB with full metadata but no embeddings (vector_hash: null). These are the answer containers. Child chunks — 128 tokens each, embedded into 384-dimensional vectors using all-MiniLM-L6-v2. These are the search targets. During retrieval, child chunks are matched against the query. But the parent chunk is what gets sent to the LLM as context. This gives the model the full surrounding paragraph while keeping the search index sharp and precise. The Hybrid Search Engine The platform runs two parallel retrieval strategies: Semantic search via FAISS: A 384-dimensional flat L2 index. For each query, the embedding model encodes the input and retrieves the top 50 nearest child chunk vectors (k=50). This catches conceptually related content even when no exact keywords match. Lexical search via BM25: An in-memory sparse search index. The same query runs against BM25 with k=50, catching exact keyword matches that semantic search might miss — especially critical for precise codes like port identifiers, document classifications, and mineral chemical names. Both result sets feed into Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which scores each candidate based on its rank position across both lists. Items appearing high in both lists receive dramatically higher scores. This merged list is then re-ranked by a Cross-Encoder, which evaluates query-chunk relevance jointly rather than in isolation. The result: high-recall retrieval with high-precision ranking. The Architecture Flow graph TD UI["React UI (JWT In-Memory)"] -->|"Bearer Token"| API["Express API Gateway (Rate Limit: 60/min)"] API -->|"Pre-Filter: User Attributes"| OPA["Open Policy Agent (Rego ABAC)"] OPA -->|"Permitted Document IDs"| SE["Search Engine Orchestrator"] subgraph "Search Pipeline" SE -->|"384-dim embedding, k=50"| FAISS["FAISS Index (Flat L2)"] SE -->|"BM25 tokenized query, k=50"| BM25["BM25 Index (In-Memory)"] FAISS --> RRF["Reciprocal Rank Fusion"] BM25 --> RRF RRF --> CE["Cross-Encoder Re-Ranking"] end CE -->|"Top-K Parent Chunks"| FW["3-Layer Prompt Firewall"] subgraph "Firewall" FW --> L1["L1: Unicode Normalizer (NFKC + Strip Bidi)"] L1 --> L2["L2: Intent Classifier (ONNX)"] L2 --> L3["L3: XML Vault (Structured Prompt Isolation)"] end L3 -->|"Sanitized XML Prompt"| LLM["Ollama LLM (Local, No Egress)"] LLM -->|"Synthesized Answer + Citations"| API API --> UI DB["MongoDB (Parent/Child Chunks + Audit Logs)"] -.->|"Chunk Retrieval"| SE DB -.->|"90-day TTL Audit Log"| OPA Sub-2-Second End-to-End Latency The pipeline delivers answers in well under two seconds: User Role Documents Permitted Latency r.sharma Port Inspector (CL2, VIZAG) 8/20 1370ms r.sharma Port Inspector (CL2, VIZAG) 8/20 1413ms s.iyer Mission Director (CL5) 20/20 1539ms The LLM synthesis step itself takes approximately 527ms. The remaining time covers embedding, parallel search, fusion, re-ranking, and firewall processing — an efficient sub-1-second retrieval pipeline. Defense in Depth: The Security Blueprint Security in the NCMM platform isn't a single gate — it's five consecutive checkpoints, each designed to fail safely and log every decision. Layer 1: JWT Middleware Every request carries a bearer token issued at login. The token encodes the user's role, clearance level, department, and — for port inspectors — their assigned port code. The middleware validates the signature and rejects expired or tampered tokens before anything else executes. Crucially, the React frontend never touches localStorage. JWTs live exclusively in React Context state, evaporating when the browser tab closes. This eliminates an entire class of XSS token theft attacks. Layer 2: The OPA Librarian — ABAC Enforcement This is the most sophisticated security layer. Before a single vector is searched, OPA evaluates a Rego policy that answers one question: which documents is this user allowed to see? The policy enforces three orthogonal constraints simultaneously: Clearance Level: A CL2 user cannot access CL3+ documents, regardless of query relevance. Department: A Port Operations inspector cannot access Logistics Analyst documents. Port Isolation: A VIZAG inspector (assigned_port: "VIZAG") is mathematically barred from retrieving JNPT port manifests, even if the semantic similarity score is high. This last constraint is what separates ABAC from simple RBAC. Two users with identical roles and clearance levels — but assigned to different ports — see completely different document universes. OPA returns a filtered set of permitted document IDs, and the search engine is constrained to only that set. Every OPA decision — allow or deny — is written to a MongoDB audit log with a 90-day TTL index. The access record is immutable and attributable. The platform passes 187 out of 194 automated tests, a 96.4% pass rate. The entire test suite runs in approximately 15 seconds. title: anan5093/SafeLink-AI: SafeLink-AI 🛡 | AI-Powered URL Safety Scanner
authors: Anand Raj

abstract: SafeLink-AI 🛡️ | AI-Powered URL Safety Scanner Project Title & Description SafeLink-AI is an intelligent, AI-powered URL safety scanner designed to protect users from malicious and phishing websites. By leveraging advanced machine learning techniques, specifically a pre-trained XGBoost classifier, the system analyzes various features extracted from URLs in real-time to determine their safety status. It provides a robust backend API for seamless integration into web applications, ensuring a secure browsing experience against online threats. Key Features & Benefits Real-time URL Scanning: Instantly checks URLs for potential threats via a high-performance API. Machine Learning Core: Utilizes a pre-trained XGBoost model (XGBoostClassifier.pickle) for high accuracy in classifying URLs as safe or malicious. Comprehensive Feature Extraction: Employs a robust set of URL features (e.g., domain properties, IP presence, URL length, random domain detection) implemented in URLFeatureExtraction.py to identify suspicious patterns. title: Android Software Malicious Detection Based on Dynamic Network Traffic Mixing API Information and Feature Importance Analysis
authors: Kang Yang; Lizhi Cai; Jian-Hua Wu
abstract: : Accurate malware identification and family categorization remain significant challenges in large-scale Android software analysis. Although deep learning has surpassed traditional machine learning in performance, its widespread adoption is hindered by the computational overhead stemming from feature redundancy and the lack of interpretability inherent in its black-box nature. To address these issues, this paper proposes DroidNTA, a DL-based detection model that fuses network traffic and API features. The model first constructs a simplified API Call Graph by extracting the intrinsic structural attributes of applications, and subsequently generates API feature vectors from invocation sequences using a Markov chain algorithm. These are then integrated with dynamic network traffic features to form a final representation vector of the Android instance. To enhance transparency, DroidNTA performs feature contribution analysis by adjusting fusion parameters and employs Shapley values to quantify global feature importance. Experimental results demonstrate that DroidNTA achieves superior performance in both binary and family classification tasks, yielding an accuracy of 99.74% and a gain of over 20%, respectively. We have released our code at https://github.com/joeyyk/DroidNTA.

title: AndroMetric: Bridging Multi-Dimensional Software Metrics and Mobile Application Security
authors: Sebastian Siedler; Karim O. Elish
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AndroMetric is a large-scale dataset designed to support empirical research at the intersection of software metrics and Android application security. The dataset contains 39,243 Android applications, including 29,208 malware samples and 10,035 benign apps, collected from publicly available repositories and analyzed using a static analysis pipeline. For each APK, 31 static code metrics are extracted to capture multi-dimensional structural and behavioral characteristics. These metrics span six categories: (i) size and dimensional structure, (ii) object-oriented design properties, (iii) control-flow complexity, (iv) sensitive operation usage, (v) Android Intent patterns, and (vi) exception handling. In addition to metrics, the dataset includes relevant metadata to facilitate large-scale analysis. AndroMetric enables research on Android malware detection, comparative analysis of benign and malicious codebases, and security-aware software quality assessment. The dataset is intended for researchers and practitioners in mobile security, software engineering, and applied machine learning. title: Annotated Encrypted Network Traffic Dataset for Application, OS, and Malware Identification
authors: Ondřej Ryšavý
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This dataset provides an annotated collection of encrypted network communication intended for research on application identification, operating system fingerprinting, and malware detection in encrypted traffic. It combines network traffic captured in controlled sandbox environments executing selected Windows applications with malware-related communication obtained from automated malware analysis reports. In addition to application and malware traffic, the dataset includes background operating system communication generated by the capture environment, enabling comprehensive and realistic modeling of host behavior. The dataset is publicly provided as Apache Parquet files containing preprocessed representations of the raw network traffic. The underlying raw packet capture data (PCAP files) are not publicly distributed but are available upon justified request. The Parquet files include extracted features and structured annotations suitable for direct use in data analysis and machine learning workflows. The format and structure of the Parquet files, including field definitions and annotation schemas, are documented in the accompanying README.md file. The dataset is versioned and designed to be incrementally extended with additional applications, operating systems, and malware samples, supporting reproducible research and long-term reuse in encrypted traffic analysis and network security studies.

title: Anomaly Detection in Encrypted Network Traffic Based on a Hybrid Machine Learning Model: ANN-SVM
authors: Amjad Mohammad Hijazi
venue: 2026 1st International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Engineering Systems (ICETES)
abstract: Encrypted network packets play a vital role in safeguarding networks and preventing attackers from intercepting sensitive information. The effectiveness of Intrusion Detection Systems relies heavily on the proper application of classification techniques, so that we can distinguish between legitimate user activities and those attempting malicious activities within network boundaries, using encrypted attacks to hide malicious activities. This poses a challenge in society. To address this challenge, machine learning models have been used to classify encrypted packets, but with limited success due to the lack of clear visibility into the contents of the network packet and the inability to inspect its content. In this research, we attempt to use the basic features of encrypted network packets as input features in the classification process, relying on a Hybrid ANN-SVM approach consisting of an ANN (Artificial Neural Network) learning method for feature extraction and a SVM (Support Vector Machine) classification algorithm. The NSL-KDD dataset was used to analyze encrypted attacks targeting common protocols comprehensively. The proposed approach demonstrated its ability to extract important values from analyzing encrypted network packets without accessing content and overcoming the limitations of encryption protocols. The hybrid model was trained on the NSL-KDD dataset, and its effectiveness was verified using encrypted network packet traffic generated from a network attack (SSL Flood Attack) in conjunction with normal encrypted network packet traffic for applications using encrypted communications (Facebook, YouTube, FTPS). The proposed hybrid approach achieved a detection accuracy (ACC) of 96.2%, a detection rate (DR) of 94.7%, a false positive rate (FPR) of 0.14%, and a detection time of 5 s.

title: APEX-IDS2026: A Real-World Network Perimeter Threat Dataset
authors: Jalal Uddin
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: APEX-IDS2026 acts as a modern, large-scale, real-world benchmark for evaluating machine learning models in network intrusion detection. Historically, research in this field relies on synthetic datasets or outdated captures. APEX-IDS2026 solves this by supplying traffic captured from a live, internet-facing /24 IPv4 honeynet over a 44-day period in early 2026. This exposes models to actual threats rather than simulated lab environments. The repository includes the data in two formats: 1. The Full Dataset (Partitioned): Contains 141.6 million records divided into three categories (Attacks, Suspicious, Normal). It includes traffic from 13,638 distinct attacking IP addresses targeting 64,084 unique ports and actual services (Redis, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, VoIP). 2. The High-Confidence Subset: A strictly filtered 69.1 million record subset containing only verified attacks (Tier 1) and verified benign flows (Tier 3). We created this subset exclusively for machine learning model training and evaluation. Real-world 'Normal' traffic often contains unclassified background noise or zero-day threats that compromise label integrity. The High-Confidence Subset guarantees a 0% false-positive ground truth on the attack class, and removes ambiguous/unverified background traffic entirely. This allows researchers to train binary classification models on verified malicious and verified benign traffic with absolute certainty regarding the labels. Features include: 5 summary Layer 7 attributes derived from over 70 raw fields extracted via the Zeek Network Analysis Framework (including HTTP, DNS, TLS, and SSH metadata). Standard NetFlow v9 attributes (byte counts, packets, flags). TCP connection states and inter-arrival time statistics. Geographical and temporal data for all connections. Note: All IP addresses are deterministically anonymized (SHA-256 truncation) to protect privacy while preserving subnet patterns for model training.

title: Application Identification with pfSense, Snort, and OpenAppID in Academic Lab Networks
authors: Minh-Khanh Vu
venue: Journal of Cybersecurity Education Research and Practice
abstract: This paper evaluates the practical capabilities and limitations of a widely used open-source network security stack—pfSense firewall, Snort Intrusion Detection System (IDS), and OpenAppID detectors—in academic cy- bersecurity laboratories and small-to-medium enterprise (SME)-like environments. In a controlled virtual testbed, we measure application-level and feature-level identifi- cation performance for major applications (Facebook, YouTube, Zoom) using the pfSense/Snort/OpenAppID configuration. The stack achieves 97% application-level identification accuracy for these applications in our lab dataset, drawing on a library of 3,374 OpenAppID detectors. However, our experiments reveal a substan- tial feature-level detection gap: specific functions such as Zoom file transfers and Facebook messaging can- not be reliably identified or blocked despite correct application-level classification. These findings clarify the architectural limitations of signature-based inspection on encrypted traffic and pfSense plug-in deployments and provide evidence-based guidance for cybersecurity educa- tors and SME administrators when selecting tools and setting realistic expectations. We argue that achieving fine-grained, feature-specific policy control will require hybrid approaches that combine traditional signatures with advanced machine-learning-based traffic classifica- tion rather than relying on signature-based methods alone.

title: Application of Machine Learning Algorithms for Early Detection of Cyber Threats
authors: Nejra Skenderović; Zanin Vejzović
abstract: Frequent cyber incidents within the public sector underscore the inadequacy of traditional, reactive defense mechanisms. This research presents the development of a model based on machine learning algorithms—specifically XGBoost, LightGBM, and Random Forest—for the early detection of threats through automated network log analysis. The focus of the study is on the classification of anomalies in HTTP status codes, utilizing authentic data (Raw Access Logs) from the information system of a local public institution. The research results demonstrate that the implemented model, by analyzing a minimal set of parameters such as IP address, HTTP method, and URL, achieves high precision in identifying suspicious requests (e.g., 403 and 404 statuses). Such anomalies are often generated by botnet activity, where compromised devices produce massive volumes of automated requests in attempts to exploit system vulnerabilities. Comparative analysis confirms the superiority of the XGBoost algorithm over other models, proving that automating the detection process drastically reduces response time and minimizes potential damage. The proposed solution offers an applicable protection model for resource-constrained institutions, enabling a transition from manual log review to an intelligent, real-time monitoring system.

title: APPLICATION OF THE PARAMETER FUZZIFICATION METHOD BASED ON REFERENCE SUBENVIRONMENTS FOR PHISHING ATTACK DETECTION
authors: А. О. Корченко; М. Г. Аскеров; І. Ірейфідж; Кирило ДАВИДЕНКО; A. Герасименко
abstract: The increasing number and complexity of phishing attacks, along with the continuous improvement of techniques for circumventing existing security mechanisms, necessitate the development of phishing detection methods capable of accounting for uncertainty in URL parameters and domain infrastructure characteristics. An analysis of current approaches has shown that methods based on threshold values, signature analysis, machine learning, and fuzzy logic have limitations in adapting to emerging types of attacks and do not provide a formalized procedure for parameter fuzzification tailored to the specific characteristics of phishing web resources. This study employs methods of system analysis, comparative analysis, mathematical modeling, and fuzzy logic. The research is based on the further development of an existing parameter fuzzification method using reference subenvironments through its adaptation to the specific characteristics of phishing URLs. For this purpose, phishing activity parameters were formalized, the corresponding linguistic terms were defined, correction reference values were established, and a fuzzification procedure was implemented for domain age, DNS change frequency, number of subdomains, URL length, and SSL/HTTPS protection status. The novelty of the study lies in extending the functional capabilities of the parameter fuzzification method based on reference subenvironments. By formalizing the transformation of current parameter values, mapping them onto two-dimensional current environments, and adapting the method to the specific characteristics of phishing URLs, it becomes possible to use the resulting fuzzified values in phishing attack detection procedures. As a result, fuzzified parameter values were obtained and used to assess the membership of current parameter values in the corresponding linguistic reference sets and to determine the two-dimensional reference region corresponding to the current level of the anomalous state induced by phishing activity. The proposed method can be used in the development of phishing attack detection systems, cybersecurity expert systems, decision support systems, and intelligent systems for phishing URL analysis. Keywords: phishing, phishing URLs, phishing attack detection systems, cybersecurity, information security.

title: Application of type 2 inflammation-related biomarkers in risk prediction models for acute exacerbations in adult asthma: a systematic review
authors: Minghao Li; Zihan Yan; Minghang Wang
abstract: Objective: To systematically evaluate how type 2 (T2) inflammation-related biomarkers are incorporated into multivariable models that predict future acute exacerbations in adults with asthma, and to appraise model performance, validation, calibration, risk of bias, and clinical applicability. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched from inception to May 2026, followed by a supplementary PubMed update through 31 July 2026. Eligible reports contained at least one adult cohort used to develop, validate, or update a longitudinal multivariable model for a future exacerbation outcome, incorporated at least one T2-related biomarker, and reported model performance or validation. Mixed-age cohorts were not counted as independent adult evidence; only performance evaluated in an adult cohort contributed to the main synthesis. Association-only studies, current-attack classification models, post-exacerbation disposition models, and post-index relapse models outside the prespecified baseline-risk setting were excluded. Data extraction followed CHARMS, and risk of bias and applicability were assessed using PROBAST. Results: = 345). Modeling approaches included logistic and elastic-net regression, gradient-boosting and deep-learning algorithms, Bayesian networks, and a mixed-effects count model. Eosinophil-related variables appeared in all eight reports but were not retained in every final model; FeNO was included in two multinational severe-asthma registry models, and serum IgE appeared as a network node in one cross-source analysis and was retained in an independently replicated metabolomics model. The metabolomics model reported AUCs of 0.901 and 0.893 in discovery and replication cohorts, whereas an RCT-derived Bayesian network achieved an AUC of 0.68 when validated in the adult ISAR cohort. Six reports were rated at high overall risk of bias, mainly because of analysis-domain limitations. Conclusion: T2-related biomarkers may add complementary information to adult asthma exacerbation-risk models, but the available evidence does not yet establish BEC, FeNO, or IgE as independently sufficient predictors or support routine implementation of an existing model. Future studies should quantify incremental biomarker value beyond established clinical predictors and prioritize adequate sample size, external validation, calibration, clinical utility, transparent handling of missing biomarker data, and reproducible model presentation. Systematic Review Registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, PROSPERO CRD420261415469.

title: Application-Layer DDoS Attacks and Defences: A Taxonomy, Comparative Evaluation Framework, and Research Directions
authors: Aditya Arsh; Priyanka Biswas; Nirmalya Kar
venue: International Journal of Wireless and Microwave Technologies
abstract: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks have gained popularity among cybercriminals as a favoured method of disruption. Application layer DDoS attacks are particularly intricate, as they overload web servers with re-quests, rendering them inaccessible to legitimate users and causing availability issues. These attacks are challenging to detect through network and transport-level security measures, making them even more concerning. This paper explores various categories of DDoS attacks, encompassing volumetric and protocol-focused attacks, with a particular focus on application-layer attacks, classifying them into Protocol-specific attacks and Generic attacks. It also delves into diverse defence strategies tailored to combat related attacks, such as HTTP Flood, DHCP starvation, SlowLoris, and others. Unlike earlier surveys, which centre on vulnerability-oriented taxonomies through 2017–2020, this work introduces an explicit, criterion-based comparative evaluation framework for attacks and defences, and extends the taxonomy with post-2020 developments containerized and cloud native low-rate attack surfaces, machine learning-driven detection and adversarial evasion, and zero-trust-based mitigation illustrated with the 2023 HTTP/2 ‘Rapid Reset’ incident. Finding that detection-only mechanisms still dominate current defences, the paper identifies recurring bottlenecks and proposes con-crete future-research directions, including detection resistant to adversarial machine learning and low-rate attack detection in containerized and serverless environments.

title: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real–Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection
authors: Amal Neji; Mohamed Fourati; Lamia Chaari Fourati
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AquaSense-ICS: a hybrid real-simulated cyber-physical dataset and leakage-aware benchmark for smart water quality monitoring and attack detection Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemically poor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. AquaSense-ICS co-registers, on a common elapsed-time axis: Real edge recording: a 25.4 h window (8.0 h of recorded data, 31.5% coverage, 23 gaps longer than 60 s) from a Raspberry Pi 5 node with a TDS probe and a Bosch BME680 ambient sensor (temperature, relative humidity, gas resistance), sampled every 1-2 s (23,688 records). EPANET-MSX simulation: a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank) simulated for 24 h, with six water-quality species (chlorine, pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, conductivity, trihalomethanes) and one wall species, plus two pulse injections (chlorine at J3, turbidity at J7). Attack and fault library: a seeded generator of five cyber-attack types (false data injection, stealthy FDI, replay, denial of service, drift) and three unintentional sensor faults (white noise, spikes, extreme values), with sample-level ground truth. Augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, released in separate files and flagged by the origin column in the fused table. They are intended for training only. The accompanying paper also shows that random row splits combined with labels computed from the input features give near-perfect but uninformative scores, and defines a leakage-aware benchmark (chronological splits, held-out attack types). title: Artifact for Open Towards Real-Time Intrusion Detection in P4-Programmable 5G User Plane Functions
authors: Akem Aristide
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Source code accompanying the paper "Towards Real-Time Intrusion Detection in P4-Programmable 5G User Plane Functions" (International Conference on Network Protocols, ICNP 2024 workshop). The paper explores how Machine Learning (ML) inference in a P4-programmable user plane can enable real-time intrusion detection in 5G networks. As a proof-of-concept, an ML model is deployed in the 5G User Plane Function (UPF) as a special Packet Detection Rule (PDR): a tree-based classifier is trained and deployed into a P4-programmable switch acting as the UPF, achieving line-rate attack detection and classification with an F1 score of up to 98% while keeping the increase in switch resource consumption under control. This repository contains the code used to train the tree-based classifier and to deploy it in the P4-programmable switch acting as the UPF, as described in the paper. The experiments use data from a 5G test network on a university campus. Paper: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14718054Source repository: https://github.com/nds-group/5G_UPF_Intrusion_Detection

title: Artificial Intelligence in Cybersecurity: Transformation of Digital Defense Paradigms
authors: Ian Khan; Ian Khan
abstract: Abstract: This paper examines the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on cybersecurity, analyzing the shift from reactive, rule-based security approaches to proactive, intelligent defense systems. The research explores how machine learning algorithms, natural language processing, and generative AI technologies are fundamentally reshaping threat detection, incident response, and vulnerability management. Through analysis of implementation patterns across geographic regions and industrial sectors, the paper identifies both the opportunities and challenges presented by AI integration in cybersecurity operations. Key findings suggest that while AI enables significant improvements in threat detection speed and response automation, it also introduces new vulnerabilities through adversarial AI attacks and creates substantial skill gaps in implementation. The paper concludes with recommendations for balanced AI adoption, emphasizing the need for ethical frameworks, human oversight, and collaborative defense networks to maximize benefits while mitigating risks in an increasingly complex digital threat landscape. Keywords: artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, machine learning, threat detection, autonomous response, digital defense, adversarial AI, security transformation Year: 2026 Version: v1.0 Original Publication: https://www.iankhan.com/ai-disruption-in-cybersecurity-redefining-the-digital-battlefield-5/ Author: Ian Khan, Independent Futurist & Researcher Author Google Scholar: https://scholar.google.ca/citations?user=a1Aiy68AAAAJ&hl=en

title: Artificial Intelligence in Next-Generation Firewalls for Discriminating Cyber Attacks from Legitimate Service Traffic Surges
authors: Samir Khanji
venue: International Journal of Information & Digital Security
abstract: Next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) sit on the critical path between public networks and production services. Their most consequential error is no longer a missed signature; it is the inability to tell a malicious flood from a genuine surge in legitimate demand. Flash crowds, seasonal campaigns, media-driven spikes, and elastic microservice fan-out can resemble distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) traffic in volume while remaining economically and operationally valid. Static access-control lists, fixed rate limits, and signature catalogs therefore produce an unacceptable trade-off: either they under-block stealthy application-layer attacks or they over-block paying users. This article reviews, compares, and synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence from 2020 onward on machine-learning and deep-learning methods that can be embedded in NGFW and software-defined enforcement points to discriminate attacks from legitimate service-intensity bursts. We organize the literature into statistical filters, classical classifiers, representation-learning hybrids, sequential models, and two-tier designs that first cheaply detect a burst and then classify its intent. Published detectors regularly report accuracy above 98% on CICDDoS2019 and related traces, yet most benchmarks omit a dedicated flash-event class, which inflates apparent performance and leaves the operationally hardest decision under-tested. Building on that gap, we propose AID-NGFW, a three-tier architecture that couples entropy and cumulative-sum screening with a calibrated three-class discriminator (benign, flash crowd, attack) and a policy engine that drops malicious flows while scaling or shaping legitimate surges. Comparative tables and figures compile reported accuracies, F1-scores, datasets, and latency–accuracy trade-offs. We argue that the scientific and engineering priority is no longer binary attack detection in isolation, but reliable, low-latency, and explainable discrimination under encrypted traffic, class imbalance, concept drift, and adversarial mimicry.

title: Attack-to-Defense IoT: A Physical IoT Security Testbed for Labeled Dataset Generation and Machine Learning-Based Attack Detection
authors: Hebert Silva; Mateus Lopes; João Luisi; Tiago A. O. Demay; Regina Moraes
abstract: The increasing adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has significantly expanded the attack surface of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), making realistic experimental environments essential for cybersecurity research. This work presents a low-cost and reproducible IoT cybersecurity testbed designed for realistic attack execution, multimodal labeled dataset generation, and Machine Learning (ML)-based intrusion detection. The proposed environment integrates ESP32-based embedded devices, MQTT/TLS communication, AWS cloud services, automated telemetry extraction pipelines, and supervised ML models. The infrastructure supports realistic attack scenarios including MQTT flooding, Sliver Command and Control (C2) beaconing, Denial-of-Service attacks, network scanning, and brute-force attacks against embedded services. The generated datasets combine PCAP-derived network traffic, MQTT telemetry, and sensor-generated events into a unified multimodal representation for intrusion detection experiments. Experimental results indicate that supervised ML algorithms, particularly Random Forest, are effective for detecting volumetric attacks and heterogeneous malicious traffic patterns in constrained IoT environments. The proposed platform contributes a reproducible physical infrastructure for IoT cybersecurity experimentation and establishes a foundation for future research involving Federated Learning (FL), TinyML, and distributed intrusion detection for CPS.

title: Automated Detection of Web Application Vulnerabilities
authors: M. Dhilsath Fathima; N. Jithendra; N. Yasaswini
venue: International Conference on Intelligent Sustainable Systems (ICISS)
abstract: Web applications are primary component of digital services but are increasingly susceptible to security threats, such as SQL Injection, Cross Site Scripting, and Cross Site Request Forgery. Manual vulnerability detection is a difficult task and vulnerable to errors, needing automation and scalable approaches. The proposed model develops an Automated Web Application Vulnerability Detection system, which uses web crawling, intelligent fuzzing, and Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) classifier to detect and prioritize vulnerabilities in real time. This model extracts features such as payload length, frequency of special character, HTTP response parameters, and response variability, and computes severity scores to guide response reduction. This system utilizes an input dataset has HTTP requests and responses, including benign and malicious payloads targeting OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities, and develops a web application, allowing user to view the output. Experimental evaluation on test dataset shows increased model performance over baseline machine learning models, achieving enhanced accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The framework adapts to obfuscated and zero-day payloads, ensuring robust detection of evolving threats. By combining automation, feature-driven ARF classification, and severity- based reporting, the proposed model provides an efficient, and actionable solution for securing modern web applications.

title: Bans that never blocked: data and analysis code for measuring silent enforcement failure
authors: Ananda Hadi Elyas; Asyahri Hadi Nasyuha; Rakhmat Kurniawan R
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Replication material for an interrupted time series study of layered compensating controls on production end-of-life scholarly publishing infrastructure, covering 14,524,327 HTTP requests over 52 analyzable days across three production servers, together with an application-side measure of bot-account creation. Contents. Pseudonymized daily and event-level data for three servers (traffic, attack events by class and HTTP outcome, per-address activity, fail2ban detections and blocks, decoy touches), the daily bot-account series with source and phase annotation, and the complete analysis pipeline: collector, daily archiver, anonymizer, public-bundle preparer, request classifier, and six analysis scripts. The deposited code reproduces every statistic reported in the accompanying article from the deposited data; this was verified by running it against these files rather than against working copies. A SHA-256 manifest covers every file. Anonymization. Network addresses are pseudonymized with a salted, truncated HMAC-SHA256; the mapping is stable per address so recidivism remains measurable, but the salt is withheld and reversal is infeasible. Reverse-DNS names keep only their registrable suffix, because cloud provider hostnames frequently embed the address itself. Site names are replaced by labels throughout: the five sites analyzed in the article keep the names used there, every other site receives a pseudonym. That is not only a matter of protecting the host institution, since the observed servers also carry sites belonging to unrelated organizations that are not participants in this study. Decoy file paths are replaced for the same reason detection thresholds are withheld. Deliberately withheld. The HMAC salt; firewall rules, jail thresholds and allow-lists; application guard configuration; per-site application versions and document roots; server environment metadata; incident, quarantine and guard logs; and honeypot payload records, whose request bodies and headers are free text supplied by attackers, were not reviewed line by line, and can carry credentials or third-party personal data. The README lists each omission with its reason. Ethics. The study is observational over data arising from normal operation. No attack was staged, no penetration test was performed, and no production change was made for the purpose of collection. Network addresses are treated as personal data under the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Law. Users of this dataset must not attempt re-identification, and must not combine it with other sources for that purpose.

title: Behavioural intelligence: Analytical frameworks for the future of threat intelligence
authors: Nicole Wong; Nathaniel Jones; Calum Hall; Daniel Levy; Adam Potter; Emma Foulger et al.
abstract: Traditional cyber threat intelligence (CTI) remains a valuable mechanism for attribution, contextualisation, and strategic awareness; however, its reliance on post-disclosure indicators imposes inherent temporal limitations. As adversaries increasingly exploit pre-disclosure vulnerabilities, legitimate credentials, and cloud-native attack pathways, indicator-driven detection models are frequently unable to provide timely defensive insight. This paper draws from real-world case studies on pre-vulnerability disclosure exploitation, multistage intrusions and nation-state activity to present behavioural intelligence as a complementary and operationally critical detection paradigm, capable of identifying malicious activity through deviations from established system and user behaviour days to weeks before traditional CTI signals emerge. It further addresses a gap in existing research, going beyond detection to interpretability by proposing two practical frameworks for operationalising behavioural intelligence within security operations centre and threat hunting workflows. These frameworks integrate unsupervised and supervised machine learning, graph analytics, and agentic reasoning to correlate low-signal anomalies into high-confidence threat narratives. The findings highlight behavioural intelligence as a necessary evolution of CTI, enabling earlier detection, improved contextual understanding, and more adaptive defence against modern, rapidly evolving adversaries. This article is also included in The Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at https://hstalks.com/business/.

title: Benchmarking Supervised and Unsupervised Machine Learning for Network Intrusion Detection on UNSW-NB15
authors: Douglas Felipe Lima Silva
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Benchmarking Supervised and Unsupervised Machine Learning for Network Intrusion Detection on UNSW-NB15 Reproducible supervised and unsupervised machine-learning benchmark for binary network intrusion detection using the official predefined UNSW-NB15 training and testing partitions. The study compares a majority-class Dummy baseline against Random Forest, XGBoost, LinearSVC, and Multilayer Perceptron classifiers. Hyperparameter selection is performed exclusively on the training partition using RandomizedSearchCV, followed by post-selection descriptive cross-validation and evaluation on the untouched official test partition. The benchmark also includes attack-family-specific detection analysis, percentile bootstrap confidence intervals over fixed held-out predictions, permutation-based feature importance, computational-efficiency measurements, and exploratory unsupervised analysis using PCA, k-Means, and DBSCAN. Attack labels and attack-family metadata are excluded from model fitting and are used only where explicitly stated for supervised targets or post-hoc evaluation. Research Questions RQ1 — How do Random Forest, XGBoost, a linear Support Vector Machine, and a Multilayer Perceptron compare for binary intrusion detection on the official UNSW-NB15 partition? RQ2 — Do aggregate classification metrics hide meaningful differences in detection performance across attack families? RQ3 — Do k-Means and DBSCAN reveal traffic structure related to normal and malicious behavior without using target labels during fitting? RQ4 — What trade-offs exist among predictive performance, model size, final training cost, and inference cost? Main Results In the archived FULL experimental profile, XGBoost obtained the numerically highest held-out F1 score (0.8943), followed closely by Random Forest (0.8907) and the Multilayer Perceptron (0.8893). Attack-wise analysis showed that aggregate performance conceals substantial variation across attack families. For the XGBoost demonstration model, Fuzzers recall was 0.8903, while several other attack families were detected almost perfectly. All non-baseline supervised models exhibited false-positive rates above one quarter of normal test traffic, emphasizing that strong recall and ROC-AUC in this controlled benchmark should not be interpreted as evidence of operational deployment readiness. The unsupervised analysis remained exploratory. k-Means with k = 2 achieved a silhouette score of 0.3335. The internally selected DBSCAN configuration produced 13 non-noise clusters, 3.18% noise, and a silhouette score of 0.2544. Post-hoc ARI and NMI remained low, indicating that the recovered cluster structure is not a close substitute for the supervised binary attack label. Methodological Safeguards The official predefined UNSW-NB15 train/test partition is preserved. No random train/test split is created. The official test set is never used for hyperparameter tuning. label is used only as the supervised target. attack_cat is excluded from model inputs and retained only for post-hoc attack-family analysis. id is excluded from all model inputs. Preprocessing is fitted within the corresponding training folds. DBSCAN model selection uses only internal, label-free clustering criteria. ARI and NMI are used only as post-hoc external diagnostics and do not participate in clustering selection. Dataset provenance is recorded through SHA-256 hashes. The FULL experimental profile uses 15 sampled hyperparameter configurations per non-baseline model, three-fold tuning cross-validation, five-fold post-selection descriptive cross-validation, and 1500 bootstrap resamples per supervised model. Scope and Limitations This work is a controlled machine-learning benchmark based on precomputed UNSW-NB15 network-flow features. It is not a production intrusion-detection system. The project does not parse raw PCAP traffic, ingest raw Syslog or NetFlow, monitor live network traffic, or claim validation in SCADA, thermoelectric, or other Operational Technology environments. UNSW-NB15 was generated in a controlled cyber-range environment. Results obtained on its predefined partition therefore characterize benchmark performance and should not be interpreted as direct evidence of operational network validity. The main supervised task is binary intrusion detection. The unsupervised component is exploratory and is evaluated on a bounded training-set sample after PCA-based dimensionality reduction. Hyperparameter search is deliberately bounded, and the reported bootstrap confidence intervals do not constitute a formal paired statistical test of model superiority. Reproducibility The associated public repository contains the source code, experiment configurations, reproducibility manifests, generated results, figures, manuscript sources, and documented QUICK and FULL experimental profiles: https://github.com/PesquisaDoug/unsw-nb15-ml-benchmark The repository state preserving the code, configuration, and reported FULL-run results is identified by Git revision: 0c44383212677a3dfc4facb3a69a495bfce412f4 Dataset integrity information is recorded in data/data_manifest.json, including SHA-256 hashes for the exact predefined UNSW-NB15 training and testing CSV files used in the study. The original UNSW-NB15 dataset is third-party data and is not redistributed through the project repository. It should be obtained from the canonical UNSW Sydney source.
