abstract: CrossPlane-5G is an open, reproducible, dual-plane benchmark dataset collected from a containerized 3GPP Release-16 5G Standalone (SA) testbed (OpenAirInterface Core & gNodeB/nrUE with RFSimulator). Dataset Links & Resources: Hugging Face Repository: alberttchalla/CrossPlane-5G GitHub NIDS Benchmark Toolkit: TchallaAlbertKwame/CrossPlane5G_Toolkit It features simultaneous, hardware TSC-aligned packet captures across two distinct observation planes: Layer-A (UE Plane): Unencapsulated user-plane PDU session tunnel telemetry (oaitun_ue1), capturing raw user intent at the UE boundary. Layer-B (N3 Transport Plane): Encapsulated 3GPP GTP-U transport telemetry with 32-bit GTP-U Tunnel Endpoint Identifiers (TEIDs), capturing physical radio dynamics and encapsulation overhead. Dataset Profile & Specifications Total Master Subflow Records: 12,252,610 (6,126,855 per observation plane) File Size: 889 MB (Compressed Apache Parquet format) / 462.52 GB (Raw dual-plane PCAP archives) Subflow Window Width: Δt = 2.0 s (Bidirectional Welford statistical moments) Feature Dimension: 46 raw features (23 per plane + GTP-U metadata) / 33 strict anti-leakage features Campaign Duration: 24-Hour continuous automated run across 26 rotational execution cycles Labeling Methodology: 100% Deterministic ground-truth via manifest port-pinning (Zero heuristic guessing) 13-Class Canonical Scenario Taxonomy The dataset includes 100% deterministic ground-truth labels across 13 canonical classes: 00_benign_baseline: Multi-thread background profile (HTTP, Video, IoT, Pause) 01_dos_icmp_flood: High-rate ICMP echo request flood 02_dos_udp_flood: High-rate UDP datagram flood 03_dos_syn_flood: Volumetric TCP SYN handshake exhaustion 04_dos_http_flood: Application-layer GET request flood 05_dos_slowrate: Low-and-slow HTTP headers exhaustion (Slowloris) 06_scan_syn: Stealth SYN port scanning 07_scan_tcp_connect: Full 3-way TCP connect scanning 08_scan_udp: UDP service discovery scanning 09_benign_embb: 3GPP eMBB high-throughput 4K video streaming 10_benign_urllc: 3GPP URLLC low-latency industrial control telemetry 11_benign_mmtc: 3GPP mMTC massive IoT telemetry 12_benign_agentic_llm: Agentic LLM multi-leg API token streaming Research Innovation & Anti-Leakage Design Anti-Leakage PII Stripping: All routing 5-tuples (IP addresses & Ports) are explicitly purged from ML feature vectors to force deep learning models to learn physical traffic dynamics rather than memorizing topological IP shortcuts. Modern Workload Realism: First 5G NIDS dataset to incorporate 3GPP slice-specific workloads (eMBB, URLLC, mMTC) alongside multi-agent LLM API token streaming. title: Cyber Attack Analysis and Awareness System using Python, Flask, React.js, Scikit-learn, Wireshark/Scapy, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis
authors: Mahmoud Rajabbek; Tarek Barhoum
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents the design and development of the Cyber Attack Analysis and Awareness System, an integrated educational and analytical platform aimed at addressing the growing complexity of modern cyber threats. The system focuses primarily on two of the most prevalent attack categories in contemporary cybersecurity: ransomware and phishing. By leveraging the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK frameworks, the system models the complete lifecycle of cyber attacks, from initial reconnaissance through final execution, providing users with a structured understanding of adversarial behavior. The proposed system incorporates a ransomware behavior simulation module capable of demonstrating encryption propagation and lateral movement within an isolated sandbox environment, alongside a machine learning-based phishing detection engine trained on real-world URL and email datasets. A comprehensive literature review of six peer-reviewed studies confirms the effectiveness of entropy analysis, API call monitoring, and Random Forest classification in achieving detection accuracy rates exceeding 96%. The platform is developed using Python and Flask for backend processing, React.js for the frontend interface, and a hybrid database architecture combining PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. System requirements are defined in accordance with NIST SP 800-61 guidelines, ensuring both functional completeness and non-functional compliance across performance, security, scalability, and reliability dimensions. The system is intended to serve both academic and professional audiences, bridging the gap between theoretical cybersecurity knowledge and practical threat mitigation. This work was conducted at Arab International University (AIU), Syria. The official website of the university is: https://www.aiu.edu.sy

title: Cyber Security and Ethical Hacking
authors: K. Aparna Preethi; I. G. Uma Maheswari; M. Vinothini; G. Hemavathi
abstract: Cyber security has become a shared concern from the server room to the boardroom, the courtroom and the national security agenda. Today, ransomware groups, or more advanced persistent threats (APT) and AI-driven adversaries can function as legitimate businesses, and challenges break down unless one knows what they are up against. This gap has been filled with the writing of Cyber Security and Ethical Hacking to provide students, early students, educators and aspiring ethical hackers clear, practical and up-to-date information and knowledge of information security, cyber resilience and cyber defence. The book starts by covering the basics of the CIA triad, cyber threat landscape, vulnerabilities, attack surface and cyber risk management, as well as relevant frameworks, regulations and data-privacy requirements. It then shifts into ethical hacking and pen testing, where vulnerability assessment, red teaming, structured methodologies like OSSTMM, provide defenders with the opportunity to embrace the thinking like the attacker mindset within their legal boundaries, clear scope of work and end responsibility. Assessment of the enemy is the foundation of defence. The chapter on cyber threat intelligence and threat hunting explains the intelligence lifecycle, the MITRE ATT&CK framework, the Cyber Kill Chain, the Diamond Model, STIX and TAXII, open-source intelligence (OSINT) and proactive hunting for hidden intrusions. Dedicated chapter on Malware, Ransomware and Advanced Persistent Threats covers Malware Analysis, Attack Campaigns, Incident Response, Endpoint Detection & Response, Digital Forensics and newer trends like AI-driven Malware and Zero-Day exploitation of Edge Devices. The next chapters are devoted to modern digital infrastructure. Network security and web application security cover firewalls, intrusion detection systems and intrusion prevention, encrypted DNS, TLS 1.3, DDoS protection, API security, the OWASP Top 10, injection flaws, broken access control and secure coding. They also discuss software supply chain security, post quantum cryptography and upcoming legislation that includes NIS2 Directive and Cyber Resilience Act. Cloud security and zero trust architecture is next, with a focus on zero trust networks, shared responsibility model, identity and access management (IAM), and container and serverless security. The final chapter explores Artificial Intelligence and machine learning in cyber security, such as Deep Learning, Large Language Models, Agentic AI, Anomaly detection, Phishing detection, Malware detection, and Security Operations Center (SOC) workflows. It also addresses adversarial machine learning and prompt injection and LLM red teaming, giving counsellors some idea on how to protect with AI and how to protect AI systems, with a nod to ethics, explainability, privacy and human oversight. All throughout, the method of discourse is intentionally simple and clear with an introduction, key words presented in the beginning of every chapter, ideas developed season by season, and linkages made to the real world. Only use techniques described in authorized, controlled laboratory areas and in accordance with the law. I hope this book provides a rock-solid grounding for those wishing to embark on a successful career in penetration testing, security operations, digital forensics, cyber threat intelligence, and cyber risk management—and fosters a culture of responsible, ethical, and resilient cybersecurity practices.

title: Cyber Threat Detection Using an Integrated AI System
authors: Devidas S. Thosar; Lakshmi Sharma; Chaitanya Jakate; Faizan Inamdar; Kisan Yadav; Saurabh Sharma
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This work presents the design and implementation of Cyber Threat Detection Using an Integrated AI System, an artificial intelligence–based framework developed for proactive cyber threat detection and analysis. The proposed platform combines network intrusion detection and phishing risk assessment into a unified architecture to address modern multi-vector cyberattacks. Benchmark datasets such as CICIDS-2017 for network traffic and URL-based datasets including PhishTank and UCI Repository will be utilized for model training and evaluation. The system employs an Unsupervised Deep Learning Autoencoder to learn normal network behavior and detect zero-day intrusions through reconstruction error analysis. In parallel, a Random Forest classifier analyzes lexical URL features such as domain entropy, special character frequency, URL length, and HTTPS validity to identify phishing websites in real time. The architecture follows a modular microservices design integrated with a FastAPI backend and an interactive dashboard interface. Additionally, Generative AI–based alert summarization provides human-readable threat explanations to reduce analyst fatigue and improve response efficiency. The expected outcome is enhanced detection of zero-day attacks and phishing threats, reduced false positives, improved situational awareness, and a scalable, intelligent cybersecurity solution capable of adapting to evolving digital threats while supporting faster and more informed security decision-making.

title: Cyber-Resilient IoT-Driven SCADA Integration for Secure and Intelligent Fuel Station Monitoring and Predictive Analysis
authors: Samuel Okperigho; Boyce Egobudiken Iyamah; Ese J. Edosio; Micheal Adawaren
venue: Journal of computer, software and program.
abstract: The paper introduces a secure, cyber-resilient IoT-SCADA convergence architecture for intelligent monitoring and control of fuel station systems. OPC UA and MQTT are utilized to provide a semantically structured supervisory control and a highly scalable telemetry system. Furthermore, deterministic field-level actuation and cloud-based analytics can be achieved. A defense-in-depth security model is implemented through OT/IT segmentation, TLS 1.3 encryption, certificate-based authentication, and machine-learning-based intrusion detection. A predictive intelligence model is developed through the implementation of a hybrid model consisting of supervised learning-based classifiers, temporal deep learning models, and a physics-informed digital twin model for detecting leaks and fraud. The proposed architecture was validated through experimentation on a representative testbed of a fuel station system consisting of four underground tanks and six dispensers. An edge gateway and a cloud-based analytics platform were utilized. Experimental results were obtained for normal operation, simulated leaks (2 L/min), meter tampering, and controlled cyberattacks. Experimental results demonstrated sub-200 ms supervisory latency, 99.97% availability, and up to 98.1% accuracy in detecting anomalies. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework to provide a highly secure and intelligent monitoring and control system for fuel station systems. This study provides a highly secure and intelligent monitoring and control system for fuel station systems. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides a highly secure and intelligent monitoring and control system for safety-critical industrial IoT applications.

title: Cybersecurity Intelligence: A Foundation Model for Proactive Network Defense
authors: Ajay Khampariya
abstract: This paper presents a foundational model engineered to bolster cybersecurity posture through advanced network traffic intelligence. Recognizing the escalating complexity of cyber threats and the limitations of traditional anomaly detection, we introduce a novel deep learning architecture that extracts profound, actionable insights from raw network flow data. This model is specifically designed to overcome challenges posed by encrypted traffic and diverse attack vectors, enabling the identification of subtle indicators of compromise. By providing a comprehensive understanding of network behavior, our solution empowers real-time threat analysis, accelerates intrusion detection, and strengthens overall cyber resilience against sophisticated and evolving digital adversaries.

title: Cybersecurity, Network Security, and Privacy: A Theoretical Evaluation
authors: Ahmet Ertuğrul; Kadir Süzme
abstract: Digital transformation has dissolved the boundaries on which conventional network security was built. Cloud platforms, remote work, mobile endpoints, and the Internet of Things have turned organizational networks into distributed, hyper-connected ecosystems in which the perimeter-based “castle-and-moat” model can no longer separate trusted from untrusted entities. Once inside such a perimeter, adversaries exploit implicit trust to move laterally, and they increasingly use algorithmic tools to automate reconnaissance and attack. At the same time, defensive architectures that depend on pervasive monitoring collide with legal and ethical obligations to protect communication privacy. Within the context of algorithmic transformation, this chapter offers a theoretical evaluation of cybersecurity, network security, and privacy. Drawing on recent literature, standards, and national and international governance frameworks, it examines three interrelated themes: the shift from perimeter defense to Zero Trust Architecture and its operationalization through microsegmentation in virtualized, containerized, and multi-cloud environments; the role of network observability, deep packet inspection, and Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems in correlating distributed telemetry; and the dilemma between comprehensive end-to-end monitoring and the preservation of privacy. The analysis shows that continuous verification, least privilege, and an assume-breach posture cannot be enforced through static rules alone; their practical viability depends on artificial intelligence and machine learning that establish behavioral baselines, adjust trust dynamically, synthesize segmentation policies, and orchestrate automated responses through SIEM, Extended Detection and Response (XDR), and Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms. The chapter treats privacy as an architectural design constraint rather than a regulatory burden and discusses how Privacy by Design, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, and federated learning can reconcile intelligent defense with data protection. Its central contribution is a conceptual reconciliation of the security-privacy trade-off: by shifting from payload inspection to encrypted traffic analysis and endpoint-centric telemetry, organizations can retain the visibility that Zero Trust requires without breaking end-to-end encryption. For security governance, this implies that cybersecurity must become a continuous, identity-driven organizational capability. The chapter also identifies the need for empirical validation against adversarial evasion and for explainable, auditable autonomous defense, and it outlines future research on autonomous policy synthesis, post-quantum Zero Trust, edge-native federated telemetry, and formal verification of defensive AI models.

title: Cybersecurity-Gated Permissions — A Pre-Query Cryptographic Admission Architecture: The Advanced Honeypot Server
authors: Lance Thomas Davidson
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Synopsis This work presents a foundational rethinking of how network security is architected at its most primitive decision point. The central thesis is not that current cybersecurity mechanisms are inadequate in isolation, but that they are all built upon a deeply entrenched structural assumption that has never been fundamentally challenged: the assumption that a system must first acknowledge and engage an incoming party before determining whether that party is legitimate. The paper argues that, across decades of technological evolution—from packet filters to stateful firewalls, next-generation inspection systems, intrusion detection platforms, and even modern zero-trust architectures—the same underlying flaw persists. Every defensive layer operates only after a connection has already been initiated. In effect, the defender is always reacting to a conversation that has already begun, which inherently grants the attacker an asymmetric advantage. The attacker expends negligible effort to initiate contact, while the defender must allocate computational resources, maintain state, and process incoming data simply to determine whether the interaction should have occurred at all. The proposed architecture, referred to as Certificate-Authority-Gated Port Stratification (CAGPS), seeks to relocate this decision point entirely. Rather than filtering or analyzing traffic after it arrives, the system enforces a cryptographic admission requirement that must be satisfied before any meaningful interaction with the protected service can occur. In this paradigm, the defended host does not respond, reject, or even acknowledge unauthorized traffic. It behaves as though it does not exist to any party that has not been cryptographically validated in advance. This relocation fundamentally alters the nature of network interaction. Every port on the system becomes an independent cryptographic entity governed by its own authority. Access is no longer determined by packet inspection or behavioral analysis but by a pre-established trust relationship verified through certificate-based challenge-response mechanisms. Only clients that can successfully complete this cryptographic admission process are permitted to interact with the real service. All other traffic is silently redirected to what the paper terms a “veneer host.” This veneer is not a traditional honeypot in the conventional sense. It is not deployed as a decoy alongside the real system in hopes of diverting some fraction of malicious activity. Instead, it becomes the default reality presented to all unauthorized actors. From the attacker’s perspective, the veneer is indistinguishable from the genuine service. It responds correctly, behaves plausibly, and exposes a full operational surface. However, it is entirely decoupled from the true system’s internal state, data, and operational pathways. This inversion is one of the most significant conceptual contributions of the paper. Traditional honeypots are probabilistic tools; they rely on the chance that an attacker will interact with them instead of the real system. The proposed architecture eliminates probability from the equation. Unauthorized users never reach the real system under any circumstance. There is no competition between real and decoy assets because the decoy is the only accessible surface for unauthenticated traffic. The implications of this shift are extensive. It collapses the conventional attack surface by removing the attacker’s ability to probe, fingerprint, or interact with the genuine system. Techniques such as banner grabbing, version enumeration, and exploit targeting become meaningless because all observable responses originate from the veneer. Even highly sophisticated reconnaissance yields intelligence that is structurally disconnected from the real environment. The architecture also redefines the role of existing technologies. Public key infrastructure, which is traditionally used to authenticate identity within an already established connection, is repositioned as the gatekeeper of whether a connection may exist at all. Similarly, protocols like TLS are no longer responsible for initiating trust during communication but operate only after trust has been cryptographically established at a prior stage. A formal stratification model is introduced to support this framework, dividing system interaction into four ordered layers: admission, communication channel establishment, service execution, and data storage. The critical constraint is that each layer must only activate after the preceding one has been successfully resolved. This ensures that no part of the system’s internal logic or resources is exposed before cryptographic validation has occurred. Beyond the technical architecture, the paper explores broader consequences for cybersecurity theory and operations. It reframes deception not as a probabilistic contest between attacker detection and defender obfuscation, but as a structural guarantee in which the attacker is permanently confined to an artificial environment. It transforms incident response from reactive damage assessment into controlled observation of contained adversary behavior. It also alters the economics of cyberattacks by ensuring that reconnaissance and exploitation efforts yield no actionable return against the real system. In essence, the work argues that the longstanding paradigm of “defend after engagement” must be abandoned in favor of “validate before existence.” By relocating the admission decision to a cryptographic layer that precedes all interaction, the architecture eliminates the attacker’s ability to ever meaningfully reach the protected system without authorization. The result is not an incremental improvement in security, but a categorical shift in how exposure, interaction, and trust are defined within networked systems.

title: DAFEX P80-k3: A Statistically Filtered Android System-Call Dataset for Behavioral Malware Analysis
authors: Faseela M H; Manjith Baby Chellam
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: DAFEX P80-k3 is a statistically filtered Android system-call dataset generated using the Direction-Aware Feature EXceedance (DAFEX) framework. The dataset corresponds to the P80 percentile threshold and k=3 voting configuration reported in the associated DAFEX study. The source dataset used in the study contains 5,820 Android application traces, comprising 2,473 benign and 3,347 malicious samples. Under the P80-k3 configuration, DAFEX identifies and filters 671 benign-labeled samples whose observed system-call behavior exhibits statistically malware-like characteristics. The resulting processed dataset contains 5,149 application traces, comprising 1,802 benign and 3,347 malicious samples. DAFEX uses interpretable statistical and behavioral characteristics of system-call traces together with direction-aware percentile thresholding and a k-of-n voting mechanism. The filtering procedure is designed to improve dataset integrity and behavioral class separability without redefining the original ground-truth labels. The underlying Android system-call traces originate from the publicly available Android Malware Detection dataset maintained by Akhilesh64:https://github.com/Akhilesh64/Android-Malware-Detection The original system-call data collection is not claimed as a contribution of DAFEX. This release provides the processed dataset corresponding to the selected P80-k3 configuration, together with supporting metadata for transparency and verification. Associated publication:Faseela, M. title: Darknet Traffic Analysis: A Machine Learning Based AI-Powered for Traffic Classification System
authors: Thandu Chandu Kollu Sai Tejaswi; D. Sandhya Rani Rahul Pajjuri
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
abstract: This paper presents Darknet Traffic Analysis, a machine learning-based system designed to classify and distinguish Onion Service traffic from standard Tor traffic using encrypted network metadata. The system leverages features such as packet size, timing, and traffic direction to identify unique patterns without accessing payload data. By integrating multiple machine learning algorithms including Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest, and an extended AdaBoost model, the framework evaluates performance across original Tor datasets, modified WTFPAD datasets, and Onion Service traffic datasets. The study addresses challenges related to traffic obfuscation techniques such as padding, dummy bursts, and traffic splitting, and analyzes their impact on classification accuracy and robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system achieves classification accuracy exceeding 99% under standard conditions, with controlled performance degradation under modified traffic scenarios. By highlighting the practical application of machine learning for encrypted traffic analysis, this work contributes to network security by enabling effective identification and monitoring of potentially malicious Onion Services..

title: DarkVortex OT: A Hybrid Behavioral–Contextual Sensor for Predictive Detection of Advanced Cyberattacks in Industrial OT Networks
authors: José Israel Nadal Vidal
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Industrial Operational Technology (OT) environments present unique and critical cybersecurity challenges due to their strict availability requirements, deterministic operational patterns, legacy protocols designed without security considerations, and limited tolerance for intrusive security controls. Traditional Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) deployed in OT networks rely primarily on signature-based or static rule-based approaches, which demonstrate significant limitations: they frequently fail to detect early-stage reconnaissance and lateral movement activities, produce excessive false positives when exposed to atypical but legitimate industrial traffic patterns, and lack the predictive capabilities necessary to prevent sophisticated multi-stage attacks before they reach critical impact phases. This paper presents DarkVortex OT, a novel hybrid behavioral–contextual sensor specifically designed for real-time detection, prediction, and classification of advanced cyberattacks in industrial control system networks. The proposed system integrates five key technological components: (1) passive network traffic capture with zero operational interference, (2) window-based behavioral feature aggregation extracting 47 distinct temporal and statistical characteristics, (3) a four-stage machine learning pipeline combining histogram-based gradient boosting, random forests, and support vector machines for progressive threat refinement, (4) adaptive evidence gating mechanisms that substantially reduce false positive rates compared to traditional approaches, and (5) comprehensive contextual interpretation aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK for ICS framework, providing SOC operators with actionable threat intelligence mapped to specific adversary tactics and techniques. The sensor operates entirely in memory without persistent storage requirements during active operation, requires no active interaction with industrial devices, supports protocol-agnostic analysis across heterogeneous OT environments (Modbus, DNP3, IEC 104, OPC UA, BACnet, and proprietary protocols), and integrates seamlessly with existing Security Operations Center (SOC) workflows through standard interfaces including Syslog, SNMP, REST APIs, and SIEM connectors. Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates consistently strong performance across multiple dimensions. Validation using the X-IIoTID benchmark dataset (1,847,623 labeled samples spanning 18 attack categories and 14 days of continuous operation) achieved a Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under Curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.985, indicating highly discriminative capability between normal operational behavior and malicious activity. The system maintains 97.3% overall detection accuracy with a precision of 95.8% and recall of 96.5%, while sustaining a false positive rate of 2.1% - representing a statistically significant 92.3% reduction (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) compared to signature-based baseline systems. Live traffic validation in a 30-day industrial testbed deployment demonstrated robust detection of all tested attack scenarios including network reconnaissance, exploitation attempts, and lateral movement patterns, with detection latency under 5 minutes and an operational unconfirmed alert rate of 0.067 per day. Performance benchmarks conducted using tcpreplay to replay captured industrial traffic at controlled rates demonstrated sustained processing capability of 1 Gbps synthetic traffic with average per-window latency of 4.2ms (±1.1ms std) using commodity hardware (Intel Xeon E-2288G, 8 cores, 32GB RAM), enabling cost-effective deployment in resource-constrained industrial environments. The primary contributions of this research include: (1) a novel multi-stage predictive architecture that separates anomaly detection from threat interpretation, reducing alert fatigue while maintaining sensitivity to emerging threats, (2) comprehensive validation demonstrating superior performance compared to existing commercial and open-source OT security solutions, (3) operational deployment guidelines based on real-world industrial testbed experience, and (4) an open discussion of limitations and future research directions for adaptive adversarial robustness and encrypted traffic analysis. This publication describes a proprietary system. The implementation, source code, trained models, datasets, and deployment configurations of DarkVortex OT are not publicly released and remain the intellectual property of the authors. This work is published for scientific dissemination purposes only.

title: Data Extraction Sheet for Systematic Review: Machine Learning Applications for IoT Intrusion Detection (Manuscript network-4470849)
authors: Majed Alzahrani; Priyadarsi Nanda; Manoranjan Mohanty; Farag El Zegil
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Structured data-extraction sheet for the 38 method papers synthesised in Table 7 of the systematic review "Machine Learning Applications for IoT Intrusion Detection: Network Dependencies, Dataset Limitations, and Regulatory Compliance—A Systematic Review" (manuscript network-4470849, submitted to Network, MDPI). Extracted per PRISMA 2020 items 9 and 10a/10b: bibliographic identifier, lead author and year, full citation, method family, application focus, gap addressed, dataset(s) used, validation approach, and QA1–QA4 quality-assessment scores. Extraction was performed by the lead author into a spreadsheet template piloted on five randomly selected full-text candidates before extraction of the full corpus began. A second reviewer independently re-extracted a random 20% sample of included studies; inter-rater agreement on structured fields reached 92%, with remaining disagreements resolved through discussion. The QA1–QA4 scores reproduced here are drawn from the independently-validated post-hoc reconstruction deposited separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22143353; this dataset combines those scores with the full extraction fields for convenience. The 8 non-method-paper included studies (foundational, methodological, and survey references) are not method-family-classified in the same way and are not included as rows here. Fields marked "n/r" indicate the detail was not specified in the reviewed evidence.

title: Data Selection Effects on Self-Supervised Learning of Audio Representations for French Audiovisual Broadcasts
authors: Valentin Pelloin; Lina Bekkali; Réda Dehak; David Doukhan
venue: International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation
abstract: Audio and speech self-supervised encoder models are now widely used for a lot of different tasks. Many of these models are often trained on clean segmented speech content such as LibriSpeech. In this paper, we look into how the pretraining datasets of such SSL (Self-Supervised Learning) models impact their downstream results. We build a large pretraining corpus of highly diverse TV and Radio broadcast audio content, which we describe with automatic tools. We use these annotations to build smaller subsets, which we use to train audio SSL models. Then, we evaluate the models on multiple downstream tasks such as automatic speech recognition, voice activity and music detection, or speaker recognition. The results show the potential of pretraining SSL models on diverse audio content without restricting it to speech. We also perform a membership inference attack to evaluate the encoder ability to memorize their training datasets, which highlight the importance of data deduplication. This unified training could bridge speech and music machine learning communities.

title: DDOS Attack Classification With Hyperparameter Tuning And Enhanced Prediction Technique
authors: A. Hemlathadhevi; C. Jackulin; C. Ramesh Kuma; T. Ani Bernish; V. Anitha; Dr.P. Deepa
abstract: Cyber-Physical Production Systems (CPPS) are integral components of Industry 4.0, enabling seamless integration between computational and physical processes. However, the interconnected nature of CPPS makes them vulnerable to cybersecurity threats, such as Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks. The technologies utilized are Machine Learning Algorithms, Rule-Based Systems, Networking Tools and Protocols, Programming Languages and Platforms, Scikit-learn, TensorFlow, or Py-Torch for model development. The current or existing model has only binary classification indicating malicious and normal attacks. And various strategies, including machine learning (ML) techniques, have been employed for DDoS attack detection. Notable approaches include deep learning models, ensemble methods, and feature selection techniques. But this existing model does not store the result logs for future reference. While these methods achieve reasonable accuracy, they often struggle with issues like class imbalance, scalability, and real-time adaptability. In the other hand the model that is being proposed works to enhance DDoS attack multi classification through suitable trained and tested datasets using LGBM algorithm. Here it would classify the normal and malicious attacks into various types of attacks such as DDOS attack, HTTP attack, traffic detection etc. A Flask-based web application for data upload and result display. Designing a database to store results and logs in file format for future use and enhancement. It operates with an average time complexity of O(log n) for both training and inference, making them highly efficient for real-time DDoS detection. The system demonstrates high classification performance, with precision and recall exceeding 99%, while maintaining a computationally efficient structure suitable for real-time implementation.

title: Decryption at the Edge: eBPF-Assisted TLS Insight for Enhanced DPI
authors: Puran Chand; Jyoti Grover; Meenakshi Tripathi; Kruttidipta Samal; Amit Yadav
venue: 2026 International Conference on Intelligent Computing, Networks, and Security (IC-ICNS)
abstract: The modern network communication is secured by the Secure Socket Layer (SSL) and Transport Layer Security (TLS), but their encryption systems are also widely used by adversaries to hide malicious activity within encrypted traffic. Current countermeasures typically rely on invasive Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) based countermeasures or machine-learning based countermeasures which are not very reliable due to lack of contextual information as the traffic is encrypted. In this paper, we suggests a host-based passive detection tool which uses Extended Berkeley Filter (eBPF) to entirely instrument TLS libraries and intercept the decrypted traffic at the endpoint. The architecture requires no change of network routes or topology and avoids the risks of decryption at intermediate devices so that privacy is never compromised. We present the basics of the SSL/TLS, explain how eBPF provides lightweight instrumentation in the user-space with user probes and outline the architecture of the system. Our assessments reveal that eBPF provides privacy-preserving visibility of encrypted sessions without any change in application behavior or network components with minimal resource consumption.

title: Deep and Parallel Network-in-Network (NIN) Model for Encrypted Network Traffic Classification
authors: K. Rambabu KADALI NAVEEN
venue: International Journal of Data Science and IoT Management System
abstract: The exponential growth of internet usage and cloud-based services has led to a dramatic increase in encrypted network traffic. While encryption ensures privacy and security, it also introduces challenges in monitoring, managing, and classifying network traffic efficiently. Traditional methods for traffic classification, such as port-based or payload inspection, are increasingly ineffective due to widespread encryption, dynamic port allocation, and evolving network protocols. Machine learning techniques, especially deep learning models, have emerged as a powerful solution to address these challenges by automatically learning discriminative patterns from traffic features without requiring manual inspection.In this study, we propose a hybrid approach combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and a parallel Deep Network-in-Network (NIN) model to classify encrypted network traffic into distinct categories. The system leverages statistical features extracted from packet-level data, which are preprocessed using standard scaling and label encoding techniques to convert categorical features into numerical representations. The CNN model acts as a baseline, providing a standard deep learning approach for traffic classification, whereas the NIN model introduces micro neural networks that perform local feature extraction and capture complex hierarchical patterns in the traffic data.The GUI-based implementation using Tkinter provides a user-friendly interface to upload datasets, preprocess data, train models, evaluate performance, and make predictions on new traffic data. Performance metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, are calculated to assess model effectiveness. Additionally, confusion matrices visualize the classification results, enabling better interpretability.Experimental results indicate that the parallel deep NIN model outperforms the standard CNN in terms of accuracy and robustness, highlighting its capability to extract complex patterns from encrypted traffic features. The approach demonstrates significant potential in real-time network monitoring and intrusion detection systems, enabling organizations to classify encrypted traffic efficiently without compromising privacy. Furthermore, the framework is scalable and adaptable, allowing integration with new datasets and evolving network protocols.Overall, this research contributes a novel methodology for encrypted traffic classification by combining deep learning techniques with practical GUI-based implementation, providing both high performance and usability for cybersecurity applications.

title: Deep Learning Approaches for Network Intrusion Detection Systems: Architectures, Challenges, and Future Directions
authors: N. RIGANA FATHIMA; D. Murugan
abstract: To adapt the increasing scope and complexity of attacks against digital infrastructure, Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) must be used to detect intrusions into a network. Traditional signature-based and rule-based IDS work effectively against known attacks, but they fail to detect new or more complex types of attacks. Recent breakthroughs in Deep Learning (DL) technologies enable an IDS to automatically detect complex patterns, allowing the system to accurately detect attacks (previously unknorwn). This research article investigates various contemporary DL-based IDS architectures (e.g. CNN, RNN, LSTM, and Hybrid models) and provides performance comparisons with other traditional IDS methods using standardized benchmark datasets. The author discusses some key issues of managing encrypted traffic, evasion tactics, and scalability when deploying IDS within large networks. Future research areas identified by the Author include creating AI with Explainable AI to improve Understanding and Reliability, and developing Lightweight Models suitable for Internet of Things (IoT) environments. The outcome exhibits the deep learning is important to contribute in the innovation of intrusion detection. Due to this impact, researchers have the privilege to work on flexible, resilient, and intelligent cyber security solutions.

title: Deep Learning for Cyberattack and Anomaly Detection in Industrial Control System Time Series on HAI 23.05
authors: Douglas Felipe Lima Silva
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 This preprint presents a controlled and reproducible comparison of four deep-learning approaches for cyberattack and anomaly detection in multivariate Industrial Control System (ICS) time series using the HAI 23.05 security dataset. The evaluated approaches comprise a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN), a long short-term memory network (LSTM), a convolutional autoencoder, and a convolutional variational autoencoder (VAE). The experimental design preserves a strict held-out evaluation protocol. HAI train1–train3 are used for normal-only reconstruction training, HAI train4 is used for normal validation and reconstruction-threshold calibration, HAI test1 is repurposed exclusively as supervised development data, and HAI test2 is reserved for final evaluation without use for model fitting, early stopping, threshold calibration, or model selection. 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 The study evaluates model behavior using complementary window-level, event-level, range-aware, and computational metrics, including: • Average Precision (AP)• ROC-AUC• F1 score• Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)• precision and recall• false-positive rate (FPR)• accuracy and balanced accuracy• attack-event recall• mean detection delay• enhanced time-series-aware precision and recall (eTaPR)• training and inference measurements Temporal windows contain 60 observations with a stride of 30 samples over 86 numeric process/control features. 𝗠𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 On 7,679 held-out HAI test2 windows, the convolutional autoencoder obtained the highest window-level F1 score (0.4380), MCC (0.4487), and Average Precision (0.3251). The VAE showed a similar reconstruction-based profile, with an F1 score of 0.4269. The CNN1D detector achieved the highest attack-event recall (0.9474) and the shortest mean detection delay (15.83 s), but this behavior was accompanied by a high window-level false-positive rate (0.6771) and low enhanced time-series-aware precision (eTaP = 0.031). The results highlight a complementary operational trade-off between broad temporal event coverage and more selective, range-precise anomaly alarms under the evaluated protocol. title: Deep Learning Framework for Prior Identification of Threats in Social Media Interactions
authors: Nageswararao Sirisala; Srinivasulu Sirisala; Anitha Yarava
abstract: Social Media Interactions are digital platforms that enable users to create profiles, connect with others, and interact through various forms of communication.These platforms facilitate social interaction, content sharing, and collaboration across geographical boundaries.Threats in Social media interactions refer to risks and malicious activities that exploit vulnerabilities in online platforms, posing harm to users, data, and digital ecosystems.These threats can impact personal security, privacy, and overall platform trustworthiness.The Deep Learning-Based Framework for Prior Identification of Threats (DLPIT) is designed to proactively detect and mitigate harmful content in social media interactions, such as hate speech, cyberbullying, and violent language, before they escalate.By leveraging a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), which is particularly effective for sequential data processing, the system analyzes Twitter language and classifies information as either harmful or non-threatening.The framework is trained on a preprocessed labeled Twitter dataset that incorporates both textual and behavioral data, ensuring comprehensive threat detection.The RNN's ability to capture contextual relationships and temporal dependencies enables DLPIT to monitor social media platforms in real time with high efficiency.Furthermore, the framework enhances detection accuracy by integrating social network interactions and user engagement patterns, which help in identifying the potential influence and reach of harmful content.To quantify the severity of a detected threat, the system calculates a Threat Level Score (TLS) based on multiple factors, including the intensity and frequency of harmful words, user history, past engagement patterns, and the influence of the content within the social network.A higher TLS signifies a greater risk, enabling moderators to prioritize intervention and take necessary actions accordingly.The performance of DLPIT is rigorously evaluated and compared with existing methods using F1-score, recall, accuracy, and precision.

title: Deep Learning Latency Attacks and Defenses: A Cross-Domain Survey of Availability Threats
authors: Zonghua Gu; Zeyu Gao; Amin Saremi; Samarjit Chakraborty
abstract: Adversarial machine learning has focused mainly on integrity, but availability is an increasingly consequential complement. Latency attacks (also energy-latency attacks) increase inference-time work, energy, or response time, causing deadline misses, throughput collapse, or resource exhaustion in vehicle controllers, interactive services, or battery-powered sensors, sometimes while preserving the nominal prediction. This survey unifies a fragmented literature spanning perception pipelines (including physical attacks on autonomous-driving detection and tracking), input-adaptive neural inference (sponge examples, dynamic networks), and autoregressive and agentic systems (output-length, verbose-image, and reasoning denial-of-service attacks on LLMs, VLMs, mixture-of-experts models, and tool-using agents). We organize attacks by exploited computational bottleneck rather than formulation, separating what makes a computation expensive from how the attacker triggers it; the delivery channel (input, prompt or retrieved content, message, poisoning, or weight tampering) is an orthogonal attribute. Many attacks share one mechanism, intermediate-work amplification, motivating a work-budget defense abstraction; we distinguish caps on the work entering an expensive stage from caps on the results leaving it. We further analyze when a model-level cost increase becomes a system-level availability failure, which depends on critical-path share, slack, existing ceilings, accumulation, resource sharing, and fallback policy, not on the amplification factor alone. We also provide a threat-model taxonomy, consolidated quantitative comparisons, a defense review by control mechanism, and open challenges such as standardized evaluation, physical realizability, and whole-system availability. Companion website: https://github.com/guzonghua/awesome-latency-attacks.

title: Deep learning models for malware traffic detection and classification: a focus on pruning and hyperband for resource optimization
authors: Sanette Penelao Sheetekela
venue: Open University of Cape Town (University of Cape Town)
abstract: Network traffic encryption is increasingly being adopted as the norm for communication technologies because of its capacity to protect privacy. Conversely, concealing data from unintended recipients presents an additional issue in the communication system, as encrypted data makes it challenging to detect malware using traditional methods such as deep packet inspection. Deep learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful technique for detecting malware in encrypted traffic flows. However, their high processing needs make it hard to use them in places with limited resources, such as Internet of Things (IoT) and edge devices. This study investigated the effectiveness of post-training weight and neuron pruning on three DL models—Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), One-dimensional convolutional Neural Networks (1D-CNN), and Long Short-term Memory Networks (LSTM)—to optimize resource usage while maintaining detection accuracy. In addition, the study integrated Hyperband, a resource-efficient hyperparameter tuning method that dynamically allocates computational resources based on intermediate performance evaluations to enhance pruned models. The CTU-13 dataset was used to assess how pruning rates influence detection performance and resource efficiency, with an emphasis on the trade-offs introduced by weight pruning (WP) and neuron pruning (NP). Our findings revealed that moderate pruning of 20% to 40% maintained or improved model accuracy while decreasing the model size by up to 40%, inference time by 30%, and memory usage by 10%. Among the models, 1D-CNN consistently provided the optimal balance between performance and computational efficiency. Regarding pruning techniques, structured neuron pruning (NP) has proven to be the most effective method, achieving significant reductions in model size and memory usage without compromising on detection performance. In contrast, unstructured weight pruning (WP) primarily reduced the number of active weights in the model by setting them to zero, which helped lower memory usage during processing; however, no compression was applied to the actual file size. Overall, the findings showed that adaptive tuning, when combined with pruning, offers an effective approach for building high-performing lightweight models that can be implemented in resource-constrained environments for encrypted malware traffic flow classification.

title: Deep Learning Techniques for Dark Web Crawling: A Comprehensive Survey for Threat Intelligence
authors: Asjad Amin; Momna Rehman; Sana Younis; Kishwar Ishfaq
