title: Making MLLMs Blind: Adversarial Smuggling Attacks in MLLM Content Moderation
authors: Zhiheng Li; Zongyang Ma; Yu Pan; Zi-Qi Zhang; Xiao Lv; Bo Li et al.
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly being deployed as automated content moderators. Within this landscape, we uncover a critical threat: Adversarial Smuggling Attacks. Unlike adversarial perturbations (for misclassification) and adversarial jailbreaks (for harmful output generation), adversarial smuggling exploits the Human-AI capability gap. It encodes harmful content into human-readable visual formats that remain AI-unreadable, thereby evading automated detection and enabling the dissemination of harmful content. We classify smuggling attacks into two pathways: (1) Perceptual Blindness, disrupting text recognition; and (2) Reasoning Blockade, inhibiting semantic understanding despite successful text recognition. To evaluate this threat, we constructed SmuggleBench, the first comprehensive benchmark comprising 1,700 adversarial smuggling attack instances. Evaluations on SmuggleBench reveal that both proprietary (e.g., GPT-5) and open-source (e.g., Qwen3-VL) state-of-the-art models are vulnerable to this threat, producing Attack Success Rates (ASR) exceeding 90%. By analyzing the vulnerability through the lenses of perception and reasoning, we identify three root causes: the limited capabilities of vision encoders, the robustness gap in OCR, and the scarcity of domain-specific adversarial examples. We conduct a preliminary exploration of mitigation strategies, investigating the potential of test-time scaling (via CoT) and adversarial training (via SFT) to mitigate this threat. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhihengli-casia/smugglebench.

title: Mal4Sight
authors: WAHIDUL ISLAM ZIAD; OMOR FARUQ; Abdur Rahman Galib
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Our Mal4Sight dataset contains a set of executable files converted into grayscale images for researching image-based malware detection. The dataset includes 16,019 samples, comprising 11,971 malware samples from 35 families and 4,048 benign samples. Each executable file is divided into distinct sections: .text, .data, other and header. Each section is turned into a grayscale image of 256 x 256 pixels with byte-level structural patterns. The dataset is organised into training, validation, and testing subsets with set splits for both malware and benign samples. Each family folder contains multiple sample folders, each folder representing a malware executable. Every sample folder contains four grayscale images. Benign files do not belong to any malware family. For this reason, the benign directory does not contain family-wise subfolders. Instead, it contains sample folders, each of which stores the four grayscale section images of a benign executable. The naming conventions for the section images for both malware and benign files in our dataset are: header.png, text.png, data.png, and .other.png. The train directory contains 8,291 malware samples and 2,833 benign samples. The val directory contains 1,833 malware samples and 607 benign samples. The test directory contains 1,847 malware samples and 608 benign samples. In total, the dataset contains 64,076 grayscale images generated from 16,019 samples, of which 11,971 are malware and 4,048 are benign files. All images are stored in PNG format to keep consistent quality. This dataset can be used to train and evaluate machine learning and deep learning models for malware detection. It also supports tasks such as feature extraction, pattern analysis, and comparisons of image-based methods across various malware families. A metadata.xlsx file is included with the dataset and contains detailed information about the images, including file_id, class, section, split, family, image_path, width, channels, dtype, preprocessing, and is_valid fields. The dataset also includes: A list of the names of all 35 malware families Raw numerical data for branch contribution analysis Source code for the Baseline CNN and ResNet training pipelines PE parsing code with a fallback mechanism included. For additional information, visit https://github.com/WAHIDUL-ISLAM/Malware_Detection_Using_Image_Processing

title: Malicious Command Line Detection
authors: Emilie Coote; Taylor Perkins; Brian Lachine; Chandra Majumdar
abstract: Given the significant amount of encrypted traffic used in enterprise environments, host-based monitoring is a necessity in any intrusion detection strategy. Important hostbased artifacts are the command lines executed on host systems, whether they are used for regular system operation and administration or for malicious purposes. Researchers have investigated various machine learning approaches to improve malicious command-line detection. This work sought to achieve detection capabilities comparable with contemporary research that could also be realistically used in a production SOC environment that continuously processes significant amounts of host data. The aim of this research was to develop a light weight malicious command line detector with effective detection performance that could be leveraged in a production SOC environment. This research used malicious command line samples from two open-source datasets and host-based data from two different corporate production networks. The developed solution did not require any de-obfuscation and first conducted data preprocessing using Bloom filters and fuzzy matching for efficient whitelisting, then used RoBERTa for text representation followed by k-NN clustering to identify malicious command lines. Four different experiments were conducted, including separate client and malicious combinations between training and testing to validate and demonstrate the generalization of the proposed solution. The implemented detector achieved results comparable to contemporary research, achieving F1 scores ranging from 97.9% to 99.3% when tested on enterprise production network data.

title: Malicious encrypted traffic identification model based on flow space-time features
authors: Shi Dong; Jiayin Zang; Khushnood Abbas
abstract: The rapid proliferation of encrypted traffic in modern networks presents significant challenges for security monitoring and threat detection. While encryption enhances privacy, it also provides cover for malicious activities, making traditional deep packet inspection ineffective. To address this challenge, this paper proposes an interpretable and efficient deep learning framework for malicious encrypted traffic identification. Our model integrates 1D-CNN, BiLSTM, and a lightweight self-attention mechanism to capture both spatial and temporal characteristics of network flows while providing explainable predictions through attention visualization. Unlike computationally intensive Transformer-based approaches, our method achieves an optimal balance between accuracy and efficiency, making it suitable for real-world deployment. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets (USTC-TFC2016 and CICIDS-2017) demonstrate that our model achieves high accuracy with 0.82 ms inference time per flow, outperforming state-of-the-art methods while offering transparency in decision-making for security analysts. The proposed approach not only enhances detection performance but also provides operational interpretability, bridging the gap between automated threat detection and human-in-the-loop security operations.

title: MalPDF-EFS: Enhanced Feature Set Dataset for Malicious PDF Detection (Benign, Old, and Recent Malicious Samples)
authors: Doo-Seop Choi; Taeguen Kim; BooJoong Kang; Eul Gyu Im
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: MalPDF-EFS is a sample of the feature data used in: D.-S. Choi, T. Kim, B. Kang, and E. G. Im, "Machine learning-based detection method for malicious PDF files: A temporal classification approach," Applied Soft Computing, vol. 189, Art. no. 114461, Mar. 2026, available online 23 Dec. 2025 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asoc.2025.114461). In the paper, malicious PDF files were collected from public malware repositories and the Contagio dataset, and grouped by creation date into old (created before 2020) and recent (created in 2020-2024) malicious PDF files. After comparing the groups, 12 new features were added to the basic feature set of 31 features, giving an enhanced feature set of 43 features. This dataset contains 1,000 randomly sampled PDF files for each of three groups (benign, old malicious, recent malicious), 3,000 in total, as two feature sets: FS31 (basic feature set) and FS43 (enhanced feature set). It is a sample of the experimental data, not the full dataset. Only extracted features are included; PDF files, file names, and file hashes are not. If you find this dataset useful in your research, please consider citing the article above.

title: MARSIM NMEA-level features and MANA baseline predictions for GPS spoofing detection
authors: Ilay Yavuz; Batuhan Hangun
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Derived data for the paper “Classical machine learning versus rule-based GPS spoofing detection at the NMEA level: benchmark, generalization limits, and a hybrid architecture”. marsim_features.csv: 138 features per recording, extracted from the raw NMEA 0183 sentences of all 43,320 pcap files of the MARSIM dataset, plus 8 metadata columns (file name, scenario A1/A2/A3, label, repetition index, attack parameter names and values). Features are aggregated over the full 120 s recording and cover receiver-1 navigation state, consecutive-epoch dynamics, and dual-receiver comparisons. mana_predictions.csv: predictions of the rule-based MANA detector (six methods, default thresholds) for every file, with per-method alert flags (pdm, pcc_sog, pcc_rot, pcc_height, cdm, cnm). mana_predictions_sample.csv: per-file MANA processing times for a stratified sample of 396 files, measured on an AMD Ryzen 7 5800X3D. All results in the paper can be regenerated from these files with the code at https://github.com/batuhanhangun/Marsim_ML_vs_MANA, which can also re-extract the features from the original MARSIM pcaps (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8202802).

title: Maximum Entropy Inverse RL for Cyber Attack Detection in IoT Networks
authors: Mohamed Massaoudi; Maymouna Ez Eddin
abstract: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has significantly expanded the attack surface for cyber threats, making effective intrusion detection systems (IDS) critical for network security. Traditional anomaly detection methods often struggle with high-dimensional network traffic data and evolving attack patterns. This paper presents a novel approach for cyber attack detection using Maximum Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning (MaxEnt IRL). The proposed method learns reward functions from normal network traffic patterns, enabling the identification of anomalous behaviors that deviate from expected normal operations. By leveraging the maximum entropy principle, the approach captures the underlying distribution of normal traffic states without requiring labeled attack samples during training. The study evaluates the performance with multiple attack types, including Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS), Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) poisoning, and Message Queue Telemetry Transport (MQTT) based attacks. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 91.18% accuracy, outperforming traditional machine learning approaches, deep learning methods, and other RL attack detection techniques. The results highlight the potential of MaxEnt IRL for robust and adaptive cyber attack detection in IoT environments. All the related codes and datasets publicly available at: https://github.com/Mmassaoudi-cell/maxent-irl-iot-ids.

title: MCP in Research and Practice: An Empirical Study of Academic Publications and GitHub Repositories
authors: Authors Anonymous
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: An empirical look at how the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is being adopted — in academic publications and in open-source code on GitHub. The goal is to track MCP's growth over time and characterize how people are actually using it: proposing/extending the protocol itself, studying or benchmarking it, securing it, or simply using it as a building block for something else. This project has two parallel tracks, each combining automated classification with manual annotation to validate it: publications.zip — MCP-related academic papers (sourced from https://www.lens.org/, analyzed for topics and classified by how they treat MCP. repositories.zip — MCP-related GitHub repositories, manually rated and cross-checked for annotator agreement on the same classification scheme. Shared taxonomy Both tracks classify each item (paper or repo) by how it treats MCP — is MCP the object of the work, or just the instrument used to build something else? Label Meaning proposes_extends Introduces MCP itself, or proposes a new protocol/specification/extension studies_analyzes Empirically studies, measures, characterizes, or surveys MCP (adoption, landscape, behavior) without proposing or securing it evaluates_benchmarks Builds or runs a benchmark, testbed, or comparative evaluation of MCP(-based systems) security_privacy Security/privacy **of MCP itself** (attacks on MCP servers/clients, tool poisoning, vulnerabilities, defenses) — not uses of MCP to build a security application uses_applies Uses MCP as an instrument: builds an agent/tool/application with it, or applies it to a domain problem mentions_only MCP is referenced only peripherally (background/related work) Classification is multi-label: an item can carry more than one role, with a single primary_label for the dominant one. publications.zip — literature analysis Four notebooks, meant to be run in order: Notebook What it does 1.MCP-topics-papers.ipynb Cleans abstracts (mojibake repair, markup stripping), filters to English via language detection, builds a word cloud, and discovers topics with BERTopic (sentence embeddings → UMAP → HDBSCAN clustering, with an interactive cluster map + intertopic distance map) 2.MCP-sample-roles-papers.ipynb Draws a random sample (n=257, seed=42) of the English-abstract subset for manual annotation. 3.MCP-roles-papers.ipynb Classifies every paper's title+abstract against the taxonomy above using GPT (OpenAI Structured Outputs), with a disk cache so runs resume instead of reclassifying. Cross-tabulates role × topic. Ships with a deterministic **mock backend** (`USE_MOCK = True`) so the pipeline runs end-to-end with no API calls or spend. 4.MCP-annotation-agreement-papers.ipynb Part 1: compares two annotators' manual labels on the 257-paper sample (agreement rate, Cohen's Kappa, confusion matrix, per-category agreement). Part 2: brings in the discussed-and-resolved ground truth and checks GPT's accuracy/agreement against it and against the humans. The corpus comprises 802 publications pulled from Lens.org; after dropping non-English abstracts, 773 enter the topic/role pipeline, of which 257 were manually annotated to validate GPT's labels. ### Data note: metadata removed, cached results provided instead The files in publications/data have had Abstract, Author/s, and other metadata fields stripped, so this repository doesn't redistribute copyrighted publisher content. Every row keeps its Lens ID, so any record can still be traced back to the full publication on https://www.lens.org/. Since notebooks publications/1.MCP_topics-papers.ipynb and publications/3.MCP-roles-papers.ipynb both need abstract text that no longer ships with the data, publications/cache provides the already-computed artifacts so the rest of the pipeline still reproduces end-to-end: cache/topics_cache — the saved BERTopic model (topic embeddings + c-TF-IDF weights). Notebook 1 can load it directly (BERTopic.load("cache/topics_cache", ...)) instead of recomputing embeddings from raw abstracts. cache/role_cache.json — GPT's role classifications from notebook 3, keyed by Lens ID, so re-running the notebook resumes from the cached labels instead of needing the original abstracts or new API calls. repositories — GitHub analysis Notebooks in repositories/notebooks_scripts, meant to be run in order: Notebook What it does data_collection.ipynb Collects the MCP repository corpus from the GitHub Search API and enriches it with contributor/commit counts, READMEs, and owner type. eda.ipynb Sensitivity analysis for the repo-selection thresholds, and the overlap between the three quality-filter conditions (stars/contributors/commits). RQ1.ipynb Evolution of MCP-adopting mature repositories over time. RQ2.ipynb Classifies each repo's MCP usage context with GPT, topic-models READMEs with BERTopic, and cross-tabulates usage × topic. discussion.ipynb Combines the repository and publication results (wave-split trends, repo-vs-publication heatmaps) for the paper's discussion. inter-rater.ipynb Inter-rater agreement for repository and publication annotations, plus GPT's calibration against the human gold labels. repositories/data/ - includes all the data required for end-to-end execution; the predominant ones are: File Contents Produced by mcp_repos_raw.parquet Raw GitHub Search API hits across all keyword/star/date query windows, before dedup. data_collection.ipynb unique_repos.parquet Deduplicated unique repos from the raw search hits. data_collection.ipynb filtered_repos_community_popularity_readme_ type_langdetect.parquet The final 33,319-repo corpus with detected language and cleaned/concatenated text added; used throughout `eda.ipynb`, `RQ1.ipynb`, and `RQ2.ipynb`. Ships pre-computed -- the language-detection step itself isn't part of this package -- repo_embeddings.npy Pooled sentence embeddings (all-mpnet-base-v2, chunked + mean-pooled) for the ~28K-repo RQ2 population, used for BERTopic clustering. RQ2.ipynb mcp_usage_llm_labels_final.parquet GPT's MCP-usage-context label for all 28,325 RQ2-population repos. RQ2.ipynb repo_topic_usage.csv Per-repo topic assignment + usage-context label, exported so discussion.ipynb can reload it without re-running RQ2.ipynb RQ2.ipynb gpt_sample_labels.csv GPT's MCP-usage label on the 380-repo calibration sample alongside the reconciled ground truth, used to compute agreement (Cohen's Kappa, Gwet's AC1) inter-rater.ipynb ## Setup Python 3.11. Install the dependencies used across the notebooks: pip install pandas numpy matplotlib plotly ftfy langdetect wordcloud scikit-learn sentence-transformers bertopic umap-learn hdbscan tqdm openpyxl GPT-based classification in `3.MCP-roles-papers.ipynb` additionally needs: pip install openai and an `OPENAI_API_KEY` in the environment. Leave `USE_MOCK = True` in that notebook to run the full pipeline offline with a deterministic keyword-based stand-in for GPT.

title: Mean FlowSpectrum: Enhancing Encrypted Traffic Classification via Mean-Based Similarity Correction
authors: Chanhyung Kim; Taeyun Kim; Jonghee M. Youn
abstract: As the majority of Internet traffic is now transmitted via encrypted protocols such as HTTPS, TLS 1.3, and VPNs, existing Deep Packet Inspection (DPI)-based security techniques are no longer able to operate effectively. Consequently, developing technologies capable of accurately classifying encrypted traffic without decryption is emerging as a core task in the field of network security. In this paper, Mean FlowSpectrum (Mean FS), a lightweight extension of the existing FlowSpectrum (FS) similarity rule, is proposed. Whereas FS uses only minimum distances between test samples and class spectra, Mean FS adds a class-mean consistency term to reduce errors caused by local spectral overlap. The method was evaluated with Semi-AE and Semi-2DCAE on ISCX-VPN2016, USTC-TFC2016, and a newly collected TLS 1.3/SSH attack-traffic testbed dataset. In a paired evaluation over five independent seeds, Mean FS improved macro F1-score in all six dataset–backbone combinations by 3.10–9.98 percentage points, and every paired improvement was statistically significant ( $p\lt 0.01$ ). Reducing the input size from $28\times 28$ to $16\times 16$ maintained comparable performance while improving memory efficiency, and Mean FS substantially mitigated the degradation caused by reducing the session size from $n=10$ to $n=1$ . GPU memory and inference time were measured for the model-side pipeline; end-to-end live-capture latency was outside the scope of this study. Mean FS therefore provides a lightweight extension to the FlowSpectrum decision rule. The measured results support its use as a decision-stage refinement for encrypted-traffic analysis, but operational validation with benign and mixed traffic is still required.

title: Mediterranean Cyclone Jolina: Near Real-Time Detection of Medicane Formation Using Multi-Sensor Earth Observation
authors: Giulia Panegrossi; ESA MEDICANES Project Team
abstract: Medicanes (Mediterranean hurricanes) are among the most hazardous high-impact weather systems affecting the Mediterranean basin, producing intense precipitation, severe winds, coastal flooding, and widespread socio-economic impacts in densely populated coastal regions. Recent advances in satellite Earth Observation are progressively transforming the monitoring of these tropical-like cyclones from retrospective classification toward near real-time physical characterization of their lifecycle and tropical-transition processes.This work presents the near real-time multi-sensor analysis of cyclone Jolina (March 2026), one of the most recent observational examples of medicane, according to the new medicane definition recently included in the glossary of the American Meteorological Society (https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/medicane/). According to this framework, a medicane is defined as a mesoscale Mediterranean cyclone exhibiting a warm core extending into the upper troposphere, spiral cloud bands, an eye-like structure, and a nearly symmetric surface wind circulation with maximum winds concentrated close to the storm center.Cyclone Jolina originated as a baroclinic disturbance and progressively evolved toward a compact, diabatically driven warm-core system approaching the Libyan coast. Infrared and passive microwave satellite observations revealed the transition from an asymmetric cold-core cyclone to a tropical-like structure characterized by upper-tropospheric warm-core signatures, spiral cloud organization, and enhanced rotational symmetry. Particularly remarkable was the occurrence of this tropical transition during an atypical season and under relatively cold sea surface temperature conditions, highlighting the complex interplay between upper-level dynamics and diabatic processes in medicane development.The analysis combines geostationary MSG-SEVIRI observations, passive microwave radiometry (e.g., ATMS, AMSU/MHS, as well as the newly available Arctic Weather Satellite and EPS-SG Microwave Sounder), scatterometer-derived ocean surface winds, and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) measurements from Sentinel-1A. Remarkably, near real-time cyclone tracking is provided through the DeMeTra deep-learning algorithm, which estimates the medicane rotational center every 5 minutes using SEVIRI Airmass RGB imagery sequences. Passive microwave observations around the oxygen absorption complex near 55 GHz are exploited to identify upper-tropospheric warm-core anomalies, while humidity sounding channels around 183.31 GHz are used to detect signatures of stratospheric dry-air intrusion and associated potential vorticity anomalies contributing to cyclone intensification and warm-core development.Beyond its meteorological significance, Jolina also demonstrated the substantial socio-economic relevance of Mediterranean tropical-like cyclones. Severe weather conditions triggered emergency measures across southern Italy and Libya, including school closures, transport disruption, flooding, landslides, evacuations, and even casualties. Interestingly, some of the strongest impacts occurred during the earlier stages of the cyclone, before the complete tropical transition occurred, emphasizing the importance of considering the whole lifecycle and both synoptic-scale interactions and medicane-scale processes in hazard assessment.This case study demonstrates the increasing capability of integrated multi-sensor Earth Observation systems, combined with artificial intelligence approaches, to identify and monitor medicane formation and tropical transition in near-real time. The methodologies developed within the ESA MEDICANES project provide new opportunities for operational monitoring, early warning, and improved risk assessment of Mediterranean cyclones under changing climatic conditions.

title: Method for Detecting Denial-of-Service Attacks Based on Statistical Analysis of the Temporal Dynamics of Network Traffic
authors: A. Nicheporuk; M. Prodeus; Andriy Drozd; Oleksii Lyhun; Olexandr Klein; Aleksandra Czupryna-Nowak
abstract: The article presents a methodology for network attacks of the denial of service type based on statistical indicators of network traffic, which allows identifying anomalous actions in corporate networks. Within the framework of the proposed method, a continuous flow of network traffic is segmented into time intervals, for each of which there is a two-tiered evaluation system: intra-window features capture instantaneous characteristics of the flow, in particular entropy and median packet size, while sixteen inter-window metrics capture the evolution of host behavior over time, yielding a total feature vector of thirty components (fourteen intra-window and sixteen inter-window) that enables detection of anomalous deviations in traffic dynamics. To ensure the operability of the method in conditions of highly loaded networks, streaming data processing algorithms were implemented, which allowed calculating complex statistical parameters without accumulating large amounts of information in memory. The resulting feature vectors belong to a machine learning model that classifies IP addresses as normal or malicious. In case of detection of malicious activity, a blocking rule based on iptables is formed. Experiments on the publicly available CIC-IDS2017 benchmark dataset, which includes normal traffic and HTTP-based DoS attack flows (Slowloris, Slowhttptest, Hulk, GoldenEye), showed that the approach increases detection reliability by capturing dynamic changes in traffic between time windows.

title: METHOD OF CONTEXT-DRIVEN DYNAMIC SOFTWARE SECURITY TESTING USING LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL-BASED AGENTS
authors: M. V. Maksimovich
abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence methods, in particular large language models and the agent-basedsystems built upon them, opens new opportunities for improving automated software security testing. Among the existingmethods, dynamic application security testing (DAST) is the most promising direction for such improvement, since itperforms end-to-end verification of a real running application and reflects its actual exploitable behaviour. At the sametime, classical DAST tools construct attack scenarios through stochastic enumeration based on predefined wordlists,which results in incomplete coverage and considerable resource consumption. The aim of this work is to develop a methodof context-driven dynamic software security testing based on agents built upon large language models, which increasesthe completeness of vulnerability detection and reduces the resource cost of scanning. The proposed method uses theOpenAPI specification as a source of semantic context, on the basis of which agents generate a set of end-to-end (E2E)security tests that act as a deterministic source of traffic and steer the dynamic scan through real business processes insteadof random crawling. The method provides two improvements: extended coverage of vulnerabilities that are unreachablefor signature-based scanners, and a reduced volume of redundant requests, since only the generated traffic is scanned. Avulnerability coverage model, the workflow, and the test scenario generation strategy are described, and metrics for evaluating the effectiveness of the method are defined. The results indicate the feasibility of the agent-based approach forextending coverage and improving the resource efficiency of dynamic testing, and outline the direction of furtherexperimental research.Keywords: dynamic application security testing, large language models, agent-based systems, OpenAPI, BOLA,IDOR, test automation. title: Method of formalizing a multidimensional reference subenvironment for detecting phishing URLs
authors: А. О. Корченко; Кирило ДАВИДЕНКО; М. Г. Аскеров; Ю.С. Журов
abstract: In modern cyberspace, phishing attacks remain one of the most dangerous threats to information security, due totheir scalability, low cost of implementation and high effectiveness of impact on users. The use of phishing URLs as atool of sociotechnical influence necessitates the development of formalized approaches to their detection. The aim of thework is to develop a method for formalizing a multidimensional reference subenvironment for detecting phishing URLsbased on the formalization of their characteristics within a multidimensional feature space. A set of parameters was usedto form the features, in particular Domain Age, Frequency of DNS Changes, Number of Subdomains, URL Length andHTTPS/SSL. The proposed method is based on the interval representation of parameters, the use of linguistic variablesand membership functions, which allows taking into account the uncertainty and dynamics of the characteristics ofphishing resources. The formalization of the reference subenvironment is carried out through the integration of thespecified parameters. The results of the study demonstrate that the proposed approach provides a transition from empiricalfeature analysis to formalized modeling of a multidimensional reference space suitable for detecting phishing URLs. Thiscreates a basis for increasing the accuracy of cyberthreat detection. The results obtained can be used to improve intrusiondetection systems and information protection tools aimed at countering sociotechnical attacks in modern cyberspace.Keywords: phishing, phishing detection, URLs, cyberattacks, cyberthreats, information security, intrusiondetection systems, cyberattack detection systems. title: METHOD OF GROUPING DEFECTS OF DAMAGED SOFTWARE INTO TECHNOLOGICALLY SIMILAR GROUPS
authors: Yurii Dobryshyn
abstract: The article considers the current scientific and practical problem of grouping defects of damaged software, whicharise as a result of cyberattacks, into technologically similar groups. It is substantiated that modern cyberattacks causecomplex software malfunctions, which are characterized by a high level of uncertainty, dynamic manifestation anddifferent criticality. It is determined that traditional methods of classifying defects do not provide sufficient efficiency inthe conditions of cyberincidents, since they do not take into account the variability of attack characteristics and thepossibility of partial belonging of defects to several groups at the same time. An analysis of modern scientific research inthe field of detecting, predicting and classifying software defects, as well as clustering and fuzzy logic methods used incybersecurity tasks, is carried out. A method of grouping defects of damaged software is proposed based on the use of the"dynamic kernels" method, which provides adaptive formation of groups of defects in a multidimensional feature space.The paper describes a mathematical model of defect representation, defines a system of feature weighting coefficients, and proposes a mechanism for assessing the degree of defect membership in the corresponding groups using elements offuzzy set theory. The practical testing of the method was performed on the example of grouping software defects after acyberattack by such features as the level of data integrity damage, system failures, and security system violations. Theresults of the study confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed approach for the automated formation of groups of criticaland minor defects, as well as the possibility of detecting defects with intermediate characteristics. It was established thatthe use of the "dynamic kernels" method and fuzzy grouping allows to increase the efficiency of the processes ofidentification, analysis, prediction, and recovery of damaged software in conditions of information uncertainty andchanges in the characteristics of cyberattacks.Keywords: grouping, method, software, defect, mathematical model, software recovery. title: Methodological Framework for Generating Synthetic, Balanced Datasets for Web Intrusion Detection using Automated Purple Teaming
authors: GABRIEL RODRIGUES
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The scarcity of high-quality, labeled datasets is a primary hindrance in the development of Deep Learning-based Web Application Firewalls (WAFs). Real-world traffic logs are often unavailable due to privacy regulations or lack ground-truth labels, leading to models that suffer from high false-positive rates. This technical report presents a comprehensive methodology for the generation of synthetic datasets through an automated "Purple Teaming" approach. By orchestrating a custom-developed offensive framework against a controlled ecosystem of vulnerable microservices, we establish a reproducible pipeline to capture, tokenize, and label HTTP traffic. This method ensures class balance between benign and malicious requests, covering the full spectrum of OWASP Top 10 threats, and provides a sustainable alternative to static, outdated public datasets.

title: Methodology Review: Intrusion Detection in Cybersecurity: A Study on Explainable Graphical Reinforcement Learning
authors: BS Arun Kumar; Rathnakar Achary
abstract: This paper provides a structured methodological review of intrusion detection systems (IDS) in the field of cybersecurity, with particular attention to Explainable Graph-Structured Reinforcement Learning (XGRL). Instead of presenting experimental evaluations, the study concentrates on analyzing design principles and methodological frameworks that influence IDS effectiveness, scalability, and resilience to zero-day and polymorphic attacks. The progression from traditional signature-based systems and classical machine learning techniques to deep learning approaches is examined, leading to recent graph-based and reinforcement learning–driven solutions. The role of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in capturing relational and topological characteristics of network traffic is discussed alongside reinforcement learning methods that support adaptive and sequential security decision-making. Special emphasis is placed on explainability mechanisms that enhance model transparency, analyst confidence, and regulatory alignment. The review identifies methodological trade-offs involving detection accuracy, computational cost, scalability, and interpretability. Challenges related to real-time operation, encrypted traffic, and system complexity are also analyzed. The paper concludes by outlining future research opportunities, including efficient explainable architectures, continual learning strategies, and federated graph-based reinforcement learning frameworks for scalable and privacy-aware IDS implementations.

title: MirageNet: A Containerized Multi-Service Cyber Deception Engine with Fail-Closed Egress Safeguard and Asynchronous Telemetry Architecture
authors: Devrishi Sharma; Hemant Jadhav; Shantanu Deshmukh; Dr.  Mohammad Muqueem
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Modern enterprise networks face severe threat asymmetry due to the inherent limitations of passive, perimeter-focused security tools such as intrusion detection systems, stateful inspection firewalls, and security information and event management (SIEM) aggregators. These traditional mechanisms suffer from reconnaissance blindness, remaining completely passive while automated scanning engines and malicious threat actors map host topologies, discover exposed software vulnerabilities, and execute brute-force credential sweeps. High-interaction honeypots mitigate this visibility gap by presenting full operating system environments, but introduce prohibitive hardware memory requirements (e.g., T-Pot CE requiring over 16 GB RAM) and catastrophic host-compromise risks if a container escape or outbound botnet pivot occurs. This paper presents MirageNet, an enterprise-grade, lightweight, multi-service cyber deception platform designed specifically for resource-constrained edge networks and Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). MirageNet features the asynchronous Hive Engine backend, which emulates six critical network application protocols (SSH, HTTP, FTP, SMB, MySQL, and Redis) concurrently on a single public IP footprint with an idle host memory footprint under 1.2 GB RAM and CPU usage below 5%. The platform incorporates a novel, kernel-level fail-closed watchdog sentinel that triggers instantaneous egress firewall drops if logging pipeline integrity degrades, mathematically guaranteeing zero outbound malware propagation. Furthermore, MirageNet integrates a log-normal synthetic timing delay model to counteract scanner round-trip time (RTT) fingerprinting and employs a Random Forest threat profiling engine that achieves 99.20% classification accuracy (ROC/AUC = 0.998) in distinguishing automated botnet sweeps from targeted human intrusions. Real-time telemetry is streamed via WebSockets to a React 19 dashboard, supporting full asciicast SSH terminal replay, automated MITRE ATT&CK mapping across 27 techniques, and STIX 2.1 threat intelligence exports. The platform further includes a rule-based MITRE ATT&CK detection engine with sliding-window correlation and an interpretable five-factor attacker risk score on a 0 to 100 scale, whose behavior is analyzed on synthetic attacker archetypes.

title: Mitigating Economic Denial of Sustainability (EDoS) Attacks in Cloud Computing Using an AI-Driven Cost-Aware Defense System
authors: Zubaidi Maytham Sahar Saeed; Anazida Binti Zainal; Fuad Abdulgaleel Abdoh Ghaleb
venue: Selamat Datang di Repository UAD (Universitas Ahmad Dahlan)
abstract: The pay-per-use billing model of cloud computing makes cloud infrastructures highly vulnerable to Economic Denial of Sustainability (EDoS) attacks, where adversaries exploit auto-scaling mechanisms to trigger excessive resource consumption and inflated operational costs. Existing mitigation approaches, such as rate limiting and conventional anomaly detection, struggle to accurately distinguish legitimate traffic from attack-traffic requests, often leading to false negative alarm and unnecessary financial overhead. This paper proposes a Cost-Aware Adaptive Defense System (CADS), a novel artificial intelligence-driven (AI-driven) defense system that integrates deep learning-based (DL-based) traffic classification, Trust-based resource access control, and Software-Defined Networking-based (SDN-based) traffic filtering to mitigate EDoS attacks while preserving economic sustainability. The Trust-based access control mechanism dynamically assigns trust scores to incoming requests and restricts suspicious entities from triggering auto-scaling, thereby preventing fraudulent resource allocation. The proposed defense system introduces a lightweight computational overhead of approximately 85 ms for detection and 210 ms for mitigation response, ensuring real-time protection with minimal performance impact. Experimental evaluation was conducted in an OpenStack-based simulated cloud environment, modeling multiple EDoS attack strategies, including HTTP flood, ICMP-based, and workload-based attacks. Results demonstrate that CADS achieves a detection performance such as 97.1% for (F1-score), 97.5% for Recall and 96.8 for Precision, indicates significantly reducing missed attacks and false alarm. More importantly, CADS reduces overall cloud billing costs by approximately 25% compared to state-of-the-art EDoS mitigation mechanisms, such as Advanced EDoS Attack Defense Shell (EDoS-ADS) and Multi-head Attention Network (MAN-EDoS). The results highlight the practical effectiveness of CADS in enhancing cloud security resilience while substantially lowering operational expenses for cloud service providers. Although CADS has not been tested in real-world environments, it demonstrates strong performance under simulated conditions. Future work will focus on large-scale real-world deployments and the integration of reinforcement learning techniques to adapt to evolving attack patterns.

title: ML-Based State of Polarization Analysis to Detect Emerging Threats to Optical Fiber Security
authors: Leyla Sadighi; Stefan Karlsson; Carlos Natalino; Marija Furdek
venue: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
abstract: As the foundation of global communication networks, optical fibers are vulnerable to various disruptive events, including mechanical damage, such as cuts, and malicious physical layer breaches, such as eavesdropping via fiber bending. Traditional monitoring methods often fail to identify subtle or novel anomalies, stimulating the proliferation of Machine Learning (ML) techniques for detection of threats before they cause significant harm. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) and Unsupervised Learning (USL) approaches for detecting various abnormal events, such as fiber bending and vibrations, by analyzing polarization signatures with minimal reliance on labeled data. We experimentally collect thirteen polarization signatures on three different types of fiber cable and process them using One-Class Support Vector Machine (OCSVM) as an SSL, and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) as a USL algorithm for anomaly detection. We introduce tailored evaluation metrics designed to guide hyper-parameter tuning and capture generalization over different anomaly types, detection consistency, and robustness to false positives, enabling practical deployment of OCSVM and DBSCAN in optical fiber security. Our findings demonstrate DBSCAN as a strong contender to detect previously unseen threats in scenarios where labeled data are not available, despite some variability in performance between different scenarios, with F1 score values between 0.615 and 0.995. In contrast, OCSVM, trained on normal operating conditions, maintains high F1 scores of 0.98 to 0.998, demonstrating accurate detection of complex anomalies in optical networks.

title: MLRan: A behavioural dataset for ransomware analysis and detection
authors: Faithful Chiagoziem Onwuegbuche; Adelodun Olaoluwa; Anca Delia Jurcut; Liliana Pasquale
venue: Journal of Network and Computer Applications
abstract: Ransomware remains a critical threat to cybersecurity, yet publicly available datasets for training machine learning-based ransomware detection models are scarce and often have limited sample size, diversity, and reproducibility. In this paper, we introduce MLRan, a behavioural ransomware dataset, comprising over 4800 samples across 64 ransomware families and a balanced set of goodware samples. The samples span from 2006 to 2024 and encompass the four major types of ransomware: locker, crypto, ransomware-as-a-service, and modern variants. We also propose guidelines (GUIDE-MLRan), inspired by previous work, for constructing high-quality behavioural ransomware datasets, which informed the curation of our dataset. We evaluated the ransomware detection performance of several machine learning (ML) models using MLRan. For this purpose, we performed feature selection by conducting mutual information filtering to reduce the initial 6.4 million features to 24,162, followed by recursive feature elimination, yielding 483 highly informative features. The ML models achieved an accuracy, precision and recall of up to 98.7%, 98.9%, 98.5%, respectively. Using SHAP and LIME, we identified critical indicators of malicious behaviour, including registry tampering, strings, and API misuse. The dataset and source code for feature extraction, selection, ML training, and evaluation are available publicly to support replicability and encourage future research, which can be found at https://github.com/faithfulco/mlran .

title: Model Web Application Firewall Berbasis Machine Learning untuk Mencegah Serangan Siber
authors: Joseray Arimateia Lopes DA CRUZ
venue: Repository Universitas Katolik Widya Mandira (Universitas Katolik Widya Mandala)
abstract: Web applications serve as the main operational foundation of various strategic sectors, yet their vulnerability to cyberattacks poses a severe threat to data security. Conventional defense mechanisms often struggle to mitigate increasingly complex new attack variations. Previous research has extensively utilized Natural Language Processing (NLP) approaches, which entail high computational complexity, making them less optimal for real-time implementation. The objective of this research is to identify the most significant features using the Feature Importance with Random Forest algorithm and to compare the performance of Tree-Based Classifiers (Decision Tree, Random Forest, GBM, and XGBoost) in classifying HTTP traffic using CSIC 2010 dataset. Evaluation using Stratified K-Fold Cross Validation and Hyperparameter Tuning demonstrated that the Random Forest model was the most superior overall, achieving an F1-score of 92.71% and a Recall of 94.95% at K-Fold = 7, despite requiring a computation time of 289.76 seconds. Conversely, XGBoost offered the best compromise with an F1-score of 92% and an execution time of only 39.45 seconds. Meanwhile, the Decision Tree model emerged as the most efficient alternative for systems prioritizing speed, with a computation time of just 2.05 seconds. Research that held proves that the non-NLP Tree-Based Classifier approach provides competitive detection performance, is lightweight, and possesses high interpretability, making it highly optimal for modern Web Application Firewall implementations.

title: Modeling an evaluation system for DDoS attack detection tools in HEI’s web resources
authors: Єлизавета ЗАВГОРОДНЯ; Yaroslav Shestak; Olena Kryvoruchko; О. М. Кулинич
abstract: This study addressed the need for a comprehensive approach to the assessment and selection of cybersecurity toolsfor protecting web resources in higher education institutions (HEIs) against modern cyber threats, particularly distributeddenial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. This study examined contemporary threats to the information security of web resourcesand justified the need for their timely identification, analysis and neutralisation in order to ensure the continuity ofinformation systems, particularly in HEIs. The academic literature review showed that traditional approaches tomonitoring and protecting information systems are inefficient in spite of modern multi-vector attacks, requiring a shifttowards integrated, adaptive and intelligent cybersecurity systems. Short-term but intense cyberattacks (e.g. DDoSincidents), can significantly disrupt service availability in the absence of proper protection measures. Additionally, wefound that effective protection of web resources requires a thorough approach that ensures the confidentiality, integrity,and availability of information, along with the ability to adapt to the changing conditions in cyber environment. A multilayered cybersecurity architecture and a hybrid DDoS detection framework were proposed. The proposed frameworkcombined signature-based, behavioural, and statistical methods to facilitate effective and modifiable threat detectionsystem. In order to support objective decision-making, a multi-criteria hierarchical evaluation model was designed. Theproposed evaluation model included nine criteria groups that were aimed at assessing technical performance, scalability,adaptability, integration capability, automation, and cost-effectiveness. The proposed method enables an organised andtransparent comparison of DDoS detection tools on specific conditions of higher research institutions.Keywords: cyber threats, SIEM systems, higher education institution web resources, DDoS attacks, cyberresilience, attack detection, provision of educational services. title: MODELS AND ALGORITHMS FOR DETECTING OBFUSCATED SQL INJECTION ATTACKS IN API REQUESTS BASED ON MULTI-SCALE HYBRID NEURAL NETWORKS AND ATTENTION MECHANISM
authors: Gayibov Islom
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In modern cloud-native and microservice information systems, data exchange is predominantly executed via REST and GraphQL Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) using structured JSON and XML payloads. However, SQL injection (SQLi) attacks embedded within nested API requests and disguised through multi-stage obfuscation evade traditional regular-expression-based Web Application Firewalls (WAFs). This paper presents a structural decomposition model for hierarchical API requests, an information-theoretic Shannon entropy estimator for obfuscation detection, and a hybrid deep learning architecture integrating Multi-Scale 1D Convolutional Neural Networks (MS-1D-CNN), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM), and a Bahdanau Attention mechanism. Character-level embedding is utilized to eliminate out-of-vocabulary (OOV) vulnerabilities, while class imbalance is mitigated via Focal Loss. Furthermore, the asymptotic computational complexity of the inline filtration algorithm is formally proved, and a rigorous comparative synthesis against peer-reviewed benchmarks on the CSIC 2010 HTTP dataset is provided.

title: Modern Network Security Architectures: A Critical Review of Networking and Cyber Defence Strategies
authors: Godson Chetachi Uzoaru; C. Nwasuka Stanley; Nwamuruamu Godswill U.; Ikechuwku Miracle; Chinkere Evangel; Eke Emmanuel Amuche et al.
abstract: Network security architecture is being reshaped by cloud computing, remote and hybrid access, software-defined infrastructure, microservices, encryption, Internet of Things deployments and increasingly adaptive adversaries. These changes have weakened assumptions that a trusted internal network can be protected principally through perimeter controls, while simultaneously creating new dependencies on identity systems, policy engines, telemetry, orchestration and external security services. This critical narrative review evaluates how modern architectural families address these conditions and where their evidence remains incomplete. Literature published from 1 January 2010 to 27 June 2026 was considered, with earlier foundational studies retained where necessary. The synthesis integrates evidence on zero trust architecture, zero trust network access, microsegmentation, secure access service edge, software-defined networking, network function virtualisation, cloud-native and service-mesh security, intrusion and network detection, encrypted-traffic analytics, distributed denial-of-service defence, routing security, moving-target defence and cyber deception. The evidence supports a transition from location-based trust towards resource-, identity- and context-centred policy, but does not support treating any single architecture as a complete security solution. Zero trust is conceptually mature yet still has limited comparative evidence on enterprise outcomes and cost-effectiveness. Programmable networks improve enforcement agility and observability but concentrate control and introduce software and orchestration attack surfaces. Cloud-native controls strengthen service-to-service policy while shifting risk towards workload identity, certificate lifecycle, configuration correctness and supply-chain integrity. Machine-learning-based detection can augment analysis, particularly when payload visibility is constrained, but performance remains sensitive to dataset realism, protocol drift and deployment context. Resilience against denial-of-service, routing attacks and adaptive adversaries requires layered mechanisms extending beyond access control. The strongest architectural position is therefore compositional: identity assurance, least-privilege segmentation, programmable policy enforcement, trustworthy telemetry, resilient routing and availability controls, and carefully governed automation should reinforce one another without creating unexamined central points of failure.

title: MSWD: Multi-Source Website Detection Dataset
authors: Joao Magalhaes
abstract: MSWD (Multi-Source Website Detection Dataset) is a publicly available dataset designed for research on malicious website detection and cybersecurity analytics. The dataset contains 5,013 collected URLs obtained from benign and malicious public sources. Each sample is represented by 54 predictive features extracted from multiple cybersecurity intelligence sources, including: • Lexical URL characteristics • DNS information • WHOIS metadata • Email-security indicators (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) • Website content features • HTTP security headers • Threat-intelligence indicators • URL entropy measurements • Homoglyph-based attack indicators The dataset was created to support research on phishing detection, malicious URL classification, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), feature engineering, and cybersecurity machine learning.

title: MTDecipher: robust encrypted malicious traffic detection via multi-task graph neural networks
authors: Fan Li; Xi Luo; Weihong Han; Binxing Fang; Lihua Yin
abstract: Abstract The widespread adoption of encrypted traffic protocols has significantly increased the challenge of detecting malicious traffic. Existing detection methods based on deep learning typically rely on fine-grained features of data packets, such as length sequences and intra-flow interaction graphs. However, these features are highly susceptible to disruption by diverse network environments and traffic obfuscation. This paper proposes MTDecipher, a robust method for detecting encrypted malicious traffic based on multi-task Graph Neural Network (GNN). MTDecipher employs a bidirectional attentive sequence encoder to mitigate the impact of diverse network environments and traffic obfuscation on packet length sequences, along with an edge-block dual sampling method and a multi-task GNN model to mitigate the training bias introduced by the unbalanced distribution of traffic. In the bidirectional attentive sequence encoder, a combination of a Bi-GRU layer and an attention pooling layer is utilized to enhance the bidirectional encoding by generating weights for each element in the sequence, thereby obtaining robust encrypted traffic sequence features. In the edge-block dual sampling method, two rounds of sampling are involved to generate more evenly distributed subgraphs as training data, which reduces the local structural bias resulting from the aggregation of malicious flows. In the multi-task GNN model, the losses for both edge and node classification tasks are simultaneously optimized, thereby minimizing the homogeneity of adjacent edges. Experimental results on two real-world datasets with traffic obfuscation demonstrate that MTDecipher outperforms eight existing methods in terms of effectiveness in detecting encrypted malicious traffic.

title: Multi-Dimensional Gram Fingerprinting: A Unified Spectral Geometric Framework for Adversarial Detection
authors: Xingmeng Song; Lan Yang; Yunxiang Wu
venue: International Conference on Computer Supported Cooperative Work in Design
abstract: The widespread use of deep learning models in critical applications like autonomous driving and medical diagnostics has revealed a major vulnerability: susceptibility to adversarial attacks. These attacks introduce subtle perturbations to inputs, causing significant mispredictions and posing safety risks. To address this, we propose the Multi-Dimensional Gram Fingerprinting (MDGF) framework, which leverages the spectral geometry of deep neural networks (DNNs) to detect adversarial perturbations. Unlike traditional methods that treat feature correlations as scalar values, MDGF models the Gram matrix geometrically, analyzing its eigenvalues and eigenvectors to capture the structure of natural images. By focusing on spectral properties such as mean activation, spectral radius, and spectral Dispersion, MDGF detects adversarial examples efficiently. Our experiments show that MDGF outperforms existing methods, especially against sophisticated attacks like AutoAttack and PGD, with significant improvements in detection accuracy (AUROC). This work provides a scalable and effective solution for enhancing the robustness of deep learning models against adversarial threats, without requiring model-specific adjustments or retraining, and contributes to a more geometric approach to adversarial defense.Our code is available at: https://github.com/songky0530/MDGF

title: Multi-Layer, Explainable Phishing Detection Platform with Domain-Disjoint Evaluation: The PhishGuard Prototype
authors: Minosh Umayanga; Manuja Nirmal; Malisha Karunarathne; Sanjana VAH
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A phishing detector that combines the address, the page and the infrastructure behind a link, and that is tested on data it has never seen, is more trustworthy than a classifier that reads only the address. We present PhishGuard, a prototype that scores a link with two calibrated machine-learning models (a character n-gram URL model and a page-content model), a sandboxed behaviour analysis, domain, TLS and brand checks, and threat-feed lookups. A risk engine merges the evidence under per-layer caps into a 0 to 100 score and a plain-language list of reasons. We evaluate the system end to end on 200 fresh phishing URLs and 200 legitimate sites that were excluded from training and tuning, with the feed lookup switched off. At the phishing threshold the system reaches 70.0% recall with no false positives; at the suspicious threshold it reaches 89.5% recall with 2.5% false positives; its ROC-AUC is 0.979 against 0.924 for the URL model alone. More than a third of the phishing URLs (75 of 200) were caught through a hosting provider's own malware warning, and without them recall at the phishing threshold falls to 52.0%. We also report two traps that inflated our early results: shortcut learning in a random URL split and a network web filter whose block pages were scored as phishing content. The contribution is a design and an evaluation method, with the limits stated.

title: Multi-Modal and CNN-Based Approaches in Cybersecurity: A Comprehensive Review
authors: Trina Banerjee; Piyush NA; Mukthikka V; Gurpreet Singh
abstract: The rapid evolution of cyber threats has necessitated increasingly sophisticated detection methodologies that transcend traditional signature-based approaches. In recent years, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and multi-modal deep learning architectures have emerged as powerful paradigms for addressing diverse cybersecurity challenges, ranging from malware detection and phishing identification to network intrusion detection and encrypted traffic classification. This paper presents a comprehensive review of 50 recent research works (20222025) that leverage CNN-based and multi-modal learning techniques in the cybersecurity domain. We systematically categorize these approaches into seven distinct groups: (1)~CNN-based malware visualization and detection, (2)~CNN-based phishing and web threat detection, (3)~multi-modal and hybrid intrusion detection systems, (4)~CNN-based IoT and botnet detection, (5)~encrypted and darknet traffic classification, (6)~adversarial and GAN-based cybersecurity methods, and (7)~multi-modal cybersecurity applications. For each category, we analyze core methodologies, architectural innovations, and performance benchmarks. Furthermore, we provide detailed comparisons of datasets, evaluation metrics, and identify critical gaps in current research. Our analysis reveals that while CNN-based visualization achieves remarkable accuracy ($>$98\%) in controlled environments, significant challenges remain in adversarial robustness, cross-domain generalization, real-time deployment, and the effective fusion of heterogeneous data modalities. We conclude by outlining open challenges and future research directions that can advance the field toward more resilient, adaptive, and deployable cybersecurity systems.

title: Multi-View Fusion for Encrypted C2 Detection: A Leakage-Controlled Measurement Study of Evaluation Pitfalls
authors: Hoang-Huy Nguyen-Huu; Van-Tri Phan; Khuong Nguyen-An
abstract: Command-and-control (C2) traffic increasingly hides within TLS, so defenders now apply machine learning to traffic metadata. Many studies assume that combining two metadata views, namely flow statistics and TLS handshake fingerprints, improves both accuracy and robustness. We tested this assumption on 17,577 TLS flows from 62 real Cobalt Strike captures. Our evaluation removes the data leakage that leads to overly optimistic reported scores. We report three findings that matter more than the fusion result itself. First, an incorrect preprocessing step increases the F1 score by 0.28. This step computes the frequency encoding across the entire dataset rather than within each cross-validation fold. The increase is about ten times larger than any real effect we measured. Second, both the labels and the behavioral features depend on the destination address. Because of this, the 17,577 flows form only 2,132 independent groups, and the positive rate of 55.1\%, which looks balanced, drops to 4.2\%. Therefore, class balance is just a result of how we analyze the data, specifically whether we count flows or endpoints, and not a real feature of the task. Third, 20 of the 62 captures (32\%) have no TLS flows to any known C2 address, so they contain only benign samples. We checked these captures directly and confirmed that this is a gap in the ground truth, not a labeling error. In this context, fusion beats the best single view by only 0.022 in F1. When an attacker forges both feature surfaces simultaneously, every model performs worse than a simple baseline that always predicts positive (F1 = 0.711). For encrypted C2 detection, the evaluation design is not a preliminary step. It \emph{is} the main result.

title: Multi-view self-supervised learning for label-flipping robustness in tabular data: a comparative study
authors: Jinhyeok Jang; Sohee Park; Seung-Soo Nam; Daeseon Choi
abstract: Tabular machine learning models are widely used in high-stakes domains such as finance, healthcare, and network intrusion detection, where their reliability depends heavily on accurate training labels. However, malicious or accidental label flipping can corrupt training data and degrade downstream model performance. Recent attacks further target decision-boundary or vulnerable local regions rather than flipping labels randomly. This paper presents a BYOL-based multi-view KNN sanitization approach for identifying suspicious label-flipped samples in tabular data. The method learns label-independent representations and examines KNN label-disagreement patterns across original and perturbed SSL embedding views. We evaluate the method on six cross-domain tabular benchmarks under both large-scale and small-scale label-flipping attacks, and compare it with existing sanitization baselines and a SCARF-based representation baseline. The results show that multi-view neighborhood probing improves suspicious-label detection and provides a practical F1-oriented trade-off, while downstream recovery remains attack- and target-model-dependent. These findings provide actionable insights for improving the robustness and label integrity of tabular machine learning systems against label-flipping attacks.

title: Multimodal Phishing Detection via Image-Text Fusion and CLIP-Based Deep Learning
authors: T. Grace Shalini; S. S. Krishika Mathi Bharathi
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: The main cybersecurity risk for people and organizations comes from phishing attacks that imitate legitimate websites with remarkable visual similarity. This leads into question the robustness of traditional detection methods, which rely on either only visual or URL features, against modern phishing techniques. The proposed paper presents a multimodal phishing detection framework that includes visual and tabular modalities. The OpenAI CLIP model uses a Vision Transformer backbone to generate 512-dimensional embeddings for visual features, while tabular features encode the features regarding URL composition, HTML structure, and SSL properties. A multilayer perceptron fuses both modalities to improve classification performance and adaptability against evolving phishing attacks.

title: MURPHY: Conversational Intent Surveillance with Arc-Based Trajectory Detection for Safe Multi-Agent AI Systems
authors: Sarkar, Gunjan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Static content moderation systems — regex blocklists and per-message classifiers — fail to detect harmful intent that emerges gradually across a conversation. A user who opens with benign questions and progressively steers toward harmful territory bypasses per-message filters trivially. We present MURPHY (Multi-layer Understanding of Risk through Phased Harm Yielding), a conversational safety intelligence layer that addresses this gap through arc-based trajectory detection. MURPHY evaluates the full conversation arc rather than individual messages, computing a deterministic arc score from four sub-dimensions: topic drift, escalation velocity, sensitive term density, and pattern similarity. MURPHY makes three primary contributions: 1. Arc-based trajectory detection: a deterministic scoring formula that evaluates the full conversation arc across four dimensions, catching slow-burn attacks invisible to per-message classifiers. 2. Self-amortising cost model: a two-tier pattern memory architecture where early LLM inference builds a reusable pattern library, progressively replacing expensive calls with near-zero-cost DynamoDB lookups. At production scale, 90% of threats are caught at near-zero cost. 3. Oracle-governed pattern learning: an external validation loop that approves new safety patterns against historical false-positive rates before activation, preventing paranoid degradation. MURPHY is designed as a surveillance layer for multi-agent AI production systems, operating asynchronously with a command authority agent to avoid blocking user-facing requests. We demonstrate MURPHY through its integration in RRQ, an autonomous YouTube production system, and show how the architecture generalises to any multi-agent deployment requiring safe human interaction.
