title: Protocol-Aware Iot Intrusion Detection Using Random Forest and CorrAUC
authors: Abdullah Abbasi; D. Hakro; Muhammad Babar; Akhtar Hussain; Danish Garg; Suad Mohammed Al Qassabi
venue: 2026 5th MEC International Conference on Advanced Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Smart Cities (ICADAAI)
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem introduces critical cybersecurity vulnerabilities through heterogeneous protocols and constrained hardware. This paper presents a protocol-aware intrusion detection system (IDS) framework validated exclusively on the Bot-IoT dataset. A Random Forest (RF) classifier is optimised through GridSearchCV with ten-fold cross-validation, combined with CorrAUC-based protocol-conditioned feature selection. The RF achieves 99.43% accuracy, 99.71% precision, 99.15% recall, 99.43% F1-score, F P R=0.28 %, and AUC=0.9944 on a 704-sample balanced test set (CV-F1 = 0.9968). XGBoost achieves comparable results (Acc =99.00 %, F1 =99.00 %), while Logistic Regression (Acc = 90.48%) and SVM (Acc = 52.27%) underperform. A paired t-test confirms RF superiority over LR at $t=15.98, p<0.001$. CorrAUC analysis identifies state (0.8765), dur (0.7825), and max (0.7710) as the top three features in Protocol-2, while the same state feature scores only 0.1090 in Protocol-3 - an $8 \times$ difference confirming the need for protocol-conditioned selection. Docker deployment validation records 107.4 MB RAM, 0.02% CPU, and successful API response (HTTP 200) during deployment validation for the containerised Bot-IoT IDS.

title: Q-FedB-HIDS for IoT Networks
authors: Logeswari G
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: TON_IoT Dataset Description The TON_IoT dataset comprises a comprehensive collection of heterogeneous data sources designed to reflect realistic Internet of Things (IoT) and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments. It integrates telemetry data from IoT/IIoT sensors, operating system logs from Windows 7, Windows 10, Ubuntu 14, and Ubuntu 18, as well as Transport Layer Security (TLS) and network traffic data. The dataset was generated within a large-scale, realistic cyber range testbed developed at the Cyber Range and IoT Labs, School of Engineering and Information Technology (SEIT), UNSW Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA). The testbed emulates an Industry 4.0 architecture comprising interconnected IoT, Edge/Fog, and Cloud layers. The infrastructure was deployed using multiple virtual machines and hosts running diverse operating systems, including Windows, Linux, and Kali Linux, to simulate real-world network interactions and system behaviors. This setup enabled the modeling of complex communication patterns across heterogeneous environments. A wide range of cyber-attack scenarios were executed within the testbed, including Denial of Service (DoS), Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS), and ransomware attacks targeting web applications, IoT gateways, and host systems. Data collection was performed in parallel across multiple sources, capturing both normal and malicious activities. The resulting dataset includes synchronized records from network traffic, Windows and Linux audit logs, and IoT telemetry streams, thereby providing a rich and diverse benchmark for developing and evaluating intrusion detection systems in IoT/IIoT environments. IoT-23 Dataset Description The IoT-23 dataset is a comprehensive collection of IoT network traffic designed for cybersecurity research, containing 23 scenarios with 20 malware captures and 3 benign traffic captures. Developed at the Stratosphere Laboratory, Czech Technical University, it includes data collected between 2018 and 2019 and published in 2020. Malicious scenarios involve executing malware samples on Raspberry Pi devices, simulating real attack behaviors across multiple protocols. Benign traffic was captured from real IoT devices, including a Philips Hue smart lamp, Amazon Echo, and Somfy smart lock. The dataset provides realistic, labeled traffic for developing and evaluating machine learning-based intrusion detection systems. UNSW-NB15 Dataset Description The UNSW-NB15 dataset was generated using the IXIA PerfectStorm tool in the Cyber Range Lab at UNSW Canberra to simulate modern normal and attack network behaviors. Raw network traffic (100 GB) was captured using tcpdump and processed with Argus and Bro-IDS to extract 49 features. The dataset includes nine attack categories: Fuzzers, Analysis, Backdoors, DoS, Exploits, Generic, Reconnaissance, Shellcode, and Worms. It contains approximately 2.54 million records across multiple CSV files, with predefined training (175,341 records) and testing (82,332 records) sets, enabling effective evaluation of intrusion detection systems.

title: QKD-Assisted Secure Transport Framework for Federated Healthcare Systems: A Software Prototype and Baseline Evaluation
authors: Fardin Muttaki; Aqeel Sahi; Shahab Abdulla
abstract: Decentralised machine learning requires authenticated transport to secure exchanged model updates. To this end, this study presents a healthcare-focused proof of concept integrating a quantum key distribution (QKD) simulation with HKDF-SHA-256, AES-256-GCM, role-based access control, replay detection, and sample-weighted federated averaging (FedAvg), and evaluates it on 42,989 medical records across 1107 synthetic patients. A trusted server decrypted authorised updates before plaintext aggregation. Centralised logistic regression achieved an F1 score of 0.7483, while a five-client FedAvg achieved 0.7333. Encrypted and unencrypted pipelines demonstrated identical model parameters. The simulated QKD protocol produced a mean quantum bit error rate of 0.2486 and successfully aborted all sessions under a full intercept constraint. Under ten independent data splits, the five-client FedAvg achieved mean F1 scores of 0.6973 (IID) and 0.6104 (non-IID). Demonstrating that transport security does not mitigate adversarial machine learning, an authenticated sign-flip attack bypassed AES-256-GCM protection and reduced the mean F1 score to 0.1185. Computationally, the QKD-assisted path averaged 0.386 ms per update compared to 0.486 ms for fresh TLS 1.3 and 0.006 ms for persistent TLS while isolating software execution from hardware constraints. Overall, this study demonstrates a reproducible proof of concept and a practical baseline for a secure machine learning approach for healthcare collaborations.

title: QR-Shield: A Malicious QR Code Detection Tool
authors: Faheem Ahmed; Isha Fatima; Mehmood ul Hassan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: QRShield is a hybrid cybersecurity framework developed to detect malicious QR codes by combining machine learning and deep learning techniques. The system analyzes both the embedded URL and the visual integrity of QR codes to identify phishing links, malicious redirects, and tampered QR images. It uses an XGBoost model for URL security analysis based on lexical, WHOIS, DNS, and HTTP features, while a ResNet-18 deep learning model detects visual tampering in QR images. The outputs of both models are combined through a fusion strategy to classify QR codes as benign, suspicious, or malicious, providing a more secure and reliable QR code detection solution for web and mobile environments.

title: QRX: A Hybrid Machine Learning and Threat-Intelligence Framework for Real-Time Detection of Malicious QR Code Links
authors: S. Shyni; P. P; H. B.; Angel Rani A
venue: 2026 International Conference on System, Computation, Automation and Networking (ICSCAN)
abstract: QR codes (Quick Response codes) are increasingly used for digital payments, authentication, ticketing, and website access because they offer quick, contactless data retrieval. However, the lack of visible information about embedded URLs allows attackers to misuse QR codes for phishing, malware distribution, and financial fraud. Recent studies show that malicious QR campaigns, also known as Quishing, are rapidly escalating in public environments, mobile banking, and e-commerce systems. This study proposes QRX (QR eXamine), a next-generation secure QR scanning application that uses threat-intelligence APIs, domain reputation checks, SSL verification, blacklist scanning, and machine-learning-based risk scoring before redirection. The goals are to help users identify links in real time and to prevent unwanted access. AI-driven reputation scoring can significantly reduce the success rates of QR-based attacks, enhancing user safety in online transactions, as demonstrated by experimental results from previous malicious URL detection frameworks. This proposed system ensures a safe user experience by providing prevent-before-redirect protection and increasing trust in frequent QR code usage.

title: QuanNetDetect: A Quantum Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Encrypted TLS Malicious Traffic Detection
authors: Nirusan Hariharan; Guhanathan Poravi
venue: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abstract: Transport Layer Security encryption protects over 95% of internet communications but creates detection challenges when malicious actors exploit encrypted channels. Classical machine learning methods struggle with the high-dimensional feature spaces characteristic of TLS metadata, achieving limited accuracy on realworld encrypted traffic. This paper presents QuanNetDetect, the first quantum hybrid deep learning framework specifically designed for detecting malicious patterns in encrypted TLS network traffic. The system integrates quantum neural networks with classical preprocessing through amplitude embedding and strongly entangling layers to process TLS handshake metadata. We implement three model architectures: a quantum neural network for multiclass classification of distributed denial-of-service attacks, a quantum neural network for binary detection of malicious VPN and Tor traffic, and a novel quantum-enhanced gated recurrent unit model for temporal pattern recognition. Evaluation on industrystandard datasets demonstrates 82.83% accuracy for multiclass DDoS classification on CIC-DDoS-2019 and 99.95% accuracy for binary malicious traffic detection on CIC-Darknet-2020, substantially exceeding previous quantum approaches to network security. The framework processes actual packet captures, performs automated feature extraction from encrypted flows, and generates detection reports suitable for security operations. Results provide empirical evidence of quantum computing advantages for analyzing complex encrypted network metadata without payload decryption

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Cybersecurity: A Taxonomy and Future Directions
authors: Siva Sai; Ishika Goyal; Shubham Sharma; Sri Harshita Manuri; Vinay Chamola; Rajkumar Buyya
abstract: ABSTRACT Context The rapid increase in cyber threats, coupled with increasingly sophisticated attack strategies and the exponential growth of data in recent years, has exposed significant limitations in classical machine learning, rule‐based, and signature‐based defense mechanisms. These approaches are often unable to scale or adapt effectively to evolving threat landscapes. Objective As a result, Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has emerged as a promising alternative, leveraging computational principles from quantum mechanics. QML enables more expressive encoding and efficient processing of high‐dimensional data, offering potential advantages for complex cybersecurity tasks. Method This survey provides a comprehensive overview of QML techniques relevant to the domain of security, such as Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs), Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs), Variational Quantum Circuits (VQCs), and Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs), and discusses the contributions of this paper in relation to existing research in the field and how it improves over them. Results It also maps these methods across supervised, unsupervised, and generative learning paradigms, as well as to core cybersecurity tasks, including intrusion and anomaly detection, malware and botnet classification, and encrypted‐traffic analytics. It also discusses their application in cloud computing security, where QML can enhance secure, scalable operations. Conclusion Many limitations of QML in the domain of cybersecurity have also been discussed, along with the directions for addressing them.

title: Quantum Support Vector Machine for Encrypted Botnet Command and Control Traffic Detection Without Payload Inspection
authors: J. S. Kumar; N. Vijay; F. Mahammad; M. Subramanyam; V. K; C. V. Kumar
venue: 2026 International Conference on Intelligent and Sustainable AI Systems (ICOSAAS)
abstract: Modern botnets use encrypted Command-and-Control (C2) communications, which poses a major challenge for network security given the fact that payloads are encrypted, which makes the use of traditional signature-based inspection methods ineffective. In this work, we introduce QSVM Shield, a hybrid quantum-classical solution for encrypted botnet C2 traffic detection purely based on network flow metadata following a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) algorithm. The proposed technique does not need to decrypt the packet payloads to detect threats, but instead uses statistical characteristics of encrypted packet flows to achieve this goal while maintaining the privacy of the communications. First, the scale variations in the essential flow attributes are reduced and feature consistency is enhanced by applying logarithmic feature transformation and MinMax normalization. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is then used to find a low dimensional representation that is compact enough for quantum encoding. The resulting reduced feature vectors are then loaded into a 4-qubit quantum feature map that is implemented using PennyLane, with parameterized quantum rotations and entanglement operations building up a nonlinear quantum kernel used to model complex relationships between the various encrypted traffic samples. The generated kernel matrix is used with a classical Support Vector Classifier that has a precomputed kernel to classify benign traffic from encrypted C2 communication of botnets. For a practical security operation, all the framework is deployed as a Flask based web application, where it enables single instance prediction, batch CSV analysis, performance visualization and scan history management. Experimental results with network flow data encrypted under the proposed hybrid quantum-classical pipeline are presented and show that the proposed hybrid quantum-classical pipeline can achieve effective detection and discrimination of malicious C2 traffic while keeping the inference process lightweight, using only flow-level information. The combination of quantum kernel learning and privacy-preserving encrypted traffic analysis creates a technically secure and practically viable solution to next generation intelligent network intrusion detection.

title: Quantum-Inspired Autoencoder and LSTM Model for Encrypted Traffic Anomaly Detection
authors: Santosh Datta Bompally
venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences and Applications (ACDSA)
abstract: The current communication systems have seen their encrypted network traffic grow exponentially and this has made the detection of malicious actions hidden under privacy-preserving protocols a significantly hard task. Traditional intrusion detection frameworks and deep learning networks like CNN, GRU, and DNN depend largely on packet payloads or the flow level statistics, thus they are not very useful in encrypted settings. In an effort to address this challenge, the present paper introduces a Quantum-Inspired Autoencoder and LSTM (QAE-LSTM) model that combines quantum-inspired feature encoding with deep time learning to detect the anomaly efficiently and with a lower false-positive rate. As in the suggested framework, quantum amplitude encoding codes classical flow features in a high-dimensional Hilbert space, increasing their representational power. The realized quantum-transformed features are compressed by the autoencoder to eliminate redundancy, and the LSTM layer is learned to identify sequential traffic patterns to distinguish normal and abnormal ones, which is proven to be more effective than conventional deep learning baselines on the CIC-IDS 2021 dataset. The experimental results on the CIC-IDS 2021 dataset exhibit the best performance with an accuracy of 94.8 %, precision of 92.8 %, recall of 94.2 % and F1-score of 93.5%, which outperforms existing CNN, GRU, and Transformer models by 3-6. The findings verify that quantum-inspired learning principles can be used to a large degree to enhance encrypted traffic analysis with higher computational efficiency and scalability.

title: QuSecVerify: Automated Verification Framework for Quantum Cybersecurity Software
authors: Shibly Sadik; Md. Ahanaf Mohosen; Mohamed Nawab; Tawhidur Rahman; Md. Farhad Rahman; Mohammad Sayduzzaman et al.
venue: 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN)
abstract: Quantum computing brings opportunities in the field of cybersecurity, yet ensuring that quantum security software is actually functional is a task of great proportions. This paper provides QuSecVerify, a verification model tailored to quantum cybersecurity applications (such as quantum key distribution, quantum-based intrusion detection, and quantum blockchain applications). We have used three methods that include formal verification over SMT solvers over a Quantum RAM model, mutation testing over security-oriented fault operators, and statistical testing as defined by repeated quantum measurements. We benchmarked the framework on key distribution on a quantum machine learning intrusion detector, BB84, and quantum consensus protocol. Our findings indicate that using our approach identifies 95.7 percent of injected faults, which is 40 percent less verification than in manual verifiability, and 23 bugs were still detected in tested implementations. The work is a bridge in the field of quantum software engineering, as it offers a practical and general tool to verify quantum code that is security-critical. title: Ranking Is Not Detecting: Operating-Region Evaluation of DDoS Detectors on Unseen Attack Families — Reproducibility Data and Code
authors: Hina Iqbal; Cristiano Premebida; Usman Haider
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Overview This repository provides the reproducibility data, experimental results, analytical scripts, figures, and supporting documentation for the research manuscript “Ranking Is Not Detecting: Operating-Region Evaluation of DDoS Detectors on Unseen Attack Families,” prepared for submission to Computers & Electrical Engineering (Elsevier). The study investigates the relationship between receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), low-false-positive-rate performance, and actual attack detection at validation-selected operating thresholds. It examines whether strong aggregate discrimination results necessarily translate into effective identification of previously unseen denial-of-service attack families. Experimental Design The study uses corrected CSE-CIC-IDS2018 network traffic-flow data and evaluates two machine-learning classifiers: Random Forest (RF) and a tabular multilayer perceptron (MLP). Models are developed using corrected traffic captured on February 20, 2018, and evaluated against corrected captures from February 15, 16, and 21, 2018. Five random seeds and three decision-threshold policies are examined: Fixed classification threshold of 0.5. Validation-selected threshold maximizing F1-score. Validation-selected threshold constrained to a false-positive rate of 0.001. The analyses consider attack-family recall, ROC-AUC, standardized partial ROC-AUC, confusion-matrix outcomes, model-seed variability, and source-address sensitivity. Principal Findings One Random Forest configuration achieves a Wednesday ROC-AUC of approximately 0.998176 while detecting none of the 1,082,293 HOIC attack flows at the fixed threshold of 0.5. Across the evaluated models, seeds, and three prespecified threshold policies, HOIC, Hulk, and GoldenEye exhibit zero recall. The study also examines 797 originally labelled LOIC-HTTP flow records that match corrected LOIC-UDP records. Their binary attack classification remains unchanged. These findings illustrate that strong ranking performance does not necessarily ensure successful attack detection at the evaluated operating thresholds. They do not establish that the studied attacks are undetectable under every alternative threshold or classifier. Repository Contents The v1.0.0 reproducibility archive contains: Saved model prediction arrays and attack-family labels. Random Forest and MLP experimental outputs across five seeds. Saved data supporting the five-address sensitivity analysis. Analysis and validation scripts. Materials supporting manuscript Tables 1–6. Publication figures and graphical abstract. Dataset provenance information and software requirements. Checksum manifests and reproducibility documentation. Reproducibility The archive supports score-based regeneration and verification of the reported experimental results. The supplied release-validation reports document successful clean-extraction execution, matching numerical results for the supported manuscript tables, and matching outputs for the three main figures and graphical abstract. Complete end-to-end model retraining from the original third-party benchmark data is not provided because the raw training datasets and original model checkpoints are not included. For Table 6, a saved Boolean mask enables recalculation of the reported source-address sensitivity results. The source-address values needed to reconstruct that mask independently are not included in this release. Data Sources and Study Limitations The original CSE-CIC-IDS2018 dataset originates from the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity at the University of New Brunswick. Corrected data originate from the DistriNet research release. The underlying third-party network-flow CSV datasets are not redistributed. The experiments provide retrospective cross-capture evaluation rather than prospective operational validation. The training protocol does not establish complete source-host independence. Reported false-positive rates reflect the defined evaluation samples and should not be interpreted as live-deployment measurements. The distinction between validation-selected thresholds and operating points derived from test ROC curves is preserved throughout the analysis.

title: Ransomware Detection in Encrypted Network Traffic Using Optimized Suricata Rules
authors: Azlinda Abdul Aziz; Nur Razia Mohd Suradi; Raja Mohd Tariqi Raja Lope Ahmad; Zuraidy Adnan; Muhammad Fairuz Abd Rauf; Suhaila Ismail et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Ransomware has emerged as one of the most serious and rapidly evolving cyber threats. This can potentially cause substantial financial losses and adversely affect organizational operations. In recent years, ransomware attacks have increasingly used methods such as encryption, hidden communication and advanced circumvention strategies. Most traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) struggle to detect encrypted traffic, leading to high false alerts and low accuracy. This limitation is more critical in modern ransomware attacks that rely heavily on encrypted command‐and‐control (C2) communication channels. This study proposes an improved method of detecting ransomware through Suricata as evidence to address these concerns. This study focuses on improving detection accuracy, reducing false positive rates and enhancing encrypted traffic analysis. This was accomplished using Suricata, an open‐source intrusion detection and prevention system. The structured methodology was implemented in three phase, which consist of design, development and testing and validation. In the design phase, the data set is prepared and IDS is configured. In the development phase, Suricata rule sets were optimized with JA3 TLS fingerprints to analyze encrypted ransomware traffic. The system was validated using real‐world ransomware datasets to ensure realistic evaluation conditions. As a result, the IDS can detect known and emerging ransomware communication patterns more effectively. Additionally, the system was optimized to achieve maximum throughput and reduce resource consumption while performing real‐time analysis. Performance evaluation was conducted using standard metrics, including detection accuracy, false positive and processing time. The proposed method achieved 96.8% detection accuracy, 2.4% false positive rate and reduced processing time from 240 to 30 s, representing a 10 times improvement compared to baseline Suricata. In addition, system performance remained acceptable while improving ransomware detection. These findings show that JA3 fingerprinting and optimized Suricata rules can improve real‐time ransomware detection in a cost‐effective and scalable way.

title: Raw data of the X3 runs related to DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23282842
authors: Stefan Trauth
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: October 2026 This preprint reports ZEUS X-Trust X3 “Shield”: the X1 live-state authentication primitive applied to AI agents. Every security layer built for agents so far protects the environment from the agent and answers what an agent may do. X3 protects the agent from its environment — from injected instructions, from tampering with its configuration, from replacement by a foreign process, and from replay of its credentials. Each agent receives its own X-Trust instance, a sphere; the identity enrolled into it is a hash of the agent itself — system prompt, tool list, task and the agent’s own code — so that the agent is the password and there is nothing to steal. A gate outside the language model recomputes that hash, verifies the calling process from the connection, checks tool and target against the task limits and asks the sphere before every tool call. Only ACCEPT executes; every error, timeout or refusal is DENY. Seven development runs between 2 and 9 October 2026 on one workstation, CPU only, from two agents and nine attacks to eighteen agents in two clusters under four hours of continuous attack, with two agents sharing one core. The one figure is the same in every run: zero calls executed without a valid identity. In the largest run the driver recorded 468 attack passes, 3,874 attack calls, among 4,574 checks. A timing probe of 184 passes found a median difference of 0.0 ms between legitimate-looking and foreign requests; 60 races returned 120 of 120 DENY; 74 late replays of consumed one-time credentials returned 74 of 74 “not mine”; 110 re-enrollments of a running member left the other seventeen agents answering throughout. Reproducibility was measured before any agent was enrolled — 190 of 190 pairs bit-identical, no tolerance window — and 189 of 189 agent-hash readout snapshots over four hours were bit-identical to their first. One gap is reported with its pre- and post-measurement: a foreign process presenting a valid agent identifier was accepted by the first build in 0.56 s and, after caller identity was added, denied in 0.053 s. Two constructions were measured side by side: the sphere as a service beside the agent, and the sphere inside the agent’s own process. With the X1 campaigns, the ZEUS X-Trust program now stands at around 750,000 attack attempts without an unauthorized acceptance. Seven figures with their numerical sources and rendering scripts accompany the paper. X3 follows X1 directly, and this preprint is filed with the Pre-X2 preprint because the reason for that step is stated there: see the versioning note below. The name X2 is kept unused. Raw data of the X3 runs (87 GB on disk, 1.4 GB packed) is deposited in this record beside the paper with restricted access; a plain-text README lists the seven runs. Access is granted on request to Info@Trauth-Research.com. The proprietary substrate — architecture, code, weights, enrolled references and credentials — is outside every deposit. Available here: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23289634 on request. ________________________________ This preprint completes the ZEUS X-Trust X1 stage and establishes the experimental basis for X2. Two additional Pre-X2 campaigns comprise 60 million measured iterations and 249,000 non-original inputs, with zero unauthorized acceptances. The first campaign forwarded 150,000 attacks across 30 classes to a sealed instance. After reconstructing a row-addressing defect in the stored amplitude data, 148,500 attack responses remained correctly addressable for the class-geometry analysis. The second campaign evaluated 99,000 altered or independent inputs and 1,000 repetitions of the original credential through a SHA-512-only input path. Under this protocol, no edit-distance gradient toward the credential was detected in response magnitude. Across the wider X1 program, the rounded totals are around 725,000 attack attempts and 140 million measured iterations. The paper outlines X2 applications for autonomous agent swarms and military drone swarms. Its first planned X2 stage couples 32 X1 spheres to a main sphere for collective live-state membership, with a reserve sphere also proposed. These are X2 architectural plans; the experiments reported here concern X1. This work continues the expanded X1 validation (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22736928). Raw measurement files are retained separately and are intended for a separate restricted-access dataset record. Raw data available with request: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22737465 as soon as Zenodo has solved his traffic topics. Note on versioning for future preprints: why X3 follows Pre-X2 directly.The Pre-X2 preprint prepared a planned generation X2: a hardened sphere, an additional watchdog, and attack-class recognition from the live-state fingerprint. X2 itself was not started. The Pre-X2 results stand as published, but they also showed that detection (ACCEPT/DENY) and classification (which attack) are separate layers, and that the layer AI agents need first is detection bound to the identity of the agent. That is X3 „Shield“, which therefore follows Pre-X2 directly. Parts of the X2 plan live on inside X3: the hardened sphere is the X3 sphere, the watchdog became the integrity ping. Attack-class recognition is deferred; whether it returns as a layer on top of X3 depends on need. The name X2 is kept unused to avoid confusion in citations.

title: REAL TIME AIML PHISHING DETECTION AND PREVENTION SYSTEM
authors: IJDIM
venue: International Journal of Data Science and IoT Management System
abstract: Phishing attacks represent one of the most persistent and dangerous cybersecurity threats in the digital era, targeting individuals and organizations by impersonating legitimate websites to steal confidential information such as login credentials, banking details, and personal data. Traditional phishing detection methods primarily rely on blacklist databases, heuristic rules, and manual monitoring systems. However, these approaches often fail to detect newly generated phishing websites, also known as zero-day attacks, due to their dynamic and adaptive nature. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes a Real Time Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) based Phishing Detection and Prevention System capable of identifying malicious websites through automated feature analysis and predictive modeling. The system collects multiple features from website URLs, domain characteristics, page content, and security indicators such as SSL certificates. These features are then processed using machine learning algorithms to classify websites as legitimate or phishing in real time. The proposed system integrates data preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, and prediction modules to ensure efficient detection and fast response. By leveraging supervised learning techniques, the system continuously improves its accuracy by learning from large datasets of legitimate and phishing URLs. Furthermore, the real-time detection framework allows early identification of malicious websites before users interact with them, thereby reducing the risk of credential theft and financial loss. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed AI/ML-based approach significantly improves detection accuracy, reduces false positives, and provides faster identification compared to traditional blacklist approaches. This system contributes to strengthening cybersecurity infrastructure by offering an intelligent, scalable, and adaptive solution for phishing detection and prevention in modern web environments.

title: REAL TIME PHISHING DETECTION USING FEATURE EXTRACTION AND HYBRID ENSEMBLE MODELS
authors: B. Kalaimathi
venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
abstract: Cyber security attacks and threats are prone among the websites used by people now a days. The most vicious threat for people surfing on the websites is phishing. Phishing is recognized as a malicious act of cybercrime to deceive users and steal important data such as Banking Credentials, ATM PINs, cards, and CVV numbers. Our proposed method is based on detecting these websites using a Hybrid Ensembler model. The URL is given as input and the feature extraction is done by thirty-one parameters which mainly include URL length, HTTPS request/response, IP address, sub-domain, etc The modal is trained using various machine learning algorithms like decision tree, K-Nearest, logistic regression, naïve bayes and hybrid ensembler and the output is obtained numerically. The model is trained in such a way that it gives more accuracy and efficiency than the existing method. The Hybrid Ensembler is used to pick a particular algorithm that gives better results for a certain dataset. Python functions are written for each feature extraction and the model is trained in google colab. The instructed modal is transfigured to a pickle file using python pickling for deployment in the flask framework. Flask framework and other UI development tools are used to create web applications where the user can enter the URL to check whether it is a Phishing website or a legitimate website.

title: Real Time Phishing Detection Using ML
authors: Sakshi Sakshi Ajit Katrajkar
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In today’s digital world, phishing attacks have become a major cybersecurity threat. Cybercriminals use fake websites, emails, and links to trick users into sharing sensitive information such as passwords, banking details, and personal data. As online services and remote work continue to grow, phishing attacks are becoming more frequent and advanced. Traditional phishing detection methods mainly depend on blacklists and predefined rules, which are not effective against new or unknown phishing attacks. Manual checking of suspicious links and emails is also slow and difficult. This project, “Real-Time Phishing Detection Using Machine Learning,” aims to develop an intelligent system that can automatically identify phishing websites and emails in real time. The system analyzes features such as URL length, HTTPS usage, suspicious keywords, sender details, and abnormal email behavior. Machine learning algorithms like Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine (SVM) are trained using phishing and legitimate datasets to improve detection accuracy. Among these models, the Random Forest algorithm gives the best performance because it can handle complex data efficiently and reduce errors. When a phishing attempt is detected, the system immediately alerts the user and provides safety guidance. This project helps improve cybersecurity awareness and provides a smart, scalable, and reliable solution for protecting users from phishing attacks. Humanity built an internet where every second link tries to steal your password. Magnificent achievement, really.

title: Real Time VPN Traffic Attack Detection and Classification
authors: N. Chidambaresh; S. Charukkesh; Dhivya G; V. Arumbu
venue: 2026 Third International Conference on Innovations in Cybersecurity and Data Science (ICICDS)
abstract: Virtual Private Networks (VPN) are used by many legitimate users all over the globe as it ensures data confidentiality over public networks. With the improvement in the current technologies the chances of misusing data over transmission is prevalent. The way in which VPN ensures confidentiality may however turn as a advantage for the data manipulators to indulge in fraudulent activities. VPN provides protection against Internet Service Providers (ISP) to avoid tracking user activities and it may provide undesirable benefit to manipulators by exploiting encrypted traffic patterns and thereby simulating cyber attacks. Therefore, to ensure the use of VPN only for legitimate users and to detect malicious activities of hackers in the presence of VPN requires a system that differentiates the suspicious and normal activity. This problem is addressed through our idea by designing a system to detect and classify the malicious activity (Port Scan or not) in the presence of VPN. The system employs a real time VPN attack simulation environment (Port Scan), Detection and Classification of Port Scan using Machine Learning Techniques. Port Scan is a network reconnaissance technique to probe target host to detect the open, closed and filtered ports. This port scan attack is detected and the system classifies if the attack is port scan or not. The real time VPN environment is setup in Linux to simulate normal, malicious traffic and Machine Learning Techniques are trained using a dataset to detect the malicious traffic and classify if its a port scan attack or not. Integrating the designed ML model on to a real time VPN environment will monitor the traffic network using pcap file and detect the presence of attack and classify the environment as port scan induced attack environment or not. This system thereby understands the VPN environment, the Port Scan attack and enhance VPN security for legitimate users.

title: Real-Time Ai/Ml Based Phishing Detection and Prevention System
authors: V. Prasad, P. Srija, M. Sahithi, Ch. Naga Shreya,P. Pujitha
venue: International Journal of Engineering Research and Science & Technology
abstract: Phishing attacks have become one of the most common widespread cybersecurity threats, targeting individuals and organizations through malicious websites, emails, and fake URLs. Traditional phishing detection techniques mainly rely on blacklist databases and manually define rules, which often fail to identify newly emerging phishing websites. This research presents a Real-Time AI/ML Based Phishing Detection and Prevention System that utilizes Machine Learning algorithms to accurately distinguish between legitimate and phishing URLs. The proposed system extracts important URL-based features, including URl length, special characters, HTTPS usage, subdomain count, IP address presence, and digit frequency, to classify websites effectively. A Random Forest classifier is trained on a phishing dataset to provide fast and reliable predictions. The system is integrated with a user-friendly web interface that enables real-time URL analysis and instant threat alerts. Experimental results demonstrate high detection accuracy and efficient performance, making the proposed solution suitable for practical cybersecurity applications. KEYWORDS: Phishing Detection, Machine Learning, Random Forest Classifier, URL Feature Extraction, Cybersecurity.

title: Real-Time Bot Detection on XCorp: Enhanced Feature Engineering with Apache Spark
authors: Hakar Mohammed Rasul; A. Jumaa; Aysar Abdulrahman
venue: passer of basic and applied sciences
abstract: The rapid growth of misinformation, spam, and automated bot activity on social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter, operated by XCorp) has created a pressing need for accurate and real-time detection systems. Bots are one of the most important challenges at XCorp. A bot on XCorp is software that sends tweets to users automatically. XCorp bots may be used for several advantageous purposes or may be created for malicious purposes such as spreading fake news campaigns, spamming, and violating the privacy of others. This study presents a scalable framework for real-time tweets analysis using Apache Spark, focusing on the integration of user-based features and context-based features to enhance bot detection performance. Three distinct datasets were utilized to build and train the proposed model, enabling robust feature learning and generalization across different data sources. A large stream of real-time XCorp data was then processed using Spark Streaming, where newly engineered features captured user and content features within tweets. The model was constructed using five PySpark machine learning techniques: Gradient Boosted Trees Classification, Linear Support Vector Machine Classification, Decision Tree Classification, Logistic Regression, and Random Forest Classification. Experimental results show that incorporating the proposed features significantly improves accuracy, precision, and recall compared with baseline models and existing studies, while maintaining a relatively stable computation time. Among the evaluated models, the Random Forest classifier achieved the best performance, reaching 99.1% precision, 99.7% recall, 99.40% F1-Score and 99.6% accuracy. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

title: Real-Time Detection of Encrypted DGA and DNS Tunneling Using DPDK on SmartNICs
authors: Sergio Elizalde; Ali AlSabeh; Samia Choueiri; Elie F. Kfoury; Jorge Crichigno
abstract: • Encrypted Domain Name System (DNS) protocols such as DNS over HTTPS (DoH) enhance user privacy by preventing eavesdropping. • However, they also enable attackers to conceal Command-and-Control (C2) communication and data exfiltration within HTTPS traffic. • We propose a real-time detection framework deployed on the NVIDIA BlueField-3 Smart Network Interface Card (SmartNIC). • Feature extraction and Machine Learning (ML) inference are offloaded to the SmartNIC, reducing host CPU intervention. • A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) classifier categorizes traffic into benign DoH, Non-DoH, DoH tunnel and Domain-Generated Algorithm (DGA). • The MLP architecture is chosen for its suitability for parallel execution. • The model operates on bidirectional flow-level statistical features. • These features are derived from packet sizes, timing behavior, and traffic pattern characteristics. • To improve robustness against evolving threats, we extend public DGA datasets with additional DoH-encapsulated samples. • ML performance is evaluated using classification accuracy and SHAP-based explainability analysis. • System performance is evaluated in terms of per-packet processing latency and throughput scalability as the number of cores increases.

title: Real-Traffic-Trained Intelligent IDS for Advanced Cyberattack Detection in Enterprise Networks
authors: Dalila Naira Chinchay; Rodrigo Calderón Ari; Liset S. Rodriguez-Baca
venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications
abstract: Early detection of cyberattacks remains a major challenge in enterprise networks due to encrypted traffic, protocol diversity, and highly dynamic service behavior. This study evaluates a machine learning-based intrusion detection system trained on real enterprise traffic captured over 20 working days under operational conditions. A total of 1,163,014 packets were collected and complemented with controlled attack traffic, including DDoS, brute force, botnet, SQL injection, port scanning, privilege escalation, and service exploitation scenarios. After flow-based feature extraction and preprocessing, six supervised learning models were evaluated under the same data partition and validation settings. Among them, Random Forest achieved the best overall performance, with precision, recall, and F1-score above 0.999 and an AUC of 0.9994 on the collected dataset. These findings suggest that training with real traffic can improve IDS performance under realistic enterprise conditions. However, further validation across additional organizations and time periods is required to confirm generalizability.

title: Reasoning Hijacking: The Fragility of Reasoning Alignment in Large Language Models
authors: Yuansen Liu; Yixuan Tang; Anthony Kum Hoe Tung
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
abstract: Current LLM safety research predominantly focuses on mitigating Goal Hijacking, preventing attackers from redirecting a model's high-level objective (e.g., from "summarizing emails" to "phishing users").In this paper, we argue that this perspective is incomplete and highlight a critical vulnerability in Reasoning Alignment.We expose the inherent fragility of current alignment techniques by proposing a new adversarial prompt attack paradigm: Reasoning Hijacking.To demonstrate this vulnerability, we instantiate it via the Criteria Attack, which subverts model judgments by injecting spurious decision criteria without altering the high-level task goal.Unlike Goal Hijacking, which attempts to override the system prompt, Reasoning Hijacking keeps the task goal intact but manipulates the model's decision-making logic by injecting spurious reasoning shortcut.Through extensive experiments on three different tasks (toxic comment, negative review, and spam detection), we demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models are highly fragile, consistently prioritizing injected heuristic shortcuts over rigorous semantic analysis.Crucially, because the model's explicit intent remains aligned with the user's instructions, these attacks can bypass defenses designed to detect goal deviation (e.g., SecAlign, StruQ), revealing a fundamental blind spot in the current safety landscape.Data and code are available at https://github.com/Yuan-Hou/criteria_attack.Goal Hijacking Reasoning Hijacking (Criteria Attack) Prompt Context Instruction (trusted) I: Classify the email as {Spam, Ham}.

title: Recent Advances in Web Application Firewall Detection: A Comparative Survey of Signature-Based, Machine Learning-Based, and Hybrid Techniques
authors: Pranav Kaluram Shinde; Yash Ranjit Ingole; Neha Pintu Tikore; Gaurav Sanjay Gosavi; Dr.  S.  B.  Chaudhari
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract - The rapid growth of web applications has significantly increased the attack surface for cyber threats such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), cross-site request forgery (CSRF), server-side request forgery (SSRF), command injection, and other sophisticated web-based attacks. Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) have emerged as a critical security mechanism for protecting web applications by monitoring, filtering, and blocking malicious HTTP and HTTPS traffic. Traditional WAF solutions primarily rely on signature-based detection techniques that provide efficient protection against known attack patterns; however, their effectiveness is limited when dealing with zero-day exploits, polymorphic attacks, and obfuscated payloads. To address these limitations, machine learning-based approaches have been introduced to identify anomalous behaviors and previously unseen attack vectors through data-driven analysis. More recently, hybrid detection frameworks combining signature-based rules with machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques have gained considerable attention due to their ability to balance detection accuracy, adaptability, and computational efficiency. This survey presents a comprehensive review of recent advances in Web Application Firewall detection techniques, focusing on signature-based, machine learning-based, and hybrid approaches. The study analyzes the working principles, strengths, limitations, and performance characteristics of each category while examining their effectiveness against modern web application threats. Furthermore, a comparative analysis is conducted to highlight key differences in detection capability, false-positive rates, scalability, and deployment complexity. The survey also identifies current research challenges, including encrypted traffic inspection, adversarial attacks against machine learning models, explainable security mechanisms, and real-time adaptive detection. Finally, emerging research directions and future opportunities for intelligent WAF architectures are discussed to support the development of next-generation web application security solutions.

title: Recursive Voting Fusion: An RFE-Based Ensemble Model for Categorizing IoT DDoS Attacks
authors: Piyush M. Prajapati; Priyesh P. Gandhi; Sheshang Degadwala; Keyur Brahmbhatt; Swapnil Maheshkumar Parikh
venue: ITEGAM- Journal of Engineering and Technology for Industrial Applications (ITEGAM-JETIA)
abstract: The rise of the Internet of Things (IoT) devices has led to an enormous vulnerability to multiple DDoS attacks, including low-rate traffic disruption and high-rate SYN Floods. This increasing menace underscores the importance of proper multi-classification methods that can detect various DDoS attack patterns. Nonetheless, most of the current machine learning models cannot provide a generalization between various DDoS types that include DDoS-ACK Fragmentation, DDoS-HTTP Flood, DoS-TCP Flood, and DDoS-SYN Flood. Non-linear Support Vector Machines (SVM) which are traditional classifiers tend to have poor performance when trying to differentiate subtle differences between these types of attacks. To overcome this drawback, this paper suggests a Recursive Voting Fusion model, which involves Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) as the method of optimum feature selection and an ensemble approach to the robust classification. The framework is a hybrid of Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Extra tree classifiers where soft voting is used. It is experimentally demonstrated that the proposed approach has 99 per cent accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and 99 per cent MCC and AUC-ROC, which is significantly higher than the baseline models. It implies that the model is highly robust and scalable to be used in real-time IoT intrusion detection and efficient mitigation of the developing DDoS threats.

title: REDESIGNING NETWORK DEFENSES TO BALANCE STRONG ENCRYPTION WITH EARLY DETECTION AND MITIGATION OF ZERO-DAY ATTACKS IN MODERN ENVIRONMENTS
authors: Maryam Siddique; Muhammad Waleed Khawar; Arslan Ali; Samra Shaheen
venue: Contemporary Journal of Social Science Review
abstract: Encrypted technologies are being increasingly used for better data protection and secure communication, but they also limit the effectiveness of existing network monitoring systems making it difficult to detect zero-day attacks. This research offers privacy-preserving approach to identify and prevent zero-day attacks in encrypted network environments while protecting user privacy. The framework integrates traffic monitoring of encrypted data with machine learning-based anomaly detection through a hybrid Random Forest (RF) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network architecture. Rather than decrypted packets, the framework uses packet and session metadata features such as packet length, session duration, and traffic patterns to detect anomalies. It includes anomaly detection, adaptive traffic classification and automated response mechanisms to support Zero Trust security. The results of a simulated approach indicate the proposed framework can enhance detection performance while keeping false alarms low, and enabling near real-time response. The paper also shows the promise of AI-based adaptive security models to overcome the limitations of signature-based approaches in encrypted traffic. The paper also explores scalability, privacy preservation and future research opportunities in federated learning, explainable AI and reinforcement-based adaptive mitigation for cybersecurity systems.

title: Region-Level Black-Box Defense Against Stealthy Embedding-Space Backdoors in CLIP
authors: Ahmed Abdelnaby; Mohamed Elmahallawy
abstract: Contrastive Language--Image Pretraining (CLIP) has emerged as a dominant vision backbone due to its strong transferability and zero-shot capabilities. However, recent studies reveal a critical vulnerability: embedding-space backdoor attacks. By poisoning only a tiny fraction of image--text pairs, adversaries can implant stealthy triggers that induce targeted shifts in CLIP's joint embedding space. Unlike conventional backdoors that manipulate classifier logits, these attacks corrupt representations directly, making them highly effective under extremely low poisoning ratios and difficult to detect. Existing defenses require access to model parameters, gradients, logits, or clean validation data---assumptions that rarely hold in realistic black-box deployments. Moreover, current black-box methods struggle to accurately localize small or out-of-distribution triggers. We propose CLIPGuard, a lightweight and fully black-box defense specifically designed to mitigate embedding-space backdoors in CLIP encoders. CLIPGuard identifies malicious regions by measuring segment-wise embedding perturbations and selectively purifies only suspicious segments via semantic inpainting, preserving benign visual content and alignment quality. Extensive experiments on STL-10, ImageNet, and diverse trigger families---including BadCLIP, BadNets, blended, patch-based, and typographic attacks---demonstrate that CLIPGuard reduces attack success rates to as low as 1.05% while maintaining clean accuracy up to 86.34%, consistently outperforming existing black-box defenses, including CleanCLIP and CleanerCLIP. Our code is available https://github.com/wsu-cyber-security-lab-ai/CLIPGuard.git

title: Replication Package and Benchmark Dataset for Temporal Coordination Learning in Distributed Web API Abuse Detection
authors: Sathish Kumar Pandian Anbalagan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Overview This repository contains the complete replication package, benchmark event traces, feature extraction pipelines, baseline models, dynamic graph implementations, and evaluation scripts for the manuscript: "Temporal Coordination Learning for Early Detection of Distributed Web API Abuse" Authors: Jasper Gnana Chandran J, Sathish Kumar P A Modern web APIs are increasingly targeted by automated business-flow abuse campaigns that hoard scarce inventory or manipulate incentives using low per-account request rates to bypass volumetric rate limiters. This package provides the full software and data pipeline for evaluating temporal coordination learning against traditional heuristic rules, tabular machine learning, sequential deep learning, and continuous-time dynamic graph neural networks (TGN and DyGFormer). Package Contents & Structure · spec/: Formal specification of the web API abuse scenario, threat models, and observable HTTP interaction attributes. · app/: Realistic transactional reservation application simulator generating high-concurrency event streams with human jitter and residential proxy IP dispersion (proxy_spread="full"). · data/: · events.jsonl & ground_truth.json: Full 35,384 interaction events across 44 discrete campaigns and benign traffic. · train_events.jsonl, dev_events.jsonl, test_events.jsonl: Strict chronological, non-overlapping partitions (60% / 20% / 20%) with zero future data leakage. · Confounder injection traces: 35 organic flash crowd surges and 40 shared NAT gateway clusters. · External transfer benchmark: YelpChi review fraud dataset (yelp_events.jsonl). · features/: Causal rolling-window feature engineering and popularity-conditioned null model (\mu, \sigma^2) estimation for standardized coordination residual calculation (z). · baselines/: Training and evaluation code for baselines B1 (Account Rate Rule), B2 (Network Rate Rule), B3 (Logistic Regression), B4 (XGBoost Individual), B4_net (XGBoost Network), and B5 (Session GRU). · coordination/: Feature control and ablation suites (C0 Individual Control, C1 Raw Coordination, C2 Popularity-Adjusted Coordination). · graph/: Continuous-time temporal graph architectures: · tgn.py: Temporal Graph Network with continuous memory modules and temporal attention. · dygformer.py: Dynamic Graph Transformer with co-occurrence neighbor patching. · evaluation/: Early detection evaluator measuring campaign recall, false alert budgets (\mathrm{FA}/10\mathrm{k}), Brier calibration scores, and pre-harm detection lead time relative to \tau_{\mathrm{harm}}. · outputs/: Model checkpoints, confusion matrices, evaluation metrics, and performance summaries. Quickstart Reproduction 1. Setup Environment pip install -r requirements.txt

title: Research on Lightweight and Lossless Detection Technology for Malicious Encrypted Traffic in Power Systems
authors: Xiao-Fei Huang; Wei Ma; Fei Shu; Jaydar Jingus; Peng Xiao
venue: 2026 IEEE 5th International Conference on Information Technology, Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (ICIBA)
abstract: This article focuses on the research of lightweight non-destructive testing technology for malicious encrypted electricity flow. Firstly, using attack detection technology based on streaming data, typical vulnerabilities are sorted out to extract features. With the help of the secondary development Snort software, encrypted traffic is collected and detected, and then alarm cleaning is performed to merge and analyze attack events; Combining active and passive information asset recognition technology, optimizing stateless scanning to avoid firewall detection, while utilizing passive encrypted traffic perception to identify asset fingerprints; Finally, based on the aforementioned data, a lightweight popular vulnerability verification framework is designed to conduct targeted vulnerability detection. This technology achieves precise and efficient non-destructive testing of popular vulnerabilities in the power system.

title: Research on Machine Learning-based Abnormal Traffic Detection and Anti-Interference Methods for Android End-to-End Encrypted Transmission in High-Reliability Application Scenarios
authors: Jun-Hao Su
venue: 2026 5th International Conference on Distributed Computing and Electrical Circuits and Electronics (ICDCECE)
abstract: Android end-to-end encrypted traffic protects payload privacy but reduces the reliability of anomaly monitoring for high-reliability services. Method: RMAI-Net is a payload-free reliable multi-view anomaly and interference network that incorporates TLS/QUIC handshake metadata, packet length-time sequences, reliability signals and session associations. The model has a reliability gate, dual anomaly/interference heads, calibration-aware risk scoring and neighbourhood consistency repair. Repeated cross-validation, perturbation testing and cross-domain evaluation were conducted on CIC-AndMal2017, USTC-TFC2016 and VPN-nonVPN in the experiments. Results: RMAI-Net achieved 0.968 accuracy, 0.957 Macro-F1, 0.986 AUC and 0.007 ECE, and increased Macro-F1 by 1.6 percentage points over the best baseline at $\mathbf{7. 8 m s} / \mathbf{1} \mathbf{k}$-session inference. Confidence Intervals and paired t-tests showed significant improvements. Conclusion: Payload decryption is not required for calibrated Android encrypted-traffic risk detection, and reliability-aware metadata modelling can support practical security monitoring without exposing sensitive content; however, open-set attacks, carrier-level drift and long-term online validation still need to be explored further

title: Research on network attack detection and defense based on deep learning algorithm
authors: Xinguang Xiao; Weijie Chen; Linjie Xing; Zhongkang Du; Yu Zhang
abstract: Traditional defense mechanisms have obvious limitations in the face of zero-day vulnerabilities, encrypted traffic attacks and counter-samples. With its automatic feature extraction and strong adaptability to high-dimensional data, deep learning provides a new solution for network attack and defense. In this paper, a CNN-BiLSTM-Attention hybrid neural network architecture is proposed, which integrates convolutional neural network (CNN), Bilstm and attention mechanisms, and is used to model the spatio-temporal characteristics of network attacks, which significantly improves the accuracy and recall rate of attack detection. At the same time, Focal Loss optimization loss function is introduced to solve the category imbalance problem, which effectively improves the model's ability to identify rare attack types. In terms of defense, this paper constructs a dynamic defense framework based on Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), which controls the attack response time within 50ms, and enhances the robustness of the model through confrontation training and model distillation technology, so that its defense success rate exceeds 85% in the face of FGSM and other confrontation attacks. The experimental results show that the detection model proposed in this paper performs well on multiple data sets, with an accuracy rate of 99.2% and a false alarm rate of only 0.3%, and shows significant advantages in dynamic defense and countermeasure robustness. This study provides an effective technical framework and practical example for AI-driven network security protection.

title: Research on network security situation awareness based on graph neural networks
authors: Zhanhong Wang; Yao Yao; Haoxiang Hu
abstract: To address key limitations in network security situation awareness, including the high dimensionality of traffic data, the increasing stealth of encrypted traffic, and the difficulty of Euclidean deep learning models in capturing non-Euclidean topological dependencies, this study proposes an adaptive spatiotemporal situation awareness framework based on a Graph Attention Network and a dynamic graph reconstruction mechanism. The model jointly represents structural dependencies and temporal evolution in network traffic, enabling an effective description of complex spatiotemporal relationships. By integrating multi-head graph attention with Temporal Convolutional Networks, the framework strengthens the detection of cross-domain interactions and short-term and medium-term temporal patterns. Experiments on the CIC-IDS2017 dataset show that the model achieves a detection accuracy of 99.96% with a false positive rate of 0.04%. On the UNSW-NB15 dataset, it attains an F1-score of 99.76%. In zero-day attack detection, it provides a 15.4% improvement compared with CNNs and LSTM models. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach maintains stable detection performance in highly dynamic and heterogeneous environments and provides an effective foundation for intelligent and adaptive network defense systems.

title: Research on the Use of Generative Adversarial Networks to SDN-Enabled Home Networks to Classify Traffic on the Internet with Encryption
authors: Rahul Kumar; D. D. Sharma; Kavita
venue: International Conference on Computing, Sciences and Communications (ICCSC)
abstract: The exponential rise in encrypted network traffic presents significant challenges for traditional classification techniques, particularly within Software-Defined Networking (SDN)-based home networks where packet inspection is limited by privacy constraints. To address this, we derive a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based framework that classifies encrypted traffic without requiring decryption, thus preserving user privacy while enhancing detection accuracy. The GAN leverages adversarial learning to model complex traffic distributions and differentiate between benign and malicious flows based on flow metadata and statistical features. Experimental evaluation using the ISCX VPN dataset demonstrates that the proposed model outperforms conventional classifiers-such as CNN, RNN, SVM, and Random Forestachieving an accuracy, precision, and recall of 98.8 %,an AUC of 0.995, and a low inference time of 2 ms. Additionally, the model maintains extremely low positive and negative rates of 0.006, confirming its robustness and reliability in dynamic, real- time environments. This research presents a scalable, efficient, and privacy-preserving solution for encrypted traffic classification in SDN-enabled home networks, paving the way for secure and intelligent network management.

title: Resilient and Interpretable Power Fingerprinting for IoT DDoS Defense
authors: Qingyu Zeng; Mingyu Yang; Yuko Hara–Azumi
venue: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
abstract: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has introduced severe vulnerabilities, notably Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks. Traditional network-layer intrusion detection relies on deep packet inspection and flow analysis, which struggle against modern encrypted traffic and raise severe privacy violations. To address these limitations, we propose a novel physical-layer framework that strictly preserves payload privacy by exploiting power side-channel signals. This study elevates the detection paradigm through three core pillars. First, we design a dynamic data acquisition and multi-domain feature engineering pipeline. Leveraging this robust feature space, our optimized XGBoost-based engine achieves an exceptional Macro-F1 score of 0.9988 for macroscopic anomaly detection and a robust 0.9658 for a multi-class identification task, seamlessly disentangling stealthy attacks from diverse legitimate IoT workloads (e.g., OpenHAB, ThingsBoard) across varying sampling scales. Second, we systematically evaluate the system’s resilience under extremely injected additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN). Even at 0 dB Signal-to-Noise Ratio, our system sustains a high anomaly detection F1-score of 0.9553, significantly outperforming traditional baselines. Third, to bridge the trust gap inherent in “black-box” machine learning, we integrate the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) framework. The comprehensive interpretability analysis demonstrates that our model generates highly transparent and trustworthy alerts, explicitly mapping complex classification decisions back to physical root causes. Furthermore, zero-shot evaluations against unseen attack tools confirm the system’s generalization, achieving a Macro-F1 of 0.9755 for anomaly detection and a Macro-AUC of 0.8928 for attack identification. Ultimately, this research establishes a transparent, highly resilient, and privacy-centric methodological framework for IoT edge security.

title: Resource-Constrained CAN Intrusion Detection with Distilled Decision Trees
authors: Amirmasoud Pourmiri; Ali Eslami; Sergio Salinas Monroy
venue: International Conference on Computer Communications and Networks
abstract: Controller Area Network (CAN) is the dominant in-vehicle bus, yet its broadcast design and absent authentication leave it exposed to injection and spoofing attacks. Existing deep-learning intrusion detection systems achieve strong accuracy but depend on ML inference frameworks incompatible with the resource budgets of production Electronic Control Units (ECUs). We present a systems-oriented pipeline that trains four neural architectures—Transformer, CNN, LSTM, and ANN—on a five-class labeled CAN dataset and distills each into a framework-free C++ decision tree via the Trustee protocol. We observe and address a systematic false-alarm collapse on Normal-class traffic: standard Trustee produces around 30% FPR-N because Normal frames constitute only 5.4% of training data. A class-balanced Trustee variant, which oversamples Normal by factor α=5, reduces FPR-N to 13.8±1.4% (three Trustee runs) while preserving 91.1±0.6% accuracy and 0.918±0.006 macro-F1 at 2.1% CPU on a Raspberry Pi 4, versus 22.6% for TF-Lite int8 and 59.4% for TensorFlow on the same board. We additionally report α and depth ablations, three-seed teacher statistics, and per-class recall for all models.Code: https://github.com/Amirmasoud-Pourmiri/Lightweight-Neural-Network-Distillation-for-Real-Time-CAN-Bus-Intrusion-Detection-in-Vehicles

title: Retrieval-Driven Training-Free AI-Generated Video Attribution
authors: Renxi Cheng; Chaolei Han; Jie Gui; Hongsong Wang
abstract: AI-generated videos are becoming increasingly realistic and difficult to distinguish from authentic ones, which facilitates malicious misuse and poses growing threats to cybersecurity and social governance. Attributing AI-generated videos to their specific generative sources is therefore of critical importance for forensic investigation and legal regulation. However, most existing visual attribution methods focus on images and particularly rely on the image generation model, thereby lacking the ability to generalize to large-scale AI-generated video data. To address these limitations, we introduce an training-free AI-generated video attribution paradigm. Specifically, we formulates AI-generated video attribution as an instance retrieval task, and design a generative fingerprint-based pipeline. This pipeline consists of an adapted orthogonal color transformation, multi-scale quantized residual generation, and temporal-semantic aggregation, progressively capturing and integrating artifacts introduced by generative models across video frames. Extensive experiments on the GenVidBench benchmark demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance in both AI-generated video detection and attribution, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods with a Rank-1 accuracy of 20.5% and a mean Average Precision of 16.6%. The code is at https://github.com/renxi-seu/Video_Attribution.

title: Review of Machine Learning Methods for Preventing False-Positive SQL Injection Detections
authors: Anuar Askarov; Samat B. Mukhanov
abstract: SQL injection remains a persistent web-application threat, yet practical detection systems often suffer from false positives that disrupt legitimate traffic and cause analyst fatigue. This review surveys machine learning methods for SQL injection detection with a focus on preventing false-positive outcomes in deployment, especially in Web Application Firewall (WAF) contexts. We define the scope across three observation layers—SQL query strings, HTTP request payloads/parameters, and derived network-flow features—and analyze how dataset design, feature engineering, and model selection influence false-positive behavior. We describe commonly used benchmark datasets and highlight limitations that hinder generalization, including synthetic traffic generation, label noise, multi-label ambiguity, and extreme class imbalance in web-attack traces. We compare classical machine learning models, deep learning approaches, hybrid systems, and anomaly-detection pipelines, emphasizing techniques that explicitly target false-positive reduction: threshold and risk-score tuning, probability calibration, cost-sensitive learning, ensemble strategies, adversarial training, and explainability for rule refinement. We summarize evaluation practices, recommending metrics suitable for imbalanced, low-base-rate settings and cost-aware decision-making. Finally, we discuss deployment constraints (latency, throughput, online learning, and concept drift) and articulate open research challenges and concrete recommendations for building reproducible, robust, low-false-positive SQL injection defenses.

title: RGB and Thermal Image based Human Intrusion Detection in Off-Road Scenarios: A New Dataset and Benchmark
authors: Reshu Yadav; Amit Mitra; Rahul Kala
venue: IEEE International Conference on Industrial and Information Systems (ICIIS)
abstract: We introduce a novel RGB and thermal dataset specifically designed for human intrusion detection in challenging off-road environments, captured using multiple synchronised RGB cameras and a thermal camera mounted on autonomous ground vehicles (AGVs). The dataset encompasses diverse terrains, varying lighting conditions, and dynamic human activities such as walking, running, and crawling. To assess its effectiveness, we benchmark several state-of-the-art object detection algorithms on this dataset, evaluating their robustness and limitations in complex, unstructured off-road scenarios. Our results provide critical insights into the capabilities of image-only perception for reliable human detection, particularly under low-light and cluttered backgrounds, which are crucial for safe AGV operation. Experimental results show that DINOv2 gives a very good performance on both RGB and Thermal images, while the performance on RGB images is generally better. The performance of transformer-based models, including Grounding DINO, DETR and RT-DETR, along with YOLOv8, is better compared to more classic deep-learning approaches. The dataset is available at https://github.com/RoitYaadav/DT

title: Robust Context-Aware Detection of Malicious Instructions in Text
authors: 刘步钊; Xinhang Ma; Yevgeniy Vorobeychik
abstract: The remarkable instruction-following ability of modern LLMs has enabled their practical use as the minds of agents that can autonomously complete increasingly complex tasks. Therein, however, also lies their vulnerability to attacks which embed malicious instructions in text, common variants of which are known as indirect prompt injection (IPI). A fundamental task in addressing this vulnerability is successful segmentation of a given text into benign and malicious sentences (if any). While a number of approaches for this task have been proposed, no detector combines query-relative detection at the segment level, and none are hardened against adaptive evasion attacks realizable in agentic executions. We address the former limitation by developing an approach for malicious sentence classification that is both context- and query-aware. Next, to harden the resulting classifier against evasion, we present two adversarial training methods. The first is directly adapted feature-space adversarial training (AT) in which evasions are approximated using projected-gradient-based optimization in the embedding space. The second simulates realizable evasion attacks in the AT loop through LLM-based paraphrasing. Crucially, we parametrize both AT variants to facilitate a smooth tradeoff between utility and attack robustness. In extensive experiments using indirect prompt injection benchmarks we show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art IPI defense baselines under static attacks, while in the case of adaptive attacks, our AT variants provide significantly higher utility, lower attack success rate, and often both. Finally, we show that the best AT parameters can depend intimately on the particular application domain. Consequently, domain-dependent tuning of malicious text detectors is likely necessary in practice. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/tavia-liu/CAD.

title: Robust Single-Trace Full-Key Extraction from Million-Point Traces With Cross-Implementation Transfer
