title: SAFECLICK:ML-Driven Phishing Detection and Analysis
authors: Gaikwad Sneha; Nagaraju Chintha; Potharaju Srihitha; Jillapalli Nikitha
venue: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
abstract: Abstract: Phishing continues to pose a significant threat to cybersecurity. This phenomenon occurs when criminals induce a person to provide their credentials using an illegitimate website. SAFECLICK: ML-Based Phishing Detection and Analysis is a research that intends to detect and prevent phishing attacks using machine learning techniques for analysis of website attributes. The technique involves harvesting data from reputable websites such as PhishTank and Tranco, and categorizing websites as legitimate or phishing. The harvested dataset is used to develop a set of features that include domain validation, SSL certificate verification, and identification of harmful content. The generated features are inputted into three supervised algorithms—Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree, and Random Forest—to determine whether the website is safe or malicious. The Random Forest model performed the best in terms of precision and recall metrics. The project develops an interactive web application that enables one to verify the legitimacy of a website using Streamlit. This technology enables individuals to understand the threats in the internet while providing a flexible and intelligent method for phishing detection. Index Terms—Phishing Detection, Machine Learning, Cybersecurity, Random Forest, Data Mining, URL Analysis, Website Classification.

title: SAFER-AiD: Saccade-Assisted Foveal-peripheral vision Enhanced Reconstruction for Adversarial Defense
authors: Jiayang Liu; Daniel Y. Ts’o; Yiming Bu; Qinru Qiu
venue: IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
abstract: Adversarial attacks significantly challenge the safe deployment of deep learning models, particularly in real-world applications. Traditional defenses often rely on computationally intensive optimization (e.g., adversarial training or data augmentation) to improve robustness, whereas the human visual system achieves inherent robustness to adversarial perturbations through evolved biological mechanisms. We hypothesize that attention guided non-homogeneous sparse sampling and predictive coding plays a key role in this robustness. To test this hypothesis, we propose a novel defense framework incorporating three key biological mechanisms: foveal-peripheral processing, saccadic eye movements, and cortical filling-in. Our approach employs reinforcement learning-guided saccades to selectively capture multiple foveal-peripheral glimpses, which are integrated into a reconstructed image before classification. This biologically inspired preprocessing effectively mitigates adversarial noise, preserves semantic integrity, and notably requires no retraining or fine-tuning of downstream classifiers, enabling seamless integration with existing systems. Experiments on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that our method improves system robustness across diverse classifiers and attack types, while significantly reducing training overhead compared to both biologically and non-biologically inspired defense techniques. Code available at https://github.com/jliu206/SAFER-AiD.

title: SambaGraph: Action-Reaction Spatio-Temporal Graphs for Soccer Tactical Response Modeling
authors: Abel A. Reyes-Angulo; Henry O. Velesaca; Steven Araujo
abstract: Soccer tactics are interactive: an attacking action changes the opponent's defensive problem, and the observed response depends on the multi-agent match state. We introduce SambaGraph, an action--reaction spatio-temporal graph dataset and benchmark for soccer tactical response modeling. From tracking and event data for all 64 matches of the 2022 FIFA World Cup, we curate 4,070 action-centered episodes represented as temporally aligned 23-node player--ball graph sequences with attack/defense views, response labels, and 26,270 split-safe attack--defense pairs. We study three questions: whether observed responses can be classified from graph episodes, whether successful defenses can be retrieved for a query attack, and whether graph-derived summaries support grounded LLM reasoning. A compact signature MLP obtains $0.796\pm0.007$ macro-F1 for response classification, while a fused graph--signature dual encoder reaches $0.471\pm0.029$ Hit@5 and $0.655\pm0.051$ Hit@10 for full-bank defensive retrieval. Hard negatives maximize pair discrimination but not retrieval quality. Local LLMs underperform supervised encoders for direct classification and do not improve over a strong original order in eight-candidate reranking, but they provide grounded tactical rationales. These results position SambaGraph as a reproducible benchmark for graph-based soccer strategy-response research. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/areyesan/SambaGraph.

title: SAMURAI: Runtime Attack Detection in AI Accelerators Using AI Performance Counters
authors: Habibur Rahaman; Atri Chatterjee; S. Bhunia
venue: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Artificial Intelligence
abstract:
AI accelerators, which improve performance for diverse AI tasks are becoming increasingly vulnerable to different adversarial attacks. These attacks, particularly Evasion attacks, introduce small, imperceptible perturbations to input data, leading to incorrect model predictions. Detecting such attacks is challenging because of their subtle nature. To address this, we propose SAMURAI, a framework designed for run-time attack detection in AI accelerators. SAMURAI features an array of AI Performance Counters (APCs) to monitor the dynamic behavior of AI models, in the same way as Hardware Performance Counters (HPCs) count hardware-related activities in modern microprocessors. It also integrates a lightweight on-chip Machine Learning (ML) engine, called TANTO (Trained Anomaly Inspection through Trace Observation). The APCs track low-level hardware events during AI processing, while TANTO concurrently analyzes these data to detect security threats and ensure secure AI usage. This approach enables run-time identification of potential threats without relying on traditional software-based methods. The study applies various adversarial attacks to both image and audio signals to assess the robustness of AI models. For audio data, both raw audio data and their 2D Mel-spectrogram representations are examined. Experimental results on image and audio datasets demonstrate that the proposed system excels in both accuracy and resilience against adversarial attacks. SAMURAI achieves a detection accuracy of 98% with minimal overhead, consumes less than 3% of the total energy, incurs less than 4% area overhead, and has a latency of 10% over the original inference time. The source code for SAMURAI is publicly available on GitHub.1

https://github.com/habiburiit/SAMURAI_Defense

title: SAND: A Self-supervised and Adaptive NAS-Driven Framework for Hardware Trojan Detection
authors: Zhixin Pan; Ziyu Shu; Linh V. Nguyen; Amberbir Alemayoh
venue: Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference (ASP-DAC)
abstract: The globalized semiconductor supply chain has made Hardware Trojans (HT) a significant security threat to embedded systems, necessitating the design of efficient and adaptable detection mechanisms. Despite promising machine learning-based HT detection techniques in the literature, they suffer from ad hoc feature selection and the lack of adaptivity, all of which hinder their effectiveness across diverse HT attacks. In this paper, we propose SAND, a self-supervised and adaptive NAS-driven framework for efficient HT detection. Specifically, this paper makes three key contributions. (1) We leverage self-supervised learning (SSL) to enable automated feature extraction, eliminating the dependency on manually engineered features. (2) SAND integrates neural architecture search (NAS) to dynamically optimize the downstream classifier, allowing for seamless adaptation to unseen benchmarks with minimal fine-tuning. (3) Experimental results show that SAND achieves a significant improvement in detection accuracy (up to 18.3%) over state-of-the-art methods, exhibits high resilience against evasive Trojans, and demonstrates strong generalization.

title: SAR-PMAE: Phase-Modulation-Guided Adversarial Example Generation for SAR Images
authors: Jiahao Cui; Wang Guo; Qi Wang; Keyi Zhang; Lingquan Meng; Haifeng Li
abstract: The presence of adversarial examples can cause SAR image classification systems to produce incorrect predictions, severely compromising their accuracy and robustness. However, existing adversarial example generation methods for SAR images often suffer from limited physical interpretability, low perturbation energy utilization, and insufficient perturbation stealthiness. To address the above issues, this paper proposes SAR-PMAE, a phase modulation-guided adversarial example generation method for SAR images. Specifically, to tackle the lack of physical interpretability, a phase modulation strategy based on the point target scattering model is employed, coupling adversarial perturbations with the EM scattering mechanism to enhance their physical interpretability; to improve perturbation energy utilization, a local focusing strategy is adopted, in which foreground targets are precisely segmented and centered via a watershed algorithm combined with morphological operations, concentrating perturbations in strong response regions and avoiding redundant energy dispersion into background clutter; and to enhance perturbation stealthiness, constraints are applied separately to the phase in the complex coherent domain, thereby maximally preserving SAR speckle statistics and improving perturbation concealment. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves an average untargeted attack success rate of 55.53% and a targeted attack success rate of 20.92% across ten classifiers based on CNN and Transformer architectures, while exhibiting strong attack transferability. The complete implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/muzhengcui/SAR-PMAE.

title: SDN-based DDoS Attack Detection and Mitigation in IoT Networks
authors: Xodjayeva Mavluda Sabirovna; Sevinch Jovlieva; Bayjanov Furkat Bakhramovich; Kalandarova Dono Usmandjanovna; Askarov Abdurashid Murodjonovich
venue: 2026 International Conference on Intelligent and Sustainable AI Systems (ICOSAAS)
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has fundamentally transformed global network infrastructure while simultaneously creating an expanding attack surface for advanced Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) threats. IoT endpoints are inherently resource-constrained, making them vulnerable to exploitation as botnet nodes for large-scale DDoS campaigns. Conventional security mechanisms including statically configured firewalls and signature-based intrusion detection systems are insufficiently scalable and adaptive for heterogeneous IoT environments. This paper proposes a lightweight, hybrid Software-Defined Networking (SDN)-based framework for real-time DDoS detection and automated mitigation. The proposed system integrates Shannon entropy-based traffic anomaly detection at the data plane with a Random Forest (RF) classifier deployed at the Ryu SDN controller. Training and evaluation are performed on the CICDDoS2019 benchmark dataset, and end-to-end validation is conducted using Mininet network simulation. Experimental results demonstrate an average detection accuracy of 98.2%, a mean false positive rate (FPR) of 1.6%, a mean F1-score of 98.2%, and a mean mitigation time of 43 ms across four DDoS attack categories: UDP Flood, TCP SYN Flood, ICMP Flood, and HTTP Flood. The proposed approach achieves a favorable accuracy-overhead balance and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in multiple evaluation dimensions.

title: SDN_IDPS: A Realistic Software-Defined Networking Intrusion Detection Dataset with SDN-Specific Attack Modeling
authors: maryam yasmin ahman
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Documentation Update This version provides an updated README, titled README (Updated), for the SDN-IDPS dataset. This document supersedes the README provided in the previous release and should be used as the authoritative reference for dataset documentation. The revisions correct and clarify the dataset column and feature counts, metadata fields, testbed host configuration, software versions, attack descriptions and ARP/MITM flow labelling procedure. The underlying CSV datasets, record counts, class labels and experimental results remain unchanged. These revisions concern the accompanying documentation only. Dataset Overview This dataset presents a comprehensive Software Defined Networking Intrusion Detection Dataset (SDN-IDPS) designed to support research in SDN security and intelligent intrusion detection systems. The dataset consists of two complementary components: Full Network Dataset – A large scale flow-based dataset derived from network traffic captured using Wireshark (PCAP format) and processed using CICFlowMeter. It contains 4,501,408 flow records and 84 columns, comprising 79 model input features, four excluded identifier/metadata fields and one target label. The dataset includes eight traffic classes covering conventional network attacks, SDN-related attacks and normal traffic. ARP and MITM Dataset – A specialised dataset derived from ARP spoofing and Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack scenarios. Packet level information was extracted using TShark and transformed into bidirectional flow records through custom feature engineering. The dataset contains 108 records and 29 columns, comprising 25 numerical model input features, three metadata fields and one target label. It includes 101 Normal records and 7 SDN_Specific records and was evaluated separately from the full network dataset. Attack Categories The full network dataset contains the following eight traffic classes: Normal DOS DDOS Reconnaissance Web_Attack R2L Malware SDN_Specific The attack scenarios include network and application layer flooding, reconnaissance, credential access attempts, web application attacks, controlled malware simulations and SDN-related attacks involving topology manipulation, flow rule abuse, Packet-In flooding and controller/API interfaces. SDN Emulation Environment The dataset was generated in a controlled GNS3-based SDN emulation environment comprising an OpenDaylight 0.7.1 controller running on Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS, five Open vSwitch 2.17.11 instances, 69 Debian/Lubuntu hosts generating benign traffic, and one separate Kali Linux attack host. Designated web application and FTP services were used to generate normal traffic and conduct controlled attack scenarios. Dataset Availability and Usage The published CSV files contain extracted flow level records without model development scaling or synthetic resampling. This allows researchers to implement their own preprocessing, feature engineering, class-balancing and machine learning pipelines. The dataset is particularly suitable for evaluating conventional and SDN-related intrusion detection, class imbalance handling, hybrid detection frameworks and minority attack class performance. Researchers are encouraged to consult the accompanying corrected README for detailed information on dataset composition, class distributions, testbed configuration, attack generation, feature definitions and recommended preprocessing procedures. title: SECDL-SEGNET: A secure Deep Learning segmentation network for intrusion detection in encrypted cyber traffic
authors: Anupama Sharma; Ruchi Gupta; Shivani Agarwal; Mili Srivastava; Aaditya Jain; José Alberto Sánchez López et al.
venue: Journal of Integrated Science and Technology
abstract: Intrusion detection on encrypted network traffic has already proven to be more difficult with the popularity of encryption protocols like TLS and HTTPS that limit the inspection of packet payloads. Although encryption grants privacy and security of data, it equally facilitates criminal activities to be hidden in the normal flow of communication. The current intrusion detectors have a high dependency on a payload-based analysis or coarse-grained statistics and therefore cannot be utilized effectively in encrypted settings. In order to overcome these weaknesses, the present paper suggests a privacy-sensitive deep learning segmentation architecture, called SecDL-SegNet, to conduct intrusion detection in encrypted traffic. The given model uses flow-level statistical properties, metadata associated with packets, and temporal patterns of communication, without the need to decipher the payloads. An architecture that is based on segmentation is presented to divide the traffic into temporal windows so that a fine-grained analysis and localization of anomalies can be performed. The framework combines convolutional encoding, temporal modeling and computing segment-level anomaly score to improve the detection accuracy and interpretability. The proposed approach is proven to be effective as extensive experiments on the encrypted traffic benchmark datasets have been done. SecDL-SegNet has an average accuracy of 97.17, precision of 96.34, recall of 96.68 and F1-score of 96.59, which is stronger than the traditional machine learning and baseline deep learning predictors. Also, the model has low false positive of 2.18% and can be run in close real-time, with an average inference time of 5.32 ms per flow. The findings indicate that SecDL-SegNet developed a scalable, powerful, and protection conscious network intrusion detection system that works in the next generation encrypted networks.

title: Secure Data Transmission Protocols for Telehealth: Improving Encryption, Authentication, and System Resilience
authors: Dr Priti Prasad Kapadni
venue: Digital health & telemonitoring advances E: 3117-6461 | P: 3117-647X
abstract: The rapid expansion of telehealth systems has revolutionized healthcare delivery by enabling remote diagnosis, monitoring, and consultation. However, this transformation has introduced significant cybersecurity challenges, particularly in the secure transmission of sensitive patient data. Ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and availability of medical information is critical, as breaches can lead to severe privacy violations and compromised patient safety. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of secure data transmission protocols in telehealth systems, with a focus on improving encryption mechanisms, authentication strategies, and system resilience. The study explores existing cryptographic frameworks, including symmetric and asymmetric encryption techniques, Transport Layer Security (TLS), and emerging lightweight cryptographic solutions tailored for resource-constrained devices. Additionally, it examines advanced authentication methods such as multi-factor authentication (MFA), biometric verification, and blockchain-based identity management systems. The paper further evaluates resilience strategies, including intrusion detection systems, fault tolerance, and secure network architectures, to mitigate cyber threats. Through a machine learning-informed perspective, the paper highlights opportunities for adaptive security mechanisms capable of detecting anomalies and dynamically responding to threats. The findings indicate that a layered security approach integrating encryption, authentication, and resilience mechanisms significantly enhances telehealth system security. Finally, the paper outlines future research directions aimed at developing scalable, interoperable, and privacy-preserving telehealth infrastructures.

title: Secure Hybrid Cryptographic and Machine Learning–Driven Framework for Automated E-Invoicing Integration in Cloud-Based ERP Systems
authors: Ritu Nagpal Udita Malhotra
venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
abstract: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) integration with government compliance systems has become a pressing need as enterprise finance rapidly turns into a digital landscape with digital taxation infrastructures. The concept of e-invoicing through the invoice Registration Portal (IRP) in India is based on the Goods and Services Tax (GST) implementation, which will involve organizations in the process of submitting invoice details for validation and generating the Invoice Reference Number (IRN). Current e-invoicing deployments are mainly based on half-automated synchronization approaches or traditional API-based communication systems that lack inherent security, synchronization issues, auditability, authorization mechanisms and heavy operational burden. In this research, a novel implementation-oriented secure e-invoicing framework for cloud-based ERP system with the implementation platform Microsoft Dynamics 365 F&O is proposed. The proposed architecture features a consistent secure outbound and inbound synchronization algorithm, which includes AES-256 payload encryption, RSA key wrapping, PBKDF2 key derivation, TLS 1.2 transport security, badge-based authentication, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), replay attack prevention, secure API orchestration, automated generation of QR-codes and audit-driven synchronization management. To boost system intelligence and adaptive security, a Machine Learning based Anomaly Detection Layer is integrated to review invoice activity from transactions, API request patterns and synchronization logs. This layer calculates dynamic risk scores to detect anomalies in normal operating behaviour, and provides proactive security enforcement in the ERP environment. This is achieved through X++ customization, REST-based API orchestration, cryptographic processing modules and native batch execution services within the ERP. Inside the ERP environment, the proposed algorithm automatically retrieves and validates invoices, issues intelligent risk ratings, encrypts them, securely transmits them, compares the content of the responses, synchronizes the acknowledgment, attaches a QR code, and logs audits. Experimental analysis shows that the proposed framework can significantly enhance the reliability of synchronization, security robustness, intelligence-driven threat detection, transparency, data integrity, scalability and operational efficiency over the traditional and existing cloud-based approach. The study presents a novel, implementation-oriented intelligent algorithmic framework for secure communication between ERP and Government portal and lays the foundation for scalable future adaptive digital taxonomies.

title: Secure Phishing Analysis and Robust Training Algorithm (SPARTA) for Phishing Website Detection
authors: Diksha Damahe; Ajay Kumar Phulre
venue: IEEE International Students' Conference on Electrical, Electronics and Computer Science (SCEECS)
abstract: The common defenses nowadays such as blocklists and hard-to-learn heuristics no longer seem to be resistant enough to keep users safe on phishing websites as the attacks grow increasingly advanced. We present SPARTA (Secure Phishing Analysis and Robust Training Algorithm) in this paper as a strong security framework where machine learning is utilized to characterize the threats and break in their paths before striking. Our hybrid feature extraction map explores far within the URL layout of a website, the HTML/JavaScript implemented within it, and the state of its own SSL/TLS certificate to establish a comprehensive computerized print. It is this rich feature set against which we then apply an ensemble of classifiers such as Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest (RF), and a Neural Network which we combine together via hardschema vote scheme in order to make a highly reliable and true-to-the-point verdict. Comparing it to benchmark datasets available on PhishTank and the UCI Machine Learning Repository, SPARTA has achievable detection rates of 99.15%. SPARTA registers as an impressive game-changer in the practical application of browsers, email gateways, and other security tools, capable of keeping pace with the constantly evolving techniques used by cybercriminals.

title: SecureSeqGuard: Transformer with Adaptive Noise Filtering for Encrypted Network Intrusion Determination
authors: D. P
venue: International Conference Trends Material Science and Inventive Materials
abstract: SecureSeqGuard is a transformer-based intrusion detection framework designed to analyze encrypted network traffic through adaptive noise filtering and sequence-level feature extraction. This method addresses the challenge of detecting malicious behavior without decrypting data, preserving privacy while improving detection fidelity. The model integrates an adaptive noise filtering module that suppresses irrelevant encrypted-traffic fluctuations, followed by a multi-head self-attention encoder that learns temporal and contextual patterns indicative of attacks. Experiments conducted on two encrypted traffic datasets demonstrate that SecureSeqGuard substantially improves detection performance. The system achieves a detection accuracy of 97.4 percent, outperforming baseline deep learning models by up to 5.8 percent, and reduces false positives to 1.9 percent, representing a 42 percent improvement in precision over conventional transformer architectures. These results highlight the potential of SecureSeqGuard as an efficient and privacy-preserving solution for modern encrypted intrusion detection.

title: Securing Enterprise APIs in Zero-Trust Architectures: Practical Implementations with Apigee and Cloud IAM
authors: Viplove Goswami
venue: International Journal on Science and Technology
abstract: The enterprise security landscape has undergone a tectonic shift as organizations transition from monolithic, perimeter-based defenses toward decentralized, cloud-native architectures. This transformation has placed Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) at the center of the modern digital ecosystem, serving as the primary conduits for data exchange and business logic. However, the exposure of these interfaces has concurrently expanded the attack surface, necessitating a security model that does not rely on network location as a proxy for trust. Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA), as formalized in NIST Special Publication 800-207, provides a framework for this new reality by mandating continuous verification, least privilege access, and comprehensive monitoring. This paper explores the practical implementation of Zero-Trust principles for securing enterprise APIs using Google Cloud’s Apigee and Identity and Access Management (IAM). By analyzing the technical mechanisms of OAuth 2.0, Mutual TLS, Workload Identity Federation, and Machine Learning-based anomaly detection, this research details how organizations can build a resilient, identity-centric security posture. The analysis emphasizes the integration of the API management layer as a robust Policy Enforcement Point that operates in concert with cloud-native identity services to eliminate implicit trust and mitigate the risks of lateral movement and data exfiltration.

title: Securing Industrial Control Systems and SCADA Networks: Protocol Weaknesses, Standards, Emerging Defenses, and Future Research Directions

title: Securing intelligent transportation systems in the internet of vehicles through an AI-driven intrusion detection framework
authors: Sajjad Salim Obaid Alshammari; Mina Malekzadeh
abstract: Abstract The integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) with modern vehicles has transformed transportation systems into intelligent, interconnected Internet of Vehicles (IoV) networks. However, this integration increases the attack surface, exposing IoV networks to threats that compromise operational reliability and passenger safety. This work introduces a configurable simulation platform for designing and evaluating IoV networks across diverse topologies and network parameters under normal and adversarial conditions. The platform supports multiple Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks across the communication stack, including application-layer Slowloris and HTTP, transport-layer SYN and UDP, and reflection-based DNS and NTP amplification. It incorporates a dataset-generation module that captures IoV behavior under benign and adversarial conditions to support training and evaluation of security models. Using these datasets, an AI-based detection framework is developed using machine learning, deep learning, and transformer models. A multi-layer evaluation combining communication and AI classification metrics demonstrates the platform’s capability to model complex IoV behavior and support security methods. It further measures deployment trade-offs involving inference latency and communication-energy cost, which reflect the practical constraints of resource‑limited devices. Experimental results show that amplification attacks are the most destructive, while cellular topology demonstrates the highest resilience, with 56.5% loss, whereas VANET and Manhattan show 87.5% loss. Under edge constraints, transformer models achieve 92–93% recovery but incur 136–181 ms inference latency, deep learning achieves 89–91% recovery with 17–45 ms latency, and machine learning provides 72–87% recovery with the lowest latency of 12–27 ms, highlighting the trade-off between detection capability and computational overhead.

title: Securing Load Balancers Against AI and Protocol Threats
authors: Shadi Radwan Albasla
venue: Stardom doğa ve mühendislik çalışmaları dergisi.
abstract: To distribute traffic across microservices and backend systems, modern cloud-native infrastructures primarily rely on load balancers and ingress controllers. Although the main purpose of these components is to increase availability and scalability, they are becoming increasingly important control points in network architecture, making them appealing targets for cyberattacks. Load balancers are frequently viewed as performance-oriented networking components rather than active security enforcement mechanisms, despite their strategic position. To support advanced cybersecurity capabilities, this thesis explores ways to improve load-balancing architecture. The study assesses the efficacy of AI-assisted Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) in identifying real-time threats, investigates the integration of machine learning techniques for proactive vulnerability discovery, and examines protocol-level security issues arising from contemporary transport protocols such as HTTP/3 and QUIC. The study also examines how load-balancing architectures can apply Zero Trust security principles to limit lateral movement in microservice environments and reduce implicit trust. The thesis proposes several defensive improvements for contemporary load balancing systems, drawing on experimental evaluation, architectural design, and security analysis. These include identity-based traffic routing aligned with Zero Trust principles, protocol-aware mitigation techniques for QUIC-specific attacks, and machine-learning-based anomaly detection using load balancer telemetry. The results show that load balancers can be made much more effective as security enforcement points in distributed cloud environments by incorporating AI-driven detection mechanisms and protocol-aware defenses.

title: SECURING PROOF OF GENERATION IN AI WATERMARKING: A KEY-FITTING ATTACK AND CRYPTOGRAPHIC COMMITMENT DEFENSE
authors: Bhoomika Sundar; D Rakshitha; Chitkala Patil; Chitra B. T
abstract: AI watermarking schemes are widely proposed as a mechanism for detecting and attributing AI-generated content (AIGC).Regulatory frameworks including the EU AI Act (Article 50) and California SB 942 increasingly rely on such schemes as enforceable transparency standards.However, a critical security gap undermines their evidentiary value: because watermark keys are private and unfixed prior to deployment, a malicious model owner can brute-force a key after observing any piece of human-generated content, causing standard detectors to falsely classify that content as AIGC.We term this a key-fitting attack.In this paper, we formalise the key-fitting threat model, prove its mathematical inevitability under order statistics, and provide the first empirical demonstration across four widely deployed watermarking algorithms: the KGW green- Securing Proof of Generation in AI Watermarking: A Key-Fitting Attack and CryptographicCommitment Defense https://iaeme.com/Home/journal/JIPRIMTL 10 editor@iaeme.comlist scheme, Aaronson Gumbel-max scheme, Tree-Ring Fourier watermarking for diffusion-model images, and DCT spread-spectrum watermarking.For text schemes, our experiments show that the standard AI-detection threshold is reliably breached within approximately 42,000 key trials on a standard CPU, requiring under ten minutes with no GPU and no model access.For image schemes, the Fourier correlation detection threshold is exceeded within approximately 5,600 key trials on a natural photograph, with no modifications to the image.We further demonstrate that this vulnerability is scheme-agnostic: it arises not from a flaw in any individual algorithm but from the structural absence of a proof-of-generation guarantee in all current watermarking frameworks.To close this gap, we propose a Merkle tree commitment protocol anchored by SHA-256 hashing, in which the model owner constructs a Merkle tree over all candidate watermark keys, deposits the Merkle root to a time-stamped, append-only public registry prior to model deployment, and later proves membership of the active key via a logarithmic-length Merkle proof.This two-layer design extends the security of SHA-256 (pre-image resistance, collision resistance, and timestamp binding) with selective-disclosure efficiency: revealing the active key requires disclosing only O(log₂ n) hashes rather than the full key portfolio.We empirically show that Merkle root computation is sub-millisecond for portfolios up to 10,000 keys, and proof verification completes in under 25 μs at any portfolio size tested (up to 2¹⁶ keys).We position this contribution against the closest prior work, including a recent governance paper that mentions key commitment only as an unformalised recommendation, and show that no prior work supplies a formal attack definition, a derived trial-count bound, a cross-scheme demonstration, or a proven commitment protocol with logarithmic-disclosure efficiency.Our protocol requires no changes to existing watermarking algorithms.

title: Security-Aware Self-Supervised Adaptive DCNN for Rice Leaf Disease Detection
authors: R. Dhivya; N. Shanmugapriya
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
abstract: Agriculture plays a critical role in global food security, yet crop production remains highly vulnerable to disease outbreaks that significantly reduce yield and crop quality. Deep learning-based models shows high performance under controlled environment; however, their reliability often deteriorates in real world environments due to variations in illumination, background complexity, and environmental noise, making the model vulnerable to the prediction error and adversarial perturbation. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel Security-Aware Self-Supervised Adaptive Deep Convolutional Neural Network (SA-SSA-DCNN) for robust rice leaf disease detection. The proposed model uses the self-supervised learning to reduce the model’s reliance over the labelled data, attention mechanism to localize the features, and adversarial training to resilient against the environmental perturbation and noise. To evaluate the model’s performance the benchmarked rice leaf dataset was obtained from Kaggle. The proposed SA-SSA-DCNN achieved 99.25% accuracy and F1 score as 0.993, Consistently outperforms the standard SSL model and randomly initialized baseline models across all evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the model demonstrates strong robustness under adversarial and noisy conditions, significantly reducing attack success rate while maintaining high prediction reliability for real-world agricultural deployment.

title: Seeing Through the Noise: Self-Supervised Reconstruction for Adversarially Robust Perception in Autonomous Vehicles
authors: Subhodeep Moitra; Deblina Banerjee; Abhijit Ghosh; Swastika Mitra; Tapan Kumar Chakraborty; Himadri Biswas
abstract: Although the Deep Learning (DL) models have been crucial in the modern-day Artificial Intelligence (AI) appliances, its susceptibility to adversarial attacks remains critical. This is mainly critical in mission-critical systems and applications like autonomous vehicles. Although most of the current defense techniques aim to enhance the classification accuracy under attacks, but they often fail to address the fundamental damage to the visual input itself. In this literature, the authors put forward an adversarial defense architectural framework that improves the robustness by reconstructing the clean images from adversarially perturbed inputs, rather than optimizing the classification operations. This architectural framework utilizes a Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) paradigm to train an autoencoder fitted with the skip connection and multi-head attention mechanisms. This allows the architectural framework to restore perceptually and structurally genuine representations of the actual scenes. Here, the authors assessed the approach utilizing the CCF BDCI Traffic Light Detection dataset under the influences of FGSM and PGD attacks, analyzing the quality of the reconstruction by MSE, PSNR, and SSIM. The results show that this architectural framework can reconstruct the critical visual information from the adversarially attacked images, providing a foundational level of defense that enables the perceptual integrity and is not dependent on classification robustness. This reconstruction-first approach paves the way for new techniques in adversarial robustness by allowing safer perception pipelines in unmanned vehicles.

title: Self-Evolving Autonomous Software Architectures Using Large-Scale Graph Neural Networks and Real-Time Big Data Feedback Loops for Economic Optimization and Cost-Efficient Resource Allocation
authors: Shoaib Hayat; Husnain Ahmed Janjua; Komal Tanveer; Muhammad Essa Siddique
venue: Journal of Business Insight and Innovation
abstract: The rapid growth of cloud-native, microservice-based, and distributed computing environments has exposed the limits of conventional software architectures that rely on static rules, manually configured resource policies, and human-driven adaptation. These limitations often produce resource overprovisioning, higher operational costs, delayed failure recovery, and inefficient use of computational capacity. This study proposes a Self-Evolving Autonomous Software Architecture (SEASA) that combines large-scale Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with real-time big-data feedback loops to enable continuous architectural learning, economic optimization, and cost-efficient resource allocation. The framework represents software ecosystems as dynamic heterogeneous graphs, where services, containers, databases, nodes, and infrastructure resources are modelled as interconnected entities, while dependencies, communication patterns, costs, and data flows are modelled as evolving edges. Runtime data were collected from Microsoft Azure Cloud workload traces, Google Cluster Workload Traces, and a synthetic microservice benchmark containing 500 services and 2.8 million interactions. Graph Convolutional Network, GraphSAGE, Graph Attention Network, and Temporal Graph Neural Network models were evaluated for anomaly detection, workload forecasting, architectural-state prediction, and autonomous adaptation. The TGNN-based framework achieved 97.4% accuracy, 96.8% precision, 96.1% recall, and a 96.4% F1-score, outperforming baseline models. It reduced adaptation latency by 38.7%, resource consumption by 24.5%, cloud operating costs by 21.8%, and overprovisioning by 27.3%. It also improved failure recovery, allocation efficiency, and service-level-objective compliance. These findings show that temporal graph intelligence and real-time economic feedback can transform software architectures into predictive, self-directed, and cost-aware computing ecosystems. title: Self-Supervised Anomaly Detection Using Contrastive Learning for Network Security
authors: A. K. M. Nuruzzaman Laskar; Md. Saifur Rahman; Arbaz Abdul; Nitin Mukhi
venue: 2026 Innovations in Machine, Engineering, and Digital Conference (IMED)
abstract: The growing popularity of encrypted network traffic, which was necessitated by privacy protection and safe communication-related protocols, has significantly limited the effectiveness of the traditional network anomaly detection systems that rely on payload examination and supervised learning. Existing models often require large labeled data, can be computationally expensive, and cannot be generalized to zero-day attacks in dynamically changing network settings. Even though current developments in self-supervised models and deep learning models have shown promise, they do not scale well and have high false-positive rates on complicated and high-throughput networks. To overcome them, a self-supervised contrastive learning-based anomaly detection model that can detect network anomalies only using flow-level mean statistics, eliminating the necessity of labeled data or payload inspection. It uses the UNet++, a more advanced feature analysis mechanism to provide effective modeling of spatial correlations of encrypted traffic attributes. An optimal dimensionality reduction algorithm of Tasmanian optimization (DSTO) is used to reduce redundancy and compute overhead. The DCL method is adopted to learn highly discriminative representations by maximizing the distance between typical and anomalous traffic patterns on a self-supervised fashion. The UNet++-DSTO-DCL was tested on the CIC-Darknet2020, ISCX VPN (non-VPN) and UNSW-NB15 data sets.

title: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning for Zero Day Cyber Threat Detection Using Network Traffic Representations
authors: V. Sharma; Garima Srivastava
venue: 2026 2nd International Conference on Sustainable Computing and Integrated Communication in Changing Landscape of AI (ICSCAI)
abstract: The fast increases in advanced and zero-day computer attacks have revealed the shortcomings of traditional Intrusion Detection System (IDS) that are dependent on manually annotated data and are incapable of extrapolating the diverse network settings. To overcome these issues, the paper introduces a powerful Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) system that employs the contrastive representation learning to perform a successful anomaly detection in cybersecurity. The presented model consists of SimCLR and MoCo encoders and one-class classifiers, including One-Class SVM and Isolation Forest, allowing the extraction of discriminative features of network traffic without labels. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets, such as CICIDS2017 and UNSW-NB15, show that MoCo-based models achieve higher accuracy (98.2%) and a 0.991 AUC on CICIDS2017, and also demonstrate better generalization across datasets. The analysis of curves on ROC and confusion matrices also confirm the accuracy of the learned representations to recognize the minority and zero-day classes of attacks. The importance of contrastive learning and data augmentation for overall system performance is demonstrated through an ablation study. The findings highlight the possibility of using SSL as a strong alternative to the fully supervised IDS, providing a foundation for further extensions based on the graph-based architecture of SSL, the multimodal approach to cybersecurity information fusion, and real-time implementation in large-scale network systems.

title: Self-Supervised One-Class Tabular Deep Learning for Intrusion Detection in Artificial Intelligence of Things Systems
authors: Thavavel Vaiyapuri; Karthiyayini Murugesan; Yassine Bouteraa
venue: Journal of Computational and Cognitive Engineering
abstract: The emergence of the artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) has led to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks. For many of these threats, labeled training data are scarce or unavailable, which increases the need for label-free intrusion detection systems. To address this issue, this study proposes a self-supervised one-class TabNet framework, termed SS-OC-TabNet, for intrusion detection in tabular network traffic. The framework combines self-supervised representation learning and one-class compactness learning within a two-stage training process. In the first stage, masked-feature reconstruction is used to learn the feature structure of normal traffic from unlabeled data. In the second stage, a hypersphere compactness objective is applied to make the latent representations of normal traffic more compact for anomaly detection. TabNet is used as the backbone to support sequential feature selection, which also improves interpretability. The proposed model was evaluated on the NSL-KDD dataset and further validated through comparison with related works on the ToN-IoT dataset, achieving an accuracy of 93.20% with a false alarm rate of 2.13%. Further, the interpretability results show which traffic features influence the model's decisions. The compact design and low computational complexity of the proposed framework also support energy-efficient deployment in resource-constrained AIoT environments. These results indicate that SS-OC-TabNet is a viable tool for label-free intrusion detection in AIoT environments. title: Selfie-Capture Dynamics as an Auxiliary Signal Against Deepfakes and Injection Attacks for Mobile Identity Verification
authors: Erkka Rantahalvari; Olli Sílven; Zinelabidine Boulkenafet; Constantino Álvarez Casado
abstract: Mobile remote identity verification (RIdV) systems are exposed to attacks that manipulate or replace the facial video stream, including presentation attacks, real-time deepfakes, and video injection. Recent European requirements, including ETSI TS 119 461 and CEN/TS 18099, motivate evidence channels beyond camera-based presentation-attack detection. This paper studies whether passive motion traces recorded during selfie capture provide auxiliary evidence for spoof screening and user verification. We introduce CanSelfie, a dataset of 375 bona fide multi-sensor sequences collected at 50 Hz from 30 participants using a commercial mobile RIdV application, together with stationary, handheld, and temporally shifted attack-proxy scenarios. We benchmark 7 multivariate time-series classifiers and 8 whole-series anomaly detectors across sensor configurations and temporal windows. For spoof screening, accelerometer-only ROCKAD obtains 0.00% FRR and 43.8% FAR, while QUANT+3-NN obtains the lowest FAR of 32.0% at 2.37% FRR; both reject all stationary proxies. For same-device and same-session user verification, WEASEL+MUSE reaches 1.07% EER using 9 channels. Raw acceleration is the most informative modality, and closed-set accuracy alone does not imply good verification because threshold calibration depends on score distributions. The findings support selfie-capture motion as a low-friction auxiliary signal, while leaving cross-device, cross-session, and real injection-attack evaluation as necessary next steps. Code and data available at: https://github.com/Ergzar/Selfie-Motion-AD-TSC.

title: Semantic Aggregated Adversarial Training Framework for Hate Speech Detection
authors: Xingwei Zhang; Hu Tian; X B Zheng; Jing Peng; Daniel Dajun Zeng
abstract: Hate speech poses a growing challenge to digital platforms with large and diverse user bases, prompting widespread adoption of deep learning (DL) models for automated detection at scale. Existing research, however, predominantly focuses on improving detection accuracy while paying limited attention to the vulnerability of DL-based detection models to adversarial attacks from malicious spreaders. To bridge this gap, we propose an adversarial training framework to improve the adversarial robustness of hate speech detection. This framework integrates imbalanced adversarial training with a novel semantic aggregation technology to learn robust yet discriminative features from hate speech corpora. We further introduce an adversarial attack generation framework to assess the performance of existing DL-based hate speech detection models under such attacks. Extensive computational experiments conducted on eight publicly available hate speech corpora demonstrate the robustness of the proposed method against attacks. In contrast, we show that existing DL-based detection models can be easily circumvented by adversarial attacks, allowing the dissemination of hateful sentiments through subtle modifications to the content. Additionally, we conduct comparative analyses of the proposed method with various adversarial training and imbalance training methods to illustrate its effectiveness in simultaneously addressing the data imbalance and feature inseparability issues inherent in hate speech detection. This study presents significant managerial implications, aiding online platforms in implementing effective measures to prevent the spread of hateful speech. title: Semi-supervised learning in Security Operations Centers: Performance, trade-offs and practical implications
authors: Felix Waschke; Alejandro Guerra-Manzanares; Risto Vaarandi
abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are under constant pressure to reduce the time required for detecting and responding to cyber threats. To support this objective, machine learning (ML) has become an increasingly valuable tool. This benchmark study explores the potential of semi-supervised learning (SSL) techniques to enhance ML performance in critical SOC tasks, including intrusion detection, malware classification, and alert handling. Five representative SSL methods, namely, self-learning, co-training, active learning, label propagation, and label spreading, are evaluated across seven diverse datasets and compared against supervised baselines. These methods make use of the unlabeled data pool in distinct ways: self-learning, co-training, and graph-based approaches extract learning signals directly from unlabeled instances, whereas active learning leverages the unlabeled pool to identify which samples should be selected for annotation. The analysis also considers key challenges related to the training data, such as limited labeled samples, labeling errors, and class imbalance. Beyond predictive performance, SSL approaches are also compared on the basis of training time and energy consumption. The results demonstrate that active learning can significantly improve detection capabilities while substantially reducing the labeling workload for human analysts, making them a promising direction for SOC automation and efficiency.

title: Sentinel Sphere: AI-Driven DoS Detection and Mitigation in Cloud
authors: Aathila M; Aamila M; Haseena K
abstract: Cloud computing has become an essential platform for hosting modern applications and services, making cloud infrastructures increasingly vulnerable to Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks that disrupt service availability by overwhelming server resources. Conventional intrusion detection systems primarily rely on rule-based techniques or machine learning models trained on static datasets, limiting their ability to detect evolving attack patterns and respond in real time. This paper presents Sentinel Sphere, an AI-driven framework for real-time DoS detection and automated mitigation in cloud environments. The proposed system continuously monitors NGINX access logs, extracts key traffic features such as Requests Per Second (RPS), IP concentration, endpoint access frequency, and HTTP error rates, and analyzes them using the Mistral 7B Large Language Model deployed locally through the Ollama runtime. Based on contextual reasoning, the framework identifies abnormal traffic behavior and automatically applies mitigation strategies, including request rate limiting and connection control within the NGINX server. The framework was evaluated using ApacheBench-generated attack traffic and benchmark datasets, including CICIDS2017 and NSL-KDD. Experimental results achieved 98.2% detection accuracy, 97.4% precision, 96.8% recall, and a 97.1% F1-score, with an average mitigation response latency of less than 1.2 seconds. The findings demonstrate that integrating Large Language Models with real-time infrastructure monitoring enables adaptive, autonomous, and scalable cybersecurity protection for cloud-hosted web services against evolving DoS attacks.

title: SentinelML: Behavioral Machine-Learning-Based Ransomware Detection with Decoupled AI Security Analysis
authors: Vasu Chowdary; Moulica Chowdary; D. M. Yashaswini; Rajashree M. Byalal
abstract: Ransomware remains a critical threat to modern enterprise and personal computing infrastructure.Traditional signature-based detection mechanisms exhibit operational degradation when confronted with previously unobserved polymorphic or zero-day variants.This paper presents SentinelML, an autonomous endpoint detection architecture that identifies ransomware activity through 19 dynamic behavioral indicators collected entirely in user space without requiring kernel-level filter drivers.By sampling filesystem Shannon entropy, process concurrency anomalies, shadow copy deletion commands, and cryptographic module bindings, SentinelML trains a local Random Forest classifier that operates as an unprivileged host daemon.To address operational triage transparency, the local classifier is coupled with an architecturally decoupled Large Language Model (LLM) advisory explainer operating via an isolated HTTPS interface.We conduct an exhaustive technical audit of the production system: confirming that Shannon entropy accounts for 41.31% of aggregate Gini importance, documenting the operational tradeoffs of heuristic user-space proxies, analyzing platform asymmetry between Windows and Linux deployments, and evaluating the system strictly as an Intrusion Detection System (IDS).Finally, we disclose that previously reported internal metrics (0.9567 accuracy across candidate algorithms) could not be independently reproduced due to unpreserved training artifacts, and establish an open empirical evaluation protocol for reproducible validation.

title: SentinelSphere: Integrating AI-Powered Real-Time Threat Detection with Cybersecurity Awareness Training
authors: Nikolaos D. Tantaroudas; Ilias Karachalios; Andrew J. McCracken
abstract: The field of cybersecurity is confronted with two interrelated challenges: a worldwide deficit of qualified practitioners and ongoing human-factor weaknesses that account for the bulk of security incidents. To tackle these issues, we present SentinelSphere, a platform driven by artificial intelligence that unifies machine learning-based threat identification with security training powered by a Large Language Model (LLM). The detection module uses an Enhanced Deep Neural Network (DNN) trained on the CIC-IDS2017 and CIC-DDoS2019 benchmark datasets, enriched with novel HTTP-layer feature engineering that captures application level attack signatures. For the educational component, we deploy a quantised variant of Phi-4 model (Q4_K_M), fine-tuned for the cybersecurity domain, enabling deployment on commodity hardware requiring only 16 GB of RAM without dedicated GPU resources. Experimental results show that the Enhanced DNN attains high detection accuracy while substantially lowering false positives relative to baseline models, and maintains strong recall across critical attack categories such as DDoS, brute force, and web-based exploits. Validation workshops involving industry professionals and university students confirmed that the Traffic Light visualisation system and conversational AI assistant are both intuitive and effective for users without technical backgrounds. SentinelSphere illustrates that coupling intelligent threat detection with adaptive, LLM-driven security education can meaningfully address both technical and human-factor cybersecurity vulnerabilities within a single, cohesive framework.

title: SessionSense: Detecting Web Attacks Through Session-Level Behavioral Feature Engineering
authors: M. Cujbă; Costin-Gabriel Chiru; Ion Bica; Alexandra-Victoria Ciuvăţ
abstract: Web-based vulnerabilities represent a substantial portion of the security exposures in modern computing infrastructure. Conventional intrusion detection approaches analyze HTTP requests in isolation, an approach that fails to capture coordinated multi-step attacks distributed across multiple requests. This paper presents a machine learning framework that addresses this limitation through session-level behavioral feature engineering. The proposed approach reconstructs user sessions from HTTP traffic using actual session cookies (JSESSIONID), yielding 97,065 sessions from 194,130 requests in the CSIC 2010 dataset. A total of 30 features are extracted across behavioral, structural, and payload categories. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that session-level features yield statistically significant improvements over request-level baselines (F1: 0.875 vs $0.864, p\lt 0.001$), with gradient boosting achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.933. Ablation analysis reveals that payload features provide the strongest discriminative signal, while structural features capturing navigation patterns offer complementary value for attack detection.

title: ShadowNet: A Multi-Protocol IoT Honeypot for Attack Detection and Behavior Analysis
authors: Mahesh S. Shinde; Vijendra Sarode; Harsh Sarulkar; Sahaz Saxena; Ujjwal Saindanvise; Sanika Luktuke
venue: 2026 4th International Conference on Sustainable Computing and Smart Systems (ICSCSS)
abstract: The rapid growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in smart homes, industries, and urban infrastructure has increased the global cyber-attack surface. Many IoT devices use lightweight communication protocols and often lack strong authentication, making them easy targets for automated cyberattacks. This paper introduces ShadowNet, a virtual IoT honeypot framework designed to capture and study malicious interactions in IoT environments. The system simulates various IoT communication services, including HTTP, SSH, and MQTT, letting attackers interact with it as if it were a real vulnerable IoT device. The framework records attacker behavior, such as login attempts, command execution, payload injections, and request metadata. To improve attack identification, the system uses a Random Forest-based machine learning model to classify network traffic as normal or malicious based on activity patterns. A web-based monitoring dashboard also visualizes attack statistics and intrusion activity by protocol. In experimental deployments, the framework captured multiple attack patterns, including SSH brute-force attempts, HTTP credential stuffing, and malicious MQTT payload injections. This shows the effectiveness of honeypot-based monitoring paired with machine learning techniques, achieving high accuracy in detecting malicious IoT traffic. The proposed system offers a scalable and cost-effective solution for real-time IoT security monitoring.

title: Shield of the Levant: Israel's Multi-Layered Missile Defense
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: When a ballistic missile launches from Iran, a complex dance of satellites, advanced radars, and high-speed interceptors begins within seconds. This episode deconstructs Israel's multi-layered defense architecture, moving from the exo-atmospheric kinetic kills of the Arrow 3 to the dual-mode precision of David's Sling. We examine the compressed OODA loop of modern warfare, the critical role of human-in-the-loop decision-making during high-pressure saturation attacks, and the growing challenge of maneuverable reentry vehicles. Beyond the physics of "hitting a bullet with a bullet," we also explore the stark economic asymmetry of defending against low-cost threats with multi-million dollar interceptors. This is a deep dive into how sensor fusion, machine learning, and rapid-response engineering are reshaping the sky over the Levant in what has become a real-time laboratory for kinetic defense and strategic survival. Show Notes Modern missile defense is a game of hyper-speed chess where the pieces move at five times the speed of sound. In the Levant, this theoretical engineering challenge has become a daily reality. The process of intercepting a ballistic missile is a multi-stage race against time, shrinking the traditional decision-making cycle—observe, orient, decide, and act—from minutes into mere seconds. ### Early Detection and Sensor Fusion The defense process begins nearly a thousand miles away from the target. Space-based infrared sensors detect the massive thermal bloom of a missile ignition almost instantly. While these satellites provide the initial alert, ground-based radar systems like the Green Pine array take over to provide precision. These active electronically scanned radars do more than just track a dot on a screen; they calculate velocity, ascent angles, and projected ballistic arcs to determine exactly where a threat will land. This data flows into a Battle Management Center, where sensor fusion occurs. Algorithms determine the "predicted impact point." If a missile is headed for the sea or an unpopulated desert, the system may stand down to conserve resources. If a city is threatened, a "kill box" is established, and the multi-layered interceptor system is activated. ### The Architecture of the Shield Israel's defense is built on a series of specialized filters. At the highest tier is the Arrow 3, an exo-atmospheric interceptor. Operating in the vacuum of space, it uses a kinetic kill vehicle—essentially a high-speed "truck" that slams into the incoming warhead. By neutralizing the threat in space, any non-conventional payloads are destroyed far above the population. If a threat slips past or operates at a lower altitude, the Arrow 2 and David's Sling systems engage. The Arrow 2 uses a proximity fuse and blast-fragmentation to destroy warheads within the atmosphere. David's Sling, often called the "middle child" of the defense family, utilizes the Stunner missile. With its distinct dolphin-shaped nose housing both infrared and radar seekers, it is specifically designed to counter maneuverable cruise missiles and medium-range rockets that are difficult to spoof. ### The Human Element and Economic Asymmetry Despite the high level of automation, the system remains "human-on-the-loop." Officers must authorize launches and manage battery logistics in real-time. This human intervention is vital during complex "saturation attacks," where an adversary launches a high volume of missiles, drones, and decoys simultaneously to overwhelm the sensors. The ultimate challenge, however, may not be physics, but economics. There is a massive cost disparity between a low-cost ballistic missile and a multi-million dollar interceptor. As attackers move toward cluster munitions and synchronized barrages, the defense must rely on AI-assisted prioritization to ensure that the most lethal threats are neutralized first. The battle for the skies has become a battle of the ledgers, where the goal is to maintain a perfect defensive record without depleting the national treasury.
